uw PS «en tae 2 LADY ANNE'S SUMMER CRUISE Thursday 7th August 'Freedom' left on her homeward voyage, taking with her memories of a very happy time spent in lots of "old familiar places" under the finest continuous spell of Sunny weather I can remember. : We spent a lazy day on the beach, but the spell was broken. The return part of the voyage was now imminent and I was itching to get going whilst the weather held fair. Bembridge is a very shallow harbour and the entrance channel all but dried out, Gonsequently we should have tO leave within two hours of high water. 5 Friday 8th August “The forecast was NE-E 4, good; fair. The morning breeze seemed firmer than of late, and if it followed: the same pattern of freshening during the day we were in for a rough ride. O800. All was stowed, the dinghy lashed on deck, kedge retrieved from the beach, a good meal inside us and we were homeward bound. We left under’ engine, but on getting outside, where it was blowing about 5 by the number of white horses, I decided to stay under engine and plug away to the Owers Lightvessel and then close reach to Newhaven. It was very rough and wet, just keeping one's balance was a major effort. The steep seas were short enough to badly hamper Lady Anne and progress was pretty slow. 1000. Alongside” the Nab Tower, at this rate ETA Owers was 1300, and it seemed that we would not be able to lay Newhaven from there. e children, despite their medicine, were showing signs of distress and I was not keen to plug away to windward for ‘he whole leg singlehanded. 1030. Decided to turn back, set headsail, stopped engine and ran back to Spithead. By this time Bembridge-entrance was too shoal. We decided to have a day out and sail to Cowes, On the way we passed the Malcolm Millar beating out of Spithead, the SS 'United States’ passed us about 300 yards off, and then we passed ‘Queen Blizabeth 2' at about a quarter of a mile. These big ships made very little wash and no noise and. present a grand spectacle on a sunny day. The children also found the large number of hovercraft ferrics absorbing, although to my ear the noise level was appaling. May we long keep them out of the Blackwater! In the evening we had a grandstand view of the traditional Cowes fireworks much to Fiona's delight. Saturday Funny wet stuff fell out of a grey sky on and off all day, the coachroof leaked, (+00 much sun), we had the dinghy on deck and the children could not go ashore. It was blowing hard most of the day, but did moderate in the evening. The forecast for SuOCe was SE3- 6, thundery showers, poor, fog patches, Not so good. Sunday 10th August _ One week left. We missed the early forecast, but the weather seemed to have settled fair again. The midday forecast gave us variable 3 fair, with moderate visibility. .

s ay es 1345. We were under way agsin bound for Newhaven.° “The breeze was fitful and we . ro did not make sail until we were well past Ryde. + 1500. I turned in below and managed to doze off for nearly two hours. 1700. ‘Frances was at the helm, taking us fairly close. to the Nab when suddenly it let out a VERY LARGE HOOT. There was a slight haze, and a liner about 3 miles off was changing course. Frances took this hoot as a personal criticism by this concrete behemoth, -and felt there was injustice in the world of seafarers. Why had it done it? What did it mean? The skipper was roused and mumbled somtething technical about fog in the western approaches, but really it was not foggy. Once started these things catch on, and soon we could hear the moan of the Owers Lightvessel off ahead of us. - 1930. ‘We had to motor the last mile to the Owers as the wind had died completely, leaving the sea like a great heaving mirror. The wind did not pick up again that night, and shortly after sunset I handed the sails. Monday. 0200. Entered Newhaven, paid our dues, moored up to yachts on B.quay, and had fried fresh mackrell as an carly breakfast. We had caught the mackrell on ww ‘spinners whilst under way. Monday was a rest day, Tuesday brought a poor forecast, E4-5, and that night we had a severe thunderstorm. Wednesday. A lot less breezy, but we could see the entrance. from the quay and there was a big sea running outside. During the evening the wind dropped almost to. nothing, and the forecast for Thursday was quite good but with other sea areas having rain and wind. Thursday. In the morning the entrance locked 0.K. and we decided to make for Dover or Ramsgate. By departing Newhaven at the correct time one can carry the flood up to nea Hastings, where the tidal streams change direction, then the ebb will also carry? yeu to the east. Hence by planning to be at Hastings or Rye about an hour after ~- H.W. Dover. a fair tide of ten hours can be achieved.— 25 ww 0830. Departed Newhaven bound for Ramsgate. Wind var.2, long swell but not uncomfortably steep. 0950. BeachyHead, out of the lee of the Seven Sisters, we found the true wind ‘to be H2-3. ETA Dungeness 1430. ; 1200. Dungeness and Beachy Med both faintly visible. “wigel and i managed to get two hours sleep. 1500. Dungeness abeam. A bit rough as we passed the point. It had now clouded over and shortly after it started to rain in earnest. Wind E3-4. ETA Dover 1830. ETA Ramsgate 2230, visibility had now decreased considerably in the héavy rain and @ very anxious lookout for steamers was kept. Three times we had to turn well off course to avoid Dover harbour traific, and as the tide was now hard against us it seemed to take an age to get clear of the harbour area High water was at 0100 and as darkness descended we headed up the lighted “Gull Stream rather than the unlit Ramsgate Channel.

ve Oe At one stage when Frances was at the helm, while I plotted a fix out of the rain, she called for advice on a strange group of lights surmounted by 2 "Qk. Fl. Or'. This phenomena was moving fast and turned-‘out to be a hovercraft bound for Pegwell Bay. 2430. We finally locked into the inner harbour, wet and tired but feeling glad to be hearer home. Friday. Another day of torrential rain, I rigged sails and covers over our leaky hatch and coachroof. The local fuel merchant supplied a BiSES bag of coke and despite the weather we got all clothing bone dry. Saturday. We locked out at high water. 1330. alongs ide fuel pontoon and took on 11 gallons. 1400. Departed eee bound for Stansgate. Forecast N-NW 2-3 Eee te f We ad 0 aotBe in a very steep short sea, which only moderated near. Tongue Sand Tower. Our track HOPE us up the S. Edinburgh channel, Mid Barrow we waited for the tide before setting off for 'home'. We picked up our mooring at 0200 “Sunday morning, 12 heune out from Ramsgate witha light headwind and @ spring ebb all across the Thames estuary. CONCLUSIONS We Had achieved the object of our cruise, by getting to and from the Solent, and in successfully meeting up with Freedom, The engine was used far more than we expected, although to be fair we had headwinds for sll but our first mornings sail. It was quite uncanny how the Easterly wind swung round to the N.East when we could at last use an easterly for our last leg homeward. The catering had panned ut very well, 2 crates (36 pints) of Long Life milk had been consumed, 7lbs. of tinned butter and 1 gallon of orange squash. Occasional fresh meat, fruit, eggs and veg. supplemented our stores, the only regular demand being for fresh bread. After a.few days we had all settled down to-live in the confines of a boat, and I was surprised how readily we fell into the new routine. We lost the boathook overboard, and one warp disappeared. Extra fenders and one more long warp would have been handy.. Also I feel that the seven gallon fuel tank is not sufficient, as we often had to refuel from cans. — Now we are laying up, but already we are planning to take Lady Anny to Holland for next summer's cruise. She did us proud this year, and we thank her. Ian G. Tate

Avril Stevens. Soc. Sec. THIS MONTH'S SATLING AT STANSGATE April 18th and 19th sees the continuation of the a Points, and the Spring Points races as outlined last month. On Saturday, April 25th is the first Pursuit Race. In this event everyone starts from the shore at staggered intervals, the slower classes first. The staggered start times are calculated so that, theoretically, everyone should cross the finishing line together at a certain time. The . Race Officer ends the race as near to, this time as possible, at the mark er} which the leading boat is about to round. The final positions are then the, finishing order of the boats participating. This race can be quite exciting as you know your position as you. approach. the finishing line, and: can maneouvre to defend or improve it. On the following morning, the 26th, is the first of the Ladies Points —_— races. This year, for the first time, there will be a series of 5 races for the Ladies Cup. (Ladies must helm but not necessarily crew). If all the races are sailed points from three will count. The trophy is an elegant little silver cup presented to the Club by Queenie Hallam, our Vice-Presi dent's. wife. -In the afternoon the first of the six Cadet Points races will be sailed. This series is for any type of dinghy, and any crew, the helmsman only must be a cadet member of the Club (over 10 and under 18 years on the lst em dee The Cup for this devies was presented to the Club by Eric Payne, another of our Vice-Presidents. ee acne eh ee acer a We are visited by a team from the Ariel Sailing Club on May 2nd. This \ is the sailing section of the B.B.Cts. Sports and Social Club. The home event will be sailed in Enterprises. This is our longest standing team fixture in which we compete for the Twin Flags sneony - a little silver mast flying both Club burgees. For those not familiar a team racing, each Club usually enters three boats, and the team scores by their boats final positions. There is often a . lot of tactical movement to slow down the opponents, and allow one's own team mates to sail through. Each Club is given a match point for each race won, that is, two races at home and two away, only in the event of a tie do “Overall boat points, for each Club, get taken into account. The Spring Points series continues on May Srd. On May 9th is another Ssingle-handed dinghy Handicap Race, while the Cruisers meet on the River ‘Roache. At a time when we are anxious to recruit and train people to man the: rescue launches, prospective helpers may find it useful to read the Re } "Suggestions and Advice to Skippers and Crews of Rescue Taunches', in the: | Publication YR3/69, as follows:- : The first responsibility of the rescue launches-is the safety of the helmsmen and crews, and they should not return to harbour until all competitors have fini shed; ‘but if the crew of a capsized boat is yee di stressed, points to be born in mind are as follows:- (a) The boats will not sink and there is no hurry. Avoidance of damage to hull and mast is an important consideration. (b) The crew should lower sails, right the boat and collect floating gear before boarding the rescue launch. (c) Once the boat is righted, the stem” :ghould be lifted as high as Beet ue to empty Mates (da) Gace can shen get into the boat, finish bailing, and, 2 rule, sail home under reefed sail or foresail only. | ee (e) Once one boat has been emptied, her crew can manage while another is assisted. “ey! Buekets and spare bailers should be carried in the rescue launches, (g) In rough or cold weter it may not be possible for the crew of the boat to lower sails. In this case, the crew should be taken on board the rescue launch,.. The crew of the rescue launch should then get hold of the mast head of the boat, unshackle the head of the - mainsail, then work down the mast and unshackle the head of the jib; then work down the forestay while righting the boat, so ending up: with the: boat upright and held by the bow. The boat should not ‘be towed on her side. Son ge FRO RR Coxswain —

This is the usual position for small visiting yachts and is. very convenient. The inimitable Albe rt the bosun, wh) weers his immaculate white topped peaked cap when the sun shines and offers his shining bald bare head to the skies when it reins, moored us to his-‘liking and ashore we went to make that telephone call. ie different from an English Sunday; the main post office was open for business, although obviously at s reduced tempo. Back to the Club for a pre-lunch drink, But first the immigretion officer accompanied by a heavily armed policeman. Passports? Yes. Ships papers? Ah, there was a difficulty. The R.Y.A. Nor, may I add, w did it at any. time in any of thethree countries we visited on the cruise, However, all was well at last and we were quite patently not listed in the lerge volume of presumably unwanted visitors carried by the »fficial, Mind yon, he looked first! In the afternoon Geof flew back home and Guocnee flew out so by tea-tine we were settled in. The next ae days, encouraged by a force 5-6 N. to N.W. wind, we sampled the delights of Ostend and chatted and drank with all our friends and acquain- tances from the Maldon River. It seemed that half the boats on the Blackwater were visiting the Continent at the same time ss us. There wes only one : evening , during the whole fortnight woen we did nt run into a local boat, and in most cases we knew the owner well, 7 By Wednesday Bet crnoen we felt we hed seen enough of Ostend and as the wind had moderated to force 3 N.wW. we casteoff and put to sea, Only for a few miles mind you. TT» Blankenburgh in fact, ere we tied up to 2 pontoon and a wandered ashore, A delightful little watering place, everyone friendly «nd, in spite of the warnings in Delmar-Morgan's "North Sea Pilstage and Harbour” quite an easy entrance. Epa Wy ar (> a2 eNe A light Northerly meant a beat out to clear the mole at Zeebrugge. The - book said clear by at least a mile. We only passed half a mile outside and 2a paid for it by being thrown about on a nasty sea which came from all directions. This in only a force 2. In astrong breeze it would have been most: uncomfortable. -As we passed the end of the mole "Theodora" the ocean Youth Club’ boat from Brightlingsea came out, The wind came more free es we approached the W., Schelde and we ran up to _ Flushing in fino style... The entrance to the lock is at the far end 6f the town _ beside the Breskens ferry terminal. Locking in was quick and efficient and by 11.30 we were in the canal, having cleared Customs whilst still in thé lock, I+ was here that we reelly noticed for the first time the simple and efficient way the Dutch have with mooring warps. None of the business of long continuous warps festooned from one end of the vessel to the other, Short orange courlene warps, ach with a large loose eye at one end and cach no longer than twenty feet or thereabouts. The loose eye is dropped or flung over the bollards with which most locks are well provided and.the other end made fast. To cast off after the water in the lock has dropped the rope is given a flick and off flies the ge to drop neatly on deck. Even the tiny children ca: do it? Four of these warps and four large fat expensive inflated fenders inbright orange plastic, and your worries about locking in,.and, out are over. . pie mean road bridge over the Kanaal Van Walcheren was closed and we ticd up to a dolphin for half an hour. It was warm and drowsy and the quick light lunch we had, with a bottle of wine made us disinclined to hurry so we were not too impatient with the bridgemaster. & loud hoot woke us from our reveric. Up went the bridge and through ceme an enormous petrol barge. And through we went in the opposite direction. The next bridge, a small. by-road opened without our. asking, but at Middleburg, a main road bridge, we tied up once again to the dolphins to wait, in company with two West Mersea boats, the owners of both of which we knew. No more bridges now, just the lock at Veere where we went through in about five minutes. Out into the Veerse Meer, a sharp turn to port and into the Stadthaven, one of the most picturesque and delightful harbours imagineble. The town is delightful as are the inhabitants, some of the more elderly of whom still-wear the traditional dress. Not asa tourist attraction, or as‘a‘ special Sunday costume, but unconsciously, evury dey. Veere has not fossilized since the Veerse meer wes dammed ond the fishing ended. -It is a lively little town whose job it is to give pleasure to the plensure seekers. Not by the provision of dance halls and juke boxes, b y being peaceful and pleasant and just ‘good ). (ine to look at As always: in Holland the Havenmeester was.icourteous and’ obliging and the Yacht Club which runs the Stedthaven, a pleasant and nice place t> have .@ drink ..........which we did, several. Friday 27th June We left Veere after lunch and sailed down the length of the Veersemeer, now fast becoming 2 giant sailing pond for full size yachts, with a number of marines either built or building. “It seeméd queer to have no tide for which to make allowances. Tame somehow, which was probably why we went agrvund. It was late afternoon and we were-fortunate that a motor cruiser came along and spotting us out of the channel came over and pulled us off. With no wind to speak of and only e 4 H.F. Stuart with a clamshell propeller we were not having much success by ourselves. At the East Scheldt end of the Veeresmeer there is an enormous new sea lock which shot us through and out into the aandkreek in record time. #e hed decided to try and meke Goes that night and clthough it was late, we motored the three miles to the sea lock at Seas van Goes, where the little canal meets the tidal estuary. Once through we motored the three miles to the main road bridge at Goes. Here however, we were unlucky, in spdte of a Telephone call made by the lock kecper at the sea lock when we entered. S5 we tiea up to a large barge and went to bed. About five in the morning, we were awakened by a thump on the cabin top and as we cast off the barge was away. It was a good job the skipper noticed us. After all, we were so smell and his vessel seemed to us to be enormous.

As it happened my son decided to spend a few days in hospital and consequently this issue is later than intended, and would have been much later still had it not been for Jill Bigden's help in typing most of the stencils for me. PE COMMODORE COMMENTS ON REGATTA Phew! its over, and what a show! What a success! What a credit to our Club! » Strains and stresses there were many, but "the few survived against all adversity including broken water mains, severed electric cables and other difficulties which might embarrass if mentioned, To those of you who gave your time, services and/or assistance, :??°)% however large or small the part you played, I would like to- say .on behalf of those who either took part, looked on or just had something é¢lse to do - Thank you! and again Thank you! ters SER ; Those of yOu who did not stay to leern of the official results will be pleased to know that the Club was thanked by the Visitors for the wonderful weekend of sailing which they sharéd with us. I am sure that the results proved the value of the competition which they gave us. Indeed the Stansgate weather persisted and supplied the whole sailing mixture of flat, good and robust conditions which always seem to appear at Regatta time. “One hundred and cighty Entries and someone said two hundred next yeart!! I won't repeat what someone else said, but, its something that needs to be said and possibly.at the Annual General Meeting of the Club when °“\: = the Membership should be asked to consider the assistance needed by the Officers and Committee if we are ever to stage another Regatta on the'° © lines of that so recently accomplished. : Fair comment? With another large event a few weeks ahead of us new helpers must be found and the amount of new help needed must not be under estimated if we are to have another success. Thanks for listening - Now H.E.L.P. . : Seen Allerton Commodore REGATTA GOSSIP A funny thing happenedto our noisy, tubby friend from Leigh - the; .., one with the Red Herald who filleée our tonts with dust as he belted up. and dow the track. n _ After most people had left Stansgate after the Regatta prize giving .. - he and his friends were having trouble with the Herald. It wouldn'.. t ~ start. After an hour or two the AA were called and the AA man agreed that petrol was not getting from the tank to the pump. "Perhaps a stone

has’:thrown up end dented the pipe"!! The AA man went away - no hooks fhe tools were in his Land Rover that had broken down. 10.00 p.m. Breakdown truck arrived. He agreed that lack of petrol was the trouble and quickly cut off a small length of fractured flexible pipe. Withing a few minutes it was all systems go. The Herald drove - SLOWLY past the dinghy park and up the road. _ More Gossip for the Regatta At the Regatta it's just as well that the Race Box crew don't work to rule. On the third -day of the Regatta they cnly had 3 mins. 39 seconds between finishing the last boat of the Third Points and the first 10 min. gun of the Fourth Points. . Kore wives than ever seemed to be involved this year, behind the Bar, in the penteys helping with Signing On and Results, and of ‘course in the Race Box and as Spotters. They were everywhere. Young sons and daughters weren't being left out either. They acted as Runners from the Club House to the Race Box, : Sc NaaRenee struck on the few days preceding the Regatta. After a storm on the Thursday thestakes holding up the marquee on the terrace had to be driven in harder - Result one burst water main and one shorted main electricity cable, After frantic shopping for bits both services were repaired temporarily. During the digging the telephone cable was~ damaged and also had to be repaircd. During the Regatta the land line to the Race Box also gave trouble for a short while but all were sorted out without holding up the Regatta. This year however the cesspools were omptied each morning end there waS no panic pumping to cope with an overflow as in previous years. JC Witter. Sa AS Ts THIS MONTH'S SAILING AT STANSGATE ~ 4 There are few events now which have not been described in previous - issues apart from the Cup races, and odd open meetings. Mona's Cup on Sunday 21st June, is the first of these Cup races. This Cup (or Mug) was presented to the club when we were at Heybridge by Mona, the proprietor of the Jolly Sailor. Since we have been at Stansgate we have kept this event as a race up river to Heybridge and back. It is an all in handicap race for cats., dinghies and cruisers. Consequently we use a long line start and finish, in accordance with special sailing instructions. ) On June 28th, Maldon Yacht Club hold their Open Cruiser race and Rum Tub from our starting line, The Rum Tub is a long dinghy handicap race around the Bench Head buoy in the mouth of the estuary, so take your lunch with you (and plenty of beer). There is a further hazard for the moorings on B row outwards, namely severe pitting of the chain. Last year_one boet went adrift due to the chain having parted. The reason was that although the chain was only a year 014d, it had been scraped across the bottom by wind and tide. SAIL SETTING At about lunch time on a very warm Sunday, a group gathered at one end of the hard, around Mr. Donald Forbes of Musto and Hyde, Sailmakers. His talk opened with a statement of priorities: Sails are the equivalent of an engine, the mast and rigging merely support the sails, and the hull is to keep your feet dry! ~ Ustng an Enterprise as a demonstration model, Mr. Forbes showed us various jib settings for various weathers, tight leach, loose foot for light winds (ccno ~ effect), and loose leach and tight foot for heavy winds. The latter setting is required so that the leach goes away at the top and does'nt backwind the main. On the Enterprise used, the sliding track needed to be fixed diagonally across the side decks a few inches aft of the shrouds, set about 3-4 inches further back on the outside, end than the inner end. The mainsail settings were also clearly described, including the order of setting. . 1. Pull miinsail up to black band. 2e Pull out foot of sail by means of the clew outhaul until the sail is a nice full’ shape - further in than you think. Se Pull dow kicking strap when afloat and close hauled. 4, Adjust Cunningham hole setting until the creases going up and back from the mast disappear. 5. Setting of track width at the stern depends on wind - in light wind it may be central. This keeps the leach tight as the sail is pulled down, ~~ A wider setting allows the main to be held down,- but the leach ean go- away at the top to reduce heeling in heavy a ee The general rules were:~ Strong wind flat sea, everything tight. — Strong tee wind lumpy sea, baggy sails and don't try sailing too close to the wind. Keep . ~ ‘sailing fast. In a light wind keep everything baggy and full. seek Another general. rule was that at any time during 2 race you are pulling - in the. mainsheet and stretching the leach, you-should also pull down the Cunningham to stretch the luff as well. In this way there are no peculiar stresses in the sail. Each time you let out the mainsheet, the Cunningham should also be lct out. 7 | Spreaders Spreaders are designed to keep the mast straight laterally whilst allowing a limited amount of bend fore and aft. Spreaders allow a thinner section of mast to be carried than would otherwise have been possible. It appears that the shroud should'nt be dead straight from hounds to chain plates but they should be pushed about 2" forward by the spreader in anything up .to hard winds, when any restriction should be removed to allow a straight ean Mr. Forbes epee dozens of questions and helped members with probloms a practical way, including taking the boats on the water... /contintied.

It may be of interest to Club Members, particularly those associated with rescue boat operation,to know that classes for the Royal Life Saving - Society Awards are held at Chelmsford Seem as: baths on aeeeney evenings by the Chelmsford Swimming Grube Normally these classes DOnGaitnnie. on the Bronze Medallion award since this is a recognised minimum qualification for those directly concerned with water safety (eg. baths attendants),and anyone of average swimming ability should be able to attain this standard. In addition there are also awards by the Amateur Swimming Association for personal survival which involve such skills as swimming in clothes, treading water, removing clothes in the water, and swimming a set distance without clothes (but with swimming costume!). The tests are in 3 grades with increasing distances and timed tests and so _ form a good basis for later life saving awards if required. The classes are very informal and include all aspects of water-safety. There is no age limit for the A.S.A. awards, but for the R.L.S.S. Bronze Medallion the minimum age is 13, for youngsters under this age there is an Intermediate award. - _ I should also add that Chelmsford Swimming Club run classes to teach children and adults to swim, In the case of children there isa long waiting - list unfortunately, but there is no harm in adding your children's names to the list. This series of articles has degenerated into a description of the Club trophies, now that the season is half over, and everyone is familiar with all the series events, so lets make the best of it. — «The Jackpot on August 2nd is for the veterans of the Club (over 40's). The Cruiser Cup is for cruisers from the same group of Clubs, and this year is to incorporate the Blackwater Clubs Cruiser Championships, making it the major cruiser race on the Blackwater this year. HOW .TO GET THE BEST OUT OF YOUR SATIS Last June, Donald Forbes from the famous firm of sailmakers, Musto and Hyde of Rayleigh, paid a visit to our club at Stansgate and we spent a most interesting and instructive day, with plenty of practical demonstration, learning how to get the best out of our sails. In the July issue of Navigans, Eleanor Witter wrote a most lucid and detailed account of the various points discussed and members are urged to male a further study of this article before embarking on next season's racing and to read it in conjunction with this less adequate description. During Donald Forbes' visit to Stansgate he dropped the hint that he would be willing to talk to us about sails during our winter lecture progranme, so our social secretary, Avril Stevens duly arranged this and the meeting was held at the main M.A.S.C. hall on February 19th. We spertt a most interesting evening with a real dinghy completely rigged on the stage to enable Mr. Forbes to demonstrate as his talk proceeded. Some eruiser owners raised various points concerning sails from their point of view, as Opposed to the main dinghy coverage. At one stage in the lecture when Mr. Forbes asked if anyone used spreaders, some amusement was caused when Eric Payne rushed forward carrying an enormcus spreader attached to a very ample stainless steel shroud from his Atalanta eruiser, which up to that point, had been discreetly hidden behind the stage and had been brought to the meeting for another purpose altogether. It was a most enjoyable evening, again with the attemdance around the 100 mark, and questions continued to be answered until a late hour and we sre most grateful to Donald Forbes for giving up his time so freely on our account. Our thanks are due to Avril Stevens for organising the meeting so efficiently - to Julian Bigden for lending his Enterprise for the demonstration - +o Nick Tovey for lending his sails and to the other members who went to the trouble of bringing their sails and dinghies to the club in reserve. ‘Our chairman for the evening was Vice-President Eric Payne and the vote of thanks to the speaker was proposed by our Rear-Commodore, John Witter. eR DINGHY BUILDING Would-be boat builders who, for a variety of reasons, are deterred from undertaking a construction will be interested in the boat building class held on the premises of Rainsford Girl's School. TO THE WESTERN ISLES VIA THE CALEDONIAN CANAL, 1970 DR. DONALD Mc KENDRICK For our summer holiday we usually tow to the Mediterranean but after repeated persuasion from friends we’ decided to join them this year in the Western Isles. With the Forth and Clyde canal closed it is quite a long haul from the Hast coast so I arranged to use one weekend prior to our holiday proper to knock off the first hundred miles. The tJayess' is a Snapdragon 27 and although bearing the official number 2 she was in fact the first one built and appeared at the Boat Show in January. She had already proved herself during a gale in our shakedown cruise in March and later during a rough passage to Holland at Whitsun. She has an Albin 12 H-P. auxiliary with the usual navigation equipment which includes a Mercia electronic log. This has the great advantage of being able to mount the speedo head in the cockpit and the log by the chart table. There are six berths and three or four can cruise in comfort for prolonged periods. On Friday July the 3rd three of us arrived at a cold ad blustery Stansgate for the first leg to Wells. I had two of my normal crew with me for this hop - my son-in-law Peter and an old friend Michael. Both would have liked to crew the whole way to Inverness but time would not allow. Peter and my daughter were to spend a week with us later in the Western Isles. We quickly got the life-raft on deck in its position at the foot of the mast and were under way by 1400 hours, deflating the 10 ft Even as-we went as we had already lost a valuable part of a spring ebb. The wind was NWS and we reached Clacton before the tide turned and the wind fell light. We had an uneventful = motor-sail past the Cork L.V. and Orford Ness, being off Lowestoft by dawn. I w decided to close the shore inside Corton sands to cheat the tide and then went below for my first sleep only to be woken in an hour by a change of motion. A quick look at the Seafarer showed we were in 10 feet instead of 4 fathoms, having come a cable or so too far off-shore. The tide turned again off Cromer. In the morning the wind had backed to the west and had given us a good sail, in fact our progress had been so good that I decided we could easily make Wells on the evening tide instead of waiting for Sunday morning as originally planned. Our course during the afternoon turned more and mare to port until the wind was on the nose and we finally motor-sailed the last five miles to the entrance. What a help Blakeney Church is in an otherwise featureless landscape. Frequent bearings gave us repeatedly good position lines which combined with echo soundings confirmed our dead reckoning. This was particularly important <s off Sheringham the speedo, which had developed a tendency to be rather optimistic over 6 knots slowed unaccountably and then dropped to zero as I was watching it. The diagnosis of the sensor unit rod falling off was easily confirmed by withdrawing the unit. A spare rod only takes a moment to fit but inserting it at sea can mean 2 or 3 pints of water in a locker so I decided to wait till we ect to Wells as we would be drying out during the night. Vv We picked up the Wells buoy at 1710 - ten minutes later than estimated. Like so many offshore harbour entrance buoys this seemed unnecessarily small and difficult to see and we were certainly within a mile of it before we were sure it was what we were looking for. Although the wind of 34 against the tide was only producing a gentle chop outside the breakers at the entrance certainly gave promise of what it could do here in a blow. The channel is not well buoyed for strangers. We followed the prescribed route closely, running in under main alone, but fluctuated from 15 to 3 feet and grounded twice, the first time well within the channel. The second time the bow was hard aground so wo dropped the hook - but it would'nt go - half the shank was sbove water! When I discovered that the stern was in 20 feet a quick burst astern put us back in the 4 knot flood to reach the quay without further trouble. There we were greeted officially and kindly by the HM. Mr. Taylor, berthed alongside and made comfortable for the night. We had an excellent chicken ghoulash, dining on a peaceful summer evening on our cockpit table before turning ii. We slept well. /continued.

A 7 me. - eo eis Ringe, oS On Sunday morning The H.M. led us to a mooring as arramged taking us ashore in his launch from where we returned to London by car. I was very satisfied. 138 miles in the first 27 hours scemed to be a good omen fcr cur holiday and we had a good northing achieved. Friday, 10th July. I arrived back in Wells at 1800 hours with my new crew, George, the .s&inest psychiatrist in the business, and a delight to have aboard any yacht, and John, a young engineer who had been introduced to me by 4 mutual friend. John has a boat of his own in the Solent but is always keen to increase his experience. He proved to be a most pleasant and extremely competent seamar, and I. ceculd not have hada better or happicr crew. There was the added bcnus that both of them have cast-iron stomachs and as I have never (yet) been sick in a small boat we felt fairly confident on that score. The tJayess' was hard aground on the sands as the H.M. had forgotten to bring her alongside as: promised. A friendly yachtsman tock us over the water in his dinghy and we took advantage of sur unexpected ground to scrub the bottom. We motored tc the quey at 2300 hours. There is about 2 ft. alongside at icw water so we sat comfortably on cur twin keels for an hour while we slept. We cast off at 0920 on Saturday llth and were soon at the outer Wells — buoy. It was a glorious warm sunny day and with a 3-4 W we made 55 - 6 knots f% under genoa and main. The Humber L.V. was abeam at 2100 haurs - 52 miles on the log in just under 12 hours of sailing. The wind increased a bit during my watch so the working jib replaced the genoa. When John took over it was Si 6 and a gale warning on the 0640 forecast came as no surprise; so we o>, altered course for Bridlington. With four rolls now we were still béing over-pressed as the wind got stronger but lazily we spilt the excess instead of tucking in more reefs 28 we were near to shelter. We tied up alongside 2 fisherman, 22 hours out of Wells with 101 miles on the clock. The H.M. greeted us during our bacon and eggs and moved us to a drying berth alongside the quey where we were comfortable enough. The Yacht Club made us very welcome end we , wallowed in their simply enormous baths. Gales persisted and kept the Rescue services busy. One yacht could not make round Flamborough but was eventually towed in safely and there was a tragic drowning in the bay. I do not normally set sail during gale warnings but by Monday evening we were getting restive and as the forecast was marginally better’I decided to press on. We left just befcre midnight and were soon round Flamborough Head. With working rig and an off- shore force 5 we had another glorious sail on « clear warm night with a few Fisherman and the odd coaster for company. During Tuesday afternoon the wind veered and increased to NW6. By 1700 hours the sky looked really awful, storm % clouds interspersed with brilliant yellows and sudden squalls. We prepared for trouble, George seeing to the storm jib and putting extra lashings on the other jibs and everything else on deck, while John rigged the trysail and I looked around to see if I could find anything else for thom to do. (Not entirely idlc, I was trying to keep the ship fairly steady!) ' The 1800 forecast was NW8© f% imminent so we downed the jib and motor sailed like hell for Sunderland which we reached at 2050 befcre the trouble started. This is a very casy entrance which would obviously offer sheltcr to a yacht in just about any conditions but the masses of empty quays made it seem a sad and rather derelict harbour. We spent a peaceful night olongside a ship quay although we would have been better to have joined the yacht moorings (which we did the next morning, Wednesday) but we could find nobody about in the whole harbour to tell us where tO 20-6 TI should mention here thet I do not in fact have a trysail but I do havo deep reef points in my mainsail. By rolling loosely down to this point and leshing the cringles with the boom topped we get = very serviceable storm sail. The reof points are just below the numbers. If a trysail is not carried I think some arrangement of this sort is essential in a cruising yacht as even with a well tapered boom there-is a limit to the number of rolis which can be put in without the boom dropping too low. When beating with this rig I think it is probably worth while keeping the topping lift just tight enough to take a little strain out of the leach. 7 | continued cverleaf/

-ee age Ree With regard tc watches, with a three man crew I prefer three hours cn and six off. This of course shifts the watches and allows for four hours sleep at a stretch (cnough at my age). I always do the navigating on my own boat so seldom get more than 2 - 3 hours consecutively anyway. We were “on a 66% (Yacht Passage Form) and had a long chat with the coastguard in his station who adviscd us to stay in Sunderland. However time was beginning to geta little short and “northerly winds were not going to be any help so we left on Wednésday at 1450 under trysail and engine with a fair tide, waving to the storm cone as we passed the C.S. station. This was not foolhardy as we could safely have run back to Sunderland had this proved necessary. In three hours the wind veered and cased to NE5-6 so the storm jib went up and we sailed into Blyth for dinner and to await the next fair tide. We were greeted by the club boatman in his launch who put us on a mooring, booked a table for us at the best local restaurant and even arranged for a club member to run us there in his car. Such kindnesses really are appreciated. Our night in Sunderland was to be our last night in harbour before Inverness although head winds from now on were to mean much motoring and hence calls for petrol. “@) THE SHADOW AND THE FUTURE Perhaps I ought to commence by apologising for kseping you in the dark - perhaps. At the A.G.M. last November I concluded my report by making the statement - "It is your Club and your decision". Perhaps in any Club such a statement should be treated with a certain amount of reserve but within the context applied I felt, have felt during the following months, and still feel that the decisions made in the “report” I am about to give were and are indeed your decisions. It was at that same meeting you all accepted without contradiction the need for the Marconi Sailing Club to exist and flourish at Stansgate and to that end agreed to pay the new rent upon a course of “succeed to buy or bust". Turning back to my opening remark therefore you can now understand why I have-not previously come forward with news of the state of negotiation, such news has either been “subject to further negotiation" or I have been in a hurry because of fear of “Busting”. As so many of these negotiations have by their netaoe been delicate I ~ would like to pay tribute to the faith and patience of my fellow officers i allowing me the freedom to negotiate “in the dark" and for supporting me to the present stage where we await permanent planning approval before the contract Ky is signed and our Sailing Site is purchased. My appreciation also goes to the Chief Executive of the M.A.S.C. and the Chairman of tho M.A.S.C. Committee slso, ee especially to the Company Property Officer = Mr. A. Hi dset » Basic Conditions of Purchase (1) The Site comprising some 7 acres is to be purchased freehold by the Marconi Athletic and Social Club for use by the Sailing Club as'a Sailing Site and for associated recreational purposes. (2) A&A Licence is to be granted to us by the M.A.S.C.e in the first place for a period of 5 years based upon a rental system of £1,000 pea. ww increasing by 10% per annum. At the end of this period rental for following years will be w ~ hegotiated. (3) All other expenses of the Sailing Section will in future be met from Section funds. There are obviously many questions.to be asked at this stage by many people but we must be patient and let things fall into their natural places as "that shadow” is not lifted until the contract is signed. Only then can we get down to the future which will bring greater responsibilities upon all members which you have signified to be acceptable as long as the Marconi Sailing Club may stay - at Stansgate. Amongst the things which may have puzzled you is the application for permanent planning permission. This‘had to go forward as obviously we wanted to buy property to use as a Sailing Site showing a new building in a different position to those at present, we obviously expect and have very good reasons to think that we shall get approval - BUT this does not mean that the building drawn up is the exact building intended neither does it mean that we shall start building in the foreseeable future, but - who knows? /continued.

a (» a This then is where we have got to, at a later date we shall no doubt show a plan of the property at Stansgate for the benefit of all concerned. in the meantime I would first appeal to all of you good members to encourage new membership amongst the Marconi ranks, .secondly I would ask you to preserve the rules of your Club regarding official visitors and outsiders (we don't want outsiders - so tell them so) and thirdly our first re-organisation will be to see thet a permanent car park is suickly established in order that the children and senior citizens may use the internal roadway and dinghy park in safety and with pleasure. Discussion revolved around finding some of the answers to the questions put to the Fleet in the April Navigans, with some of the conclusions summarised below:- Most fleet members considered themselves to be in the beginner or ‘not terribly skillful" class. This meant that, if racing were to be encouraged ‘and enjoyed, lengths of courses and the prevailing conditions if adverse might deter many helmsmen from racing. It was concluded that more laps of fairl;: short courses (similar tc those for Mirrors) would be advantagcous and would enable boats to retire if their crews became fatigued. PATTER To recap, dear reader, you will remember how three boats and umptocen persons trailed to Broxbourne for the first of the Traveller's Trophy Meetings on 2nd May, now read on. uoty = tMe boats came to the line - and it was crowded. The lake is shaped roughly like a kidney bowl, the narrow part being about 30 ft. wide and the whole area being something like our dinghy and car park joined together. The wind adopted guerrilla tactics - it was very frustrating - Blackjack retired during the second race. Norman Palmer and Dave Draper continued and secured 12th and 9th overall places respectively, Blackjack taking 18th position in the lst race. There were numerous capsizes caused by sudden gusts which although not particularly strong came from totally unexpected directions - they were invariably followed by a flat calm. Typical observed incident - two boats were running side by side on opposite jibes with spinnakers set - sudden East - one boat capsized and the other shot straight up the bank into a blackberry bushe Our general opinion was that pond sailing probably has its good points, the chap in the blackberry bush certainly found some, but we could not. On the following Sunday the 9th May, the same group of persons visited Leigh-on-Sea S.C. This was just a social visit really although we did join in > one of their points races (20 boats on the line). . ww ww This was a much more enjoyable affair as far 1s Blackjack was concerned, we finished 5rd. Dave and Norman dithered about a lot and then blamed me for not pointing out where the marks were, which was rather unfair since I put ina ereat deal of effort in order to show them the way round - part of the burdensome load of high office, I suppose. Tempus fugited on and paused awhile whilst Norman Palmer won the Saturday single handed race. During this event Ken Beavins managed to successfully set his spinnaker - as far as I know even Elvestrom has not tried single handed spinnaker work in a dinghy. The last two races of the spring points series held a double interest. The first was that Blackjack had to beat Hanging Five in both races to win the series; the second was that these two races were part of the invitation series with Stone S.C. Blackjack won the first race but capsized after overtaking Hanging Five = in the second, a rapid recovery and some superb sailing by the crew of Blackjack took her right through the 12 stone fleet to finish Srd, one place behind Hanging v Five. Consistency pays - congratulations to Dave and Gary on winning the Spring - Points series. (I hear that the ban on that hat has been lifted as a result). ; w The Stone G.P. fleet njoyed their visit and we look forward to meeting them again. Stan Atkins 7531 managed to break his tiller extension and soon afterwards went overboard when a toe drap broke, he made a rapid recovery however end only lost one place. Gordon Parr caused Norman to capsize 2 *C" mark, Anne bruised her ribs and Gordon in fear of his life retired to the safety oF the Stone §.C. Somewhere I have managed to miss -out the Pilots Cup. So -— Pilots Cup won by Dave in Hanging Five, Norman in third place, the rece being sailed in very light airs and taking 6 hours to complete. Regatta Very enjoyable. Honging Five gaining several places to take 8th overall. Blackjack gained 6th and 17th on Sunday and retired through lack of wind on Monday. Ken Beavins set off in his boat on Saturday with son Nick and cruised round to the River Crouch, spent the night there and sailed back again on Sunday morning - I have not seen Ken to enquire about the trip but it must have been a wonderful dovmhill ride back along the coast. Peter Baines has purchased NWN. Palmers boat “Whiplash”, and another new boat in the fleet is 6278 cwned by Geof Wright - we look forward to seeing them both on the line in the near future. Pat Black.

_—_— Letter to the Editor of Navigans. 12th June, 1972. NEW CLUB HOUSE As an Ordinary Member I feel entitled to answer Peter Foremants comments in the last Navigans in an Ordinary Member's capacity. Peterts thoughts are in accord with my own. The original idea (born 1968) was for a single storey Club House built on pillars (storage etc. underneath) with a commanding view of the river from the lounge. Other facilities included would be adequate changing rooms, toilets and showers, also bar and galley facilities, in fact this was the type of buildings included in our planning application last year. I feel that - as Peter suggests - the building should be adequate but not large and built only for summer or seasonal usuge. The point raised re building on the river side of the sea wall would never be entertained. In fact even if we were able to get over the dead bodies of the Wentworth Days in the area and build we would certainly suffer from shifting foundations. I havo been an advocate for finishing races off the hard for some time ‘7 but of course this does mean a control in two places due to the unfavourable conditions for starting races from the shore anywhere but as at present. (Signed) S.R.Allerton. Commodore. A A A Planning and Dave?.opment of Stansgat: Site It is said that a little knowledge is dangerous. Mary, in her Editorial last month, drew attention to an article regarding the new Club House which was very welcome and will it is hoped provoke others to follow suit, indeed the "murmurings in the bush" are beginning to be heard, so much so that "secret plans" cnd “decisions without reference to membership" are being referred to. “Gctting the right advice" has also heen mentioned, but I am sure that all of this is well intentioned and fecl that the following facts and detail will fill you all in on what has been happening during the last six months. A Planning & Development Sub-Committce was formed as agreed at the Annual General Meeting. This Sub-Committee first met in January when agreement was reached as follows:-- "That the objectives cf the sub-committee would be to plan for ‘Devel opmer:t of the Stamsgate Site! to the benefit of the Marconi Sailing Club according to the terms of the Planning permission within five Yours. Further extension of Planning Rights would also be considered. The development plans shall includce:- (i) Clubhouse - size, design, facilities ete. (ii) Precincts (all factors). (iii) Launching facilities, haré@ and foreshore. (iv) Moorings. (v) -The use of large field. /continued.

CONMODORE'S NOTES In spite of the fact that we did not hold our Open Day when originally planned, it was certainly most successful in terms of enjoyment, weather and new. larconi members. We changed the date to avoid clashing with the H.4.S.C. Barbecue, and then discovered we'd clash with the Essex Show, and several away meetings. I. must adnit I was apprehensive half way through the afternoon when Geof Farnie told me he'd only had one application, but thereafter. business was much more brisk, and we were delighted to end up with at least twelve new members. Hany thanks to all our helpers, sailors and organisers. The sailing deronstrations were well received, and the boat trips exceedingly popular. Incidentally, Jack Bigden's appeal qver the P.A.- for new members was heard by the crew of 2 passing cruiser, who came ashore and asked for an application form: For the benefit of our Associate liembers, the main idea of the Open Day

~2~ is to"show off" the club to Marconi people, in order to attract more ordinary menbers. This, incidentally may also allow us to take more associates, whilst still maintaining our membership ratios. The detailed plans for the clubhouse have now been completed, and subrnitted to four builders for quotations and to various authorities. There are likely to be some modifications regarding siting, but at present these don't seem serious. By far the most important consideration is the cost and we won't know this for a week or two yet. The weather has been most kind to us this ycar, and this has been reflected in the sailing activity. In particular, the cruiser fleet has been much more active. The lst Barnacle points heda record entry of seven boats, and the cruise to Brightlingsea (dare I say Pin 1ii11?) was a great success. Dennis Byatt. Commodore. OPEN DAY The "Boat Trip" side of Open Day was well supported both by boat owners and visitors. About 5 dinghies, 7 cruisers and the new Rescue Boat took over 50 adults and over 40 children out for a sail or motor. Other members: lent lifejackets and as a result of all these. cfforts several families have now ’ become sailing club menbers. The visitors were very appreciative of the kindness of club members in taking theia out for what for many of them was their first trip in a smallish boat. , a Eleanor Witter. LHIS AND THAT! The warm sunny weather has encouraged many more swimmers this year, especially as the Blackwater really does seem much cleaner now. The children, especially, have enjoyed themselves. However, please note that the tide rip can be very strong past the hard, and when dinghies are coming in it can be hazardous, especially. when races are finishing. Witha force six behind us and a turned tide against us it was one long run, Frank holding the boom and I manning the tiller and clutching ny life jacket. We decided to put in to the bank opposite, have a cup of coffee and nake ourselves respectable for. the grand entry - Frank never having been to 'B' before. In August I joined the sailing barge Marjorie at Maldon for a 4 .. day Cruise.. Marjorie. is -a common sight on the Blackwater.as‘she ; ; Sails. to and.from the Hythe Quay, Maldon, with charter ‘parties aboard. “and is casily recognizable by the white cross in her “topsail, she is a: coasting barge built for R & W Paul of: Ipswich in 1902, rth. a length of 86.ft.:. and a -beam of. 20ft.The.:hold has ‘been fitted out to provide cabin accomodation for.1l2 charterers, a spacious saloon and.a' well-appointed: gallery... The crew. (skipper and mate) _ live.in. the. traditional skipper's: cabin but eat. with. the charter Ww ie “party (who. supply and: cook the food). The barge has a kctch rig, the ‘mizzen being sheeted to the rudder blade to assist. steering and countcract the force of the foresail and “""Staysail. “Our party consisted of 5 chaps, including myself, the rest. of the party having backed down, There is a moral there for any one interested . in. organising a charter party. However, the smaller ‘party is an " Advantage as it gives plenty of opportunity “to be involved in the semaanines and Lie of the barge. “We were Sones ‘away from Hythe Quay at 5.20 am. on Howey chow the 20th. by a small tug. The tide had just started to ebb, but the > Wind was almost. non-existent. All the sails were set off Heybridge, we chartocrers being given various ropes and told to pull, and the tug cast off. We drifted rather than sailed down Colliers Reach and some extemely strong language was used to attempt to 'whistle-up a — wind', It became apparent as the days progressed that little could WW be achieved in or around the barge without the use of certain quaint old barging phrases and sayings, although no harsh words were ever directed at the barge herself, she being almost sacred amo. ng vessels, Such was the rate of progress that we had time to start cooking breakfast off Northey Island and to be washing it down with a cup of tea whilst passing otansgate. At last the tide turned at Bradwell and it started to rain, and wc anchored to catch up on some sleep. The wind freshened in the afternoon and at 4pm. we hoisted sail and- raised anchor. The barge set off towards Mersea at a grand space, A few of us climbed into the barge's dinghy and-spent some time ‘circling the barge taking photos as she. sailed. She looked splendid under sail, close-hauled, and I took some fine colour slides. That ni ght “found us anchored off Brightlingsea in company. with: Dawn, Walter Cook's other charter barge. . Next morning we left Brightlingsea at 9.30am. and headed down the Colne for the Spitway. There was a fresh easterly breeze blowing and ‘Marjorie. ploughed her way out of the Blackwater -estuary. Heavy rain and rough water made navigation difficult and it was a comfort that at least the crew appeared .to -know-the way. The seas in the Spitway were quite rough.and confused andthe old barge creaked and. groaned .eclow decks. I4 was the: first time I.have ever made tea when the cups wouldn! t.. stay where I-put them. Our’ cruiser colleages.-aré,no- doubt, used.to this.We hadito.go.about twice in the: ininiiins ‘to clear the “/ continued.

“11-. the Buxey sands, this was8 quite:as memorable. experience in the cond- .Swin' into the ‘Thames, crossed over to the Medway channel:and anchored [op Gillingham 63 hours after -leaving a Ceortainly @ «3 journey: for a dinghy sailor. to remember. Wednesday we spent anchored at Gillingham where we weent ashore for a few hours in the morning, and:went up to Hoo Marina in the dinghy jin the.afternoon. As the tide was to turn about 6pm. it was” decided to move down river to Stansgate Creek (near Shcerness) ae evening. . we had a.fine sail, tacking down the Medway with the tide in our favour. We were eraced with a fiery sunset, and the lights from the ‘navigation buoys and tankers at the refineries made a colourful picture. It was quite dark whem we anchored in the entrance to Stansgate Creek but by now I knew my. way around the deck well cnough to avoid tripping over the umpteen bits and pieces that are oe i make ra barge gow eee were cae Hs ete me eee tere ee ome mF He Next — Chumeden, was our last= and we had to be at Southend . Pier by“the afternoon to change’-places with the next charter party: Marjorie was to Stay in the Thames as she was to sail in the Surbhend Barge Match the following weekend, Thursday morning we up-anchored (a back breaking bu siness, by far the worst job on the barge).,.‘and oo headed back into the Thames. Once clear of the Medway I got my ¢hance 4 to take the wheel under the guidance of a watchful barge skipper. This indeed was sailing in grand style as we tacked our way down river just off the Kent coast. The sea was choppy and the “breeze fresh, and the wheel kicked like a mule. I soon found it was better to le 4 her have’ her own way” whem‘she kicked making alterations in| between times. I continually cast anxious glances from the bob th the sails, ever conscious of the gaze of the crew. Putting the barge about was certainly different to tacking my GP 14, but the principle appeared to: be much the’ same. A Héarty "Leé-Oh' to warn the crew tending the foresail bowline, then helm hard down and around she goes. The foresail is backed by means of a bowline which pushes the- barge S bows cleanly through the wind. Once on the new tack the bowline is | let go and the foresail whips across the horse and away she goes. .~ 411 good things must come to an end and the barge was handed back to her crew and course set for Southend Pier via the South Shoebury - buoy and the Essex coast. The holiday was. over when the. barge. dinghy landed us on Southend Pier with all our gear, 4 days and 60 colour- ~ slides after leaving Maldon. ‘ If my tale has whetted anybody ' S appetite and tempted them to ~~ organise ‘a charter party, I would ‘itdke the following suggestions, one is to book early as chartcring is very popular and the second is to be sure of your party and see the colour of their money before you commit yourself. In the early summer of 1973, an increasing diserchantment with dinghy racing '( perhaps not unconnected with a conspicuous lack of success Since 1972 ), together with crew problems, led me to consider wider sailing excursions in my GP 14, Lady Clare, What follows has, I hope, sufficient of the characteristics of a log- to qualify it as a Mamgu Trophy entry,. but it is priorarily a pie of-ce’ personal writing. ° The choice of crew presented a problem. Nik and I have in the .. past made several successful short sailing/camping trips, the most recent having been in 1971, when we. visited Burnham and Foulness island.But this year he was not available. The only other person ~With whom I have achieved that instinctive, intuitive, rapport in the boat which is essential was also not available, so I concluded that this trip would have to be single handed. . The planned trip was.a five-day north easterly excursion up the issex coast. The first and last nights would be spent, sleeping in the boat in the general vicinity of Colne Point, and the other two farther North at pre-arranged accomodation ashore. The planned times of departure, -passing and arrival, taking into account tidal flows were set down on paper in terms of High water rather than clock times in order to allow(prophetically, oe it turned out) for slippage of dates. Each day's sheet of paper also had a column in which I was to log the actual times. That column : remains blank to this day- and the paper looks as though it had seen more sea water. than ink.. By converting the HWD based times to clock and calendar times, | I found that.the only suitable dates when I could be free, were : between the 6th and the 10th of August, and in mid-July I committed myself by giving to a somewhat incredulus wife and family a statement of my intention and to the Almighty a fervent prayer for good weather, : Because of the planned overnight stays in the boat, a sleeping bag, the boat cover, rudimentary cooking gear and two thermos flasks were to be taken. Food would include milk, coffee, sugar; soup, orange juice, biscuits, cheese, nuts and dried fruit. Each morning the flasks would be charged one with coffee, and the other with soup for consumption at the-end of the day. Midday food would be contained in a plastic airtight box and consist of biscuits, cheese, nuts and fruit. Brandy would also be. taken. »% : I planned to take. extra sailinggear, including. the small | headsail, a second anchor,.all the spare line I could find,’a small compassand my knife/marlin.spike which doubles as an identity disc. The latter two items were worn around my neck. I borrowed Clare's - M.W. transistpgr radio and took alist of BBC M.W. weather forecast (23.45 Radio is best I also purchased ). a red hand flare. (Use when aireraft or vessel is sighted). It remains unused. I did not take the spinnaker..I wore my wet suit and bouyancy jacket all-the sailing time. INTRODUCTION This account.is constructed from the day-to-day working log of SUZANNE-MARIE, our Drascombe Lugger, and covers our holiday cruise from, 16th. June to 29th. June 1973. The aims of the cruise were to explore the Kent coast from the Downs to the Medway, and if circumstances permitted, to pop across the channel to Calais. The fact that these aims were not quite fully realised did not detract from a very enjoyable and successful cruise -.not the least because we actually. had some sun this year! SATURDAY 16th. June. The Sailing Club Open Day - also the first day of our holidays! & fine morning gave promise to a successful Open Day, which indeed it was. We dutifully did our bit by taking prospective members for a spin in SUZANNE-MARIE but by 1630 we could dally no longer, and md slipped off downstream with a salty beat into the fresh easterly .. : breeze. Our first night destination was only Tollesbury Fleet, so it-was not long before the Nass was rounded and we were running up to the Leavings, where we brought up at 1815.We were glad to get our tent strung up between the two masts, as the breeze and the thickening haze had made it decidedly chilly for the last hour-or- so, SO we settled down to-our first night of the cruise - always, I think, the most exciting whilst still getting accustomed to the motion of the boat again, and with the prospact of the holiday before you. And especially as tomorrow we were hoping th make the long haul down to Ramsgate, Als SUNDAY 17th. JUNE. Up at 0500 to be greeted by the first accident of the holidays — I had slept on my spectacles and broken one of the arms!. Luckily. I had actually thought to bring a spare pair with me- a thing I usually forget. ~ The day promised fair again, although the wind had veered SW overnight, and a lot of altocumulus cloud was in evidence. We set off at 0620 ghosting down Tollesbury Fleet whilst receiving a reassuring shipping forecast -—- S, F3-4, veering W.. Round the Nass we had a fresh sail in a strengthened breeze for a while,- until it dropped right off again. To maintain our schedule we had to start the motorw to take us over the young flood to the Spitway,, from whence we continued under sail again. At 1020 we rounded the Barrow Beacon and set off in the gentle SW breeze to crab across the channels and shoals that radiate out from the Thames. The sea was mori the sun was warm, not another boat in sight and life was good ‘Inspite ofa developing haze pilotage was easy - a matter of-- buoy hopping, allowing for tidal drift by keeping two buoys in transit. However, as we were crossing the Black Deep, life became not so good! The wind had been falling steadily so we resorted to the motor again, but before -long it coughed and spluttered to a halt. Whilst I was effecting temporary repairs to a spark plug connector, a tanker loomed out of the haze towards us and caused us to heave ‘to and have lunch while it passed. All the time the cloud cover had been increasing, trapping a sultry atmosphere under it, vessel ele

Mean: and in particular the blackness amassing in the Kent direction made us somewhat apprehensime. However, the motor working again, we. set . off to enter. the 5, Edinburgh Channel. Suddenly, we..found ourselves. wallowing in’a wave system of outrageous proportions! We were in .fact cutting across some shoals to beat the last of the flood tide, and had not realised that the tide at this point Flooded at least an hour or two after HW. Also, the channel do_hg a neat righi angle bend herc, the tide tends to take a short cut over the shallows, causing these alarming overfalls. We battled through with no mishaps, but were glad the @ngine ‘did not falter again! Sagar The tide was against us all the way down the S. Edinburgh, but once out of it the -going was easier, although the motor remained on: until the N. Foreland was close to. It was still overcast and sultry, but sufficient breeze piped up at this point to get. sailing again. The peace and quiet was most appreciated after hours of motoring. The last stretch was a pleasant close reach along the coast and _ at 1730 we motored through Ramsgate. harbour entrance witha feeling Sof achievement that ~is only possible with a small open boat, and were directed alongside an old fishing boat in. the outer harbour. After setting our clearance and paying our dues, we celebrated the successful voyage with a slap up meal ashore and a stroll.along the prom, in the evening sun, ( the clouds having cleared again!),. MONDAY 18th, JUNE. Our first night in Ramsgate was not a success! Our little SUZANNE- MARIE was being smashed up against the rusty old fishing boat . (alias salvage vessel, “I believe) by the swell in the harbour; there seemed to be a party on a nearby yacht; and then the lifeboat maroon went off right over our heads. This all resulted in us seeking refuge in the inner harbour at 0030m when the gate was open for HW; Here ~’ we did eventually get to sleep,in spite of the trucks trundling along the quays loading cargo at all hours of the night. The day was a lazy affair, although I got to know Ramsgate quite well whilst searching around for a replacement part for_the outboard motor. It was ideal holiday weather - indeed so hot that sue actually succeeded in dragging me in for a swim! Ramsgate is lucky in having a good beach so close to the harbour.© TUESDAY 19th, JUNE.’ Having gone’ to bed early the evening before, our plan was to _ : lock out on the midnight tide in readiness for the cross channel trip during the day. However, an 0030 shipping forecast of S, F5-6 was enough in our heavy-eyed state to persuade ourselves to stay where’we were, : So another day was ‘spent ashore, mainly in shopping and a stroll nlong the cliff top into Pegwoll Bay. Tho day. was, fine, again and the F5-6 never materialised, so we were somewhat kicking ourselves :for not locking out. In the late afternoon it ‘startad becoming overcast — and cooler, but we still went to bed early again with the hope of locking out in the night. WEDNESDAY 20th. JUNE. All thoughts of locking out were quickly dispelled bya crack of thunder at 0020. The wind was a good F6é now, even in the inner harbour, ond the rain was bucketing down. On top of this, the forecast was gloomy again, so back to sleep! . a continued/ i

-l10— The rain‘had eased off in the morning, ‘and. the wind.with it. We were beginning ‘to get “fed up with Ramsgate by,.noOw, and were. : determined to lock-out with the edrly afternoon tide. Besides, the continual noise around the harbour, SUZANNE-MARIE was slowly. being buried under a layer of Russian peat moss dust froma recent cargo‘stacked close by. on the quay. So at.1350 we vuttered: out. . behind a ‘continental coaster loaded with Fordson tractors (it | seems we do export something! i and set off for Sandwich as it was too late to think of ¢hannel crossings in our. little boat today. After negotiating the rather alarming swell at’‘the harbour entrance, we notor-sailed against a light headwind,.wanting.to negotiate tho | shallow unknown River’ Stour before the tide fell too far. Whilst changing a fouled up’ sparking’ plug (the bane of my, life!) misfortune struck again and took the spark plug spanner down ‘to. the sea bed. with it! After that the engine had to run with the clean spark plug screwed in only hand tight. | After’ one. small argument. with a sandbank -‘at the entrance, we headed. upstream to- discover a very attractive and unspoilt river..When we- : reached it at 1600; we thought the. same’of Sandwich too, excgpt for yt ~) the burden-of heavy through » traffic that quaint little town Ss Ones: A quick rush around the town rgulted in another plug spanner, of which of course, could not be made to fit the intricate recesses of our outboard notor.: Attempted modification with a broken _ hacksaw; blade brought no improvement so we resigned ourselves to*angther =" idle day whilst. A: visit. to a nearby - ‘engineering works resulted in even more drastic modification of the spanner’= all to no effect, but! the final ‘successful solution was to attack the’ engine covering.Sages pi ewite eRe BREST to drop neatly into its: slot. : : The rest of the day was spent in exploring Sandwich and its environs, although we wero hindered by a thick hazy nist: which ‘otonk= eted the soft country scenery. We would probably have run, into fog trouble at sea anyway ; if we had attempted our ‘channel »crossing today, FRIDAY gona. JUNE. tie asia bs Pelle pay beh er Up at 0500 to attenpt ‘our belated crossing, sities Bes ar aia after a favourable forecast, except Oy poor 9 Ee We motored downstream into. the wind, enjoying:“thio fine et to the morning. However ,approaching. Pegwell Bay, .we- ‘could, see fog... banks rolling in lazily from the sea, and what with a Crewing halo round the sun, we regrctfubly turned back ‘and gave ‘Up ali: ideas. of crossing the channel. 3 The northerly vreeze gave us a fair wind to help-punch against” the tide up the Stour again. The tide runs strongly in the. Stour, and at Sandwich ebbs: for nine hours out of every twolvel The river twists like a demented snake ‘and ‘is véry. shallow in placés,. but we. managed to sail nearly ‘all the way back to Sandwich, only using the gngine on 2. couple of unfayourabie reaches,

ee 1 We were back at Sandwich by lunchtime, and after a quick shopping spree we.set off to explore the upper reaches of the Stour. This neant lowering the masts to go undér the occasional bridge, but after. one long reach where the river doubles back on itself almost to the mouth again, we raised the mainnmast, stopped the engine, and proceeded to sail the rest of the way up the Stour. The sky had cleared. again .. but the wind had increased steadily during the day, and as we sailed inland, strong gusts would hit us and send us. creaming along at an exhilarating pace .between the narrow banks. We were now sailing from an 0.5. map instead of a chart, and were glad to know when to expect bridges so that we could drop the mast in tine! Wg sailed through lush rural countryside, raising a few angling eyebrows, then the Kent coalfield, and then a reservoir! Above the 1 reservoir the river: becane progressively choked with water Jilies and barely three miles from Canterbury we came to a cloggy Halt, and. returned back to Groveferry, a pretty little spot with riverside- er and a pub. We drew up by. the river bank and retired to. the pub for refreshment, only.to. be disturbed by the water bailiff who... vanted us to move SUZANNE<M;RIE. It would seem that we'd moored up .t the prize angLing spot of his stretch of the river! | Pais SATURDAY 23rd.. JUNE. This was the second black night of the holliday! The Stour would appear to be above dll an angling river, and.an:all night fishing party insisted on getting as close as possible to us, dnd despite entreaties, kept a shouting conversation going all night. I thought nglers wero searchers’ of “peace and solitude.too! We had intended to spend another. night at Groveferry, > but.it was-first necessary to find a quieter mooring. An alternative berth suggested by the bailiff casually ‘remarked that he was expecting ten coach loads on the 3 following day. This was all too much for us, so we quickly set off and motored back downstream to Sandwich.for the night. WUNDAY 24th, JUNE. a We were beginning to yearn for the open sea again, and fortune smiled on us with a clear sky but little wind. We set off from sandwich, motoring downstream against the last of the flood, but on ° ~~ rcaching Pegwell Bay we hoisted the sails and beat our way up the coast past Ramsgate. There was some swell from yesterdays strong winds, but todays wind was light and when the tide turned we had to resort to the: moter to push us round the N. Foreland. 2 COMMODORES NOTE .~» Membership renewals have been coming in at a gratifyinz rate, and our foolish fears that the general alarm and despondancy . would extend to sailing appear to be groundless, thank goodness. Neverthe less, we are anxious to increase our ordinary membership, so do encourage your friends in the company to join us, even if they haven't a boat. Many of you are aware of the enthusiasm and hard work that Bruce Long has put into building and encouraging thé.development of the 18° Sydney Barbour Skiffs. However, you may not be aware that these boats are maintained in part by sponsorship, which involves advertising brand names on the sails. Bruce has applied for his boat to sail from the club, as an M.8.C. registered boat, but our club rule 24 states, 'Members shall not display gross forms of advertising at the club, or on or about boats registered with the club." Furthermors, the R.Y.4. have a similar rule, and we ave affiliated to the R.Y.A. We are informed by the Skiff Class that 7 the R.Y.a. are considering a change in their rules rezarding sponsorship. Your committee have made the following decision. Bruce ~ will be allowed to sail his boat from Stansgate for this season, without prejudice to future action. We will have to arrange an Extraordinary General Meeting (or at the 4.G.i.) to consider the clubs feeling regarding our own rule, and take action accordingly. Our action may be influenced by the R.Y.A. decision. No doubt there will be plenty of discussions on this point during the season, but most of us felt our decision the best compromise in the circurstances. DENNIS BYATS. SOCIs4L SCREED. 36 SPRING BANK HOLIDAY REGATTA 25 -27th May I974. Last year our Annual Spring Bank Holiday Regatta attracted a record entry of 200 boats from 34 clubs. If we are again lucky enough to have fine weather, the entry this year could be even higher. Throughout the year many of our members visit other clubs when cruising, compet¢ing in dinghy open events or perhaps when on holiday. Invariébly they are made extremely welcome and offered all the facilities of the club. Our club differs from many others in that we do not hold a series of Open Meetings throughout the year. The Regatta therefore is the one occasion in the year when we can repay that hospitality by sharing our facilities with visiting yachtsmen and also give those of our dinghy fleets who do not travel, the chance to sail in a large competative event. \For those who do not sail dinghies there is an oppotunity to view the spectacle of 200 sails across the water and join in the social scene. Whilst an event of this size does involve us in a lot of work, it only becomes a burden if it is left to a few ‘'regulars'. MANY HANDS MAKE LIGHT WORK! !!!!- if every member were to give one hour of their time everybody could participate and enjoy the weekend to the full. Please offer your services to any committee member or complete the attached tear-off slip and send it to me. Help is particularly needed at the pre-regatta working party and with Bar, Galley, Race Box/Spotting, Results and Reception duties over the weekend.
