6. SOUTH SEA SAGA Members of casti— Rick Anstey, Bill Baker, Roy Battye, Vic Braybrook, Dave Harper, Vic Tate and Keith Taylor. The Master Plan It was towards the end of the evening of the last Laying-Up Supper that the Mirrormen in a fit of misguided inspiration, decided that a cruise around the Isle of Wight would be a good starter for the 1975 season. Little more was said until early 1975 when things gradually hardened up into a climax in the planning of these affairs with a meeting under Rick's roof in January. Kathy did her little piece for the evening with a supply of ham sandwiches, and the rest of us did our little piece with a shower of compliments and a nice excess of cans of beer. What with the large quantities of sandwiches eaten and the even larger quantities of canned beer consumed, there was a very noticeable deterioration in the quality of the atmosphere as the evening wore on —- and this was without our Rear Commodore present, who later on during the cruise was to give us an overpowering demonstration in this area. Dave produced an excellent agenda for the meeting and this covered a number of subjects such as :- "The need for rubber boots " "What do we do when we get there?" "Colour of bow tie to match dinner jacket" and a number of other similar mind bending questions. The date was set for the cruise, the idea being to start from Lymington, round the I.0.W. to Cowes to collect the milk, then Cowes to Poole, and Poole back to Lymington - a distance of about 100,000 fathoms as the crow flies. The real business of the evening was enacted fairly swiftly when Bill was downing a Scotch, after which he found that he'd been unanimously elected skipper by a majority of 14 votes. We appreciated what an inspired choice we'd made when bill, realising what had happened, desperately called for a double and pulled out a new copy of the Great Midland Canel Guide to Seamanship. Seriously though, Bill was an obvious choice since Gloria, his wife, had magnificently volunteered to do the provisions and we thought that electing him skipper was the least we could do in appreciation. A cook was the other outstanding posts the call for a volunteer produced a deathly hush (e log o) broken only by the faint sound of gastric disturbances (perhaps in antici- pation). Someone plucked up courage and commented on how well Keith was handling his ham sandwich, whereupon Keith, no doubt trying to divert everyone's attention, volunteered for the job. It was fairly late when we emerged into the fresh air, and I can only blame it on the shock of this truamatic experience for not seeing the skip. It says something for British workmanship, because following the collision and picking myself up from the back seat (yes, reversing at the time), I examined the skip (made in Hong Kong) and did not find a dent in it anywhere. The Departure -— Friday March 14th When Dave, Keith and Vic T. arrived to pick me up, the cocks had barely fallen off their perches, in fact I reckon they were only just thinking of getting up. Bill and Vic B. were travelling together from Brentwood, and Rick was travelling on his own by way of Liverpool, but that's another story. My bags were packed and ready so it was a simple matter for all four of us, combined weight 50 stone, acting with split second timing to force them into the boot of the Volvo, and then we were away from Galleywood on time at 06.40 and by 09.00 were on the M3 with the first stop Fleet for breakfast. Approaching Fleet the call of nature began to get stronger and then to dominate our thoughts despite the need to concentrate on locating speed traps, which were reliably rumoured to be operating in the area, before they located us. On arrival there was unanimous expressions of great relief, followed by fried breakfast where we enjoyed the fascinating sight of Vic obviously a man of great compassion for animals and birds, stroking the sausage, bacon and ese with his beard before eating them.

Te Off again and all was well until Dave casually remarked that we were nearly out of petrol (on the M3.) and asked us to look for a filling station that: accepted Access Cards, sold 5 star Martell, gave 10 fold Green Shield stamps and a free car wash, otherwise he wasn't interested in stopping. This slightly concerned the rest of us, since we would have to push, and there was only a fair chance of finding such a station before running dry. However, as you might guess, he compromised when we got down to the last drop and had to get a refill. As we were leaving, I noticed that Keith wasn't with us, someone said “Look, he's at it already" and sure enough there was Keith sprinting down the road after a girl in a car, and succeeded in catching and stopping her. When he came back he mumbled something about her not paying, which rather surprised us since it is usually the other way round. However, it turned out he meant for the petrol. It was near 10.30 when we approached Lymington feeling slightly peckish and looking forward to "opening time”. The Arrival We ran into Bill and Vic B just coming out of the Lymington Yacht Marina. They had established that the boat,a Rival 34 was being prepared and would be handed over at 13.00. J ‘ince the pubs opened at 11.00 that gave us half an hour to run up to the off-licence, complete the provisioning and rejoin the others at the pub next to Peter Webster's boat yard. Quantities are always a protlem to decide on but we devised a simple formula to deter- mine the quantity of booze to take on board, this being proportional to the reciprocal of the ambient temperature. Some might remember that weekend was exceedingly cold. By 11.00 we were on the steps of the pub just as the doors were opened. The beer was good, the company also, and by 13.00 nothing was too daunting, so we departed for the Marina and the boat, with Bill's words ringing in our ears — walk steadily and don't let him see the booze. "Suge" was a lovely boat, and it did not take long to load the provisions albeit with bottles of gin etc. tucked out of sight in Wellington boots or well wrapped up in coats. Friday 14th March - Time -— 24 hours after opening. With the good ship "Euge" vittled and made ready for sea, the high spirited crew ( beer and gin soaked) cautiously motored out of Lymington Marina - when there, right before our very eyes, it was upon us - an enormous ‘erection' rising out of the mud bank "hard on' our port bow. The notice on top stated that this was "HARPHRS POST", Once we were clear of the river and out in the cold breezy Solent sails were hoisted, main and large reaching genoa - course was set for Egypt point, Cowes, Isle of Wright. Two and a half bottles of Booth's later, we thrashed into the Medina River under full canvas. The Southampton Ferry was just leaving the Pier, so about we must go — but NO we missed stays and had to beat again towards the shore and pier. A quick decision was made that Cowes was not large enough for us, 80 we ran for the vast open waters of the Solent, once again to feel the full effects of the northerly 3-4. Two nameless crew got their heads down, effects of cold, gin and mal—de-mer; the motion,alcohol and foul wind were different on & Rival 34 than on a Mirror. The pangs of hunger and thirst overcame, so into my tumbler of Booths, large hunks of bread were dunked. Our more refined crew members settled their empty stomachs on digestive biscuits and cake. All this time "Euge" romped along towards the safety of her own berth. What a wonderful experience she was having with her all male crew — No —- she was not satisfied and scraped her bottom on the ground just off the entrance to the Lymington river.The purpose of our return was to collect Rick, our seventh crew member. Sails were lowered just in time. Yarmouth 1.0.W. Lymington ferry was ploughing down the narrow channel bottom of the spring tide, we missed it by 5'3". As will be seen by an inside photograph, Dave holding the wire says, it pays to advertise. The next event was an excellent fish and chips tea in a local shop; the Mirror section providing the entertainment for the take-away customers.. A visit wasthen made to an historic public house before we proceeded back to the pub next to Peter Webster's boat yard to meet up with Rick at 8.30pm. 10.40pm. closing bell —- no Rick - so we decided to return to "EKuge" for supper.

8. Sleeping bags were prepared but the blankets were found to be soaking wet. Vic gave his usual assurance ~ "No problem boys, it will be just like a water bed". Eventually we all managed to get to sleep. However, we were woken fairly early by Keith and Roy snoring, and the beads of condensation falling upon us from the coach roof. Saturday 15th Maroh It was a beautiful morning, Keith prepared a first class breakfast and David and Vic'T made for a telephone to try and establish the whereabouts of the elusive Rick. (To cut a long story short, we found that he had stayed the night in Andover with a fun seeking auntie and would meet us at Poole later that day). Still no Rick. Note on Volvo for Rick. Plan course on chart table -— Wind force 2 to 3, forecast 5 to 6, high water unknown. Off we go. Hoisted the geneoa and main and impressively overtook large craft which later turned out to be anchored. Castle Point. The Needles. Quite thrilled with previous prediction of E.T.A. at the Needles Sea buoy, only 5 mins. error i.e. less than 3%. Broad reach to Poole. Arrival at Poole 3.26pm. and lunch. (Dinner jackets not worn on this occasion). Sedate evening in Poole We met up with Rick at Poole harbour just after "Euge" had flown in. God, were we cold. So cold in fact, that Vic Tate's beard was growing inwards and Vic Braybrook's face was moulting. So the scene was set for a further 1+ 'daze' of sailing, sampling and sleeping, ( at times some of the crew were doing all three at once). Before we go any further, it must be emphasised that the idea of the trip was solely for the purpose of furthering our ability to handle a boat - what a ridiculous idea. Keith volunteered to be cook and immediately set about preparing a meal in rather cramped surroundings.Watching Keith handle a spatula, one is reminded of Adrian Boult suffering from St. Vitus Dance in the middle of "Pomp and Glory". Keith proudly announced the meal was ready. Vic said he didn't feel well. Roy asked if there was a hamburger stall nearby. Bill pretended to be asleep and Dave had since been told by the Nurse that he can come out next week. Vic Braybrook and myself heaved our share over the side and next morning we hauled out 20 stone of dead fish. Seriously though, Keith provided excellent food and we're looking forward to his first book on the subject. The next procedure was to prepare for the evening's activities. First task was a shave, followed by a shower and shampoo followed by a liberal dose of nut dust. The only effect it had was to get us thrown out of the first two pubs before we even got the rounds in. The target for the evening was the "Harbour Heights" - a rather refined dinner danc establishment, but we missed the target. Well it's only natural we should grace such a place with our presence. We were shortly to find that our intentions would not be fulfilled. Things started normally, pints in quick succession and clarity of speech rapidly deteriorating. Rick boldly ventured to ask a lady to dance and after three attempts decided to give up.The lady was heard th mutter "I wish these damn foreigners would learn to speak English before they come over here". The grandiose meal we intended in fact turned out to be - what else. Fish and chips served by a friend from Pakistan in the current edition of the "Morning Star". Rick was disturbed to find that this establishment, renowned worldwide for the rubbish it sells, refused his out of date Diners Card. End of Part 1.

EDITORIAL At last all the "Official business" is over and the committee can stop twitching and get down to the real thing - sailing. Even the weather is with us and the weekend produced two of the best sailing days I have ever known, and on Sunday, our Commodore was seen to brush the cobwebs off his Enterprise and sail away into the sunshine. The good weather also brought out the trippers and our gate lock proved a very effective deterrent against strangers bringing their cars into the club grounds. A couple of reminders, can members keep the grass around their boats in the dinghy park and on the sea wall cut fairly short, a few appear to be sailing in the Sargassa Sea. When a collision occurs between dinghy and cruiser, the incident should be reported to the 0.0.D. If there is no 0.0.D. on duty then a short entry in the log and please, contact the cruiser owner, who would like to know if his boat is in any danger of sinking. I speak from experience for Snowgoose has a hole in her bow, just on the waterline, probably wused during Regatta, but only discovered when I retrieved some rusty baked bean tins ~om the bilges. . We hope to move the old life boat, kindly donated by Joe Daff from the bottom of the dinghy park to the climbing tree for the children and make this into a children's play area. There is also an old packing crate that will make a super Wendy House and Robbie Sims has generously given a climbing frame and a swing. Any father willing to give an hour of his time helping to build the children's play area, please contact me. Brenda Tate. Cover photograph:- Arthur and Stephen Hodges with "Red and Reckless". Inside cover:- left right Julian Bigden preparing to take out "All ashore that's going ashore" Chris Cooper's new Laser, Mike Turner being the perfect gentleman.

2 COMMODORES NOTES In the last month two major events have ocoured in the activities of the Club. The first being the formal opening on May 17th, in our 25th year, of the New Cluhouse by Sir Eric Eastwood, which proved to be a very successful evening and was enjoyed by all who attended. The guests included representatives of the Company, the M.A.S.C. and various other bodies who have been instrumental in helping us build our new home. Commodores of the other Clubs on the river and neighbours were also present and guests were received by members of the Committee and Club. The formal ceremony of unveiling the plaque commemorating the event was undertaken by our President, who during the proceedings provided some interesting background on the early days of the club. Commemoration plaques were presented to Mr Ron Rider of the Building and Facilities Group and Mike Taylor, who built the club, as a mark of our appreciation of the services given and we are very grateful to our President for performing these ceremonies. The formal part of the evening was concluded by Vice President Eric Payne recalling some of the amusing incidents in the early days of the club. I would also like to express our thanks to Margaret Cottam and Clare Urry and their helpers, who prepared the refreshments for the evening, also to Alf Cottam who organised the magnificent floral displays for the Clubhouse, which were done by a Steeple village resident. The second major event was the Spring Bank Holiday Regatta which was once again a weekend of which the Club can be proud. Despite the strong North winds, the weather held fine for the Sunday and Monday and exhilarating sailing was enjoyed by visitors and members alike. I would like to express my appreciation for the help given by members both during the weekend and at the Wednesday working party before the event, when lots of members turned out to prepare for the weekend. Much help was also given by those who stayed on after the weekend to clear up, and I am pleased to say that as well as clearing up after the Regatta, the old clubhouse and sheds were cleared ready for demolition and the grass on the sea wall was reduced to a manageable length. In the next month or so there are three more annual activities which are always popular with members and guests. Open Day on June 22nd has this year been moved to a Sunday, to make it an event which will provide an opportunity for both non-sailing members and guests to get trips in boats of their choice. We shall, of course, need lots of boat owning members there to provide help and rides in boats. The weekend of June 28th and 29th brings the annual visit from our sailing colleagues at Rochester when once again we expect about five cruisers to come round from the Medway and eight dinghies to be brought overland for the traditional races on Saturday. This visit is looked forward to by our visitors and usually provides a very enjoyable weekend. The third event is the annual Barbecue on July 12th when, as usual, help will be required to set up on both the Friday evening and Saturday and for clearing up on the Sunday morning. In order to make this event as enjoyable as possible for members, the Committee have decided that camping will be allowed on the site for the Saturday evening and it is hoped that those who do camp will give as much help as possible with the preparation and clearing up. John Witter, Commodore. SOCIAL SCREED Another successful regatta behind us, and again the weather was friendly but cool, and with the high winds on Monday the rescue services were fully stretched Although the marquee was 20 ft. longer this year, it was still crowded for the disco on Saturday night, where Exodus did a splendid job with the music, and then Sunday saw the clubhouse turned into a cinema which was well attended. Open Day is in 3 weeks time ( June 22nd) which this year is a Sunday. Boats will be exhibited, there will be boat rides, demonstrations etc., let's hope our visitors find it @ lively day. The Barbecue is to be held on Saturday July 12th at Stansgate, on the hard, from 8pm to midnight, with disco. There should be no shortage of wood for the bonfire since clearing out the old boathouse, and of course there will be a supply of charcoal cooked food. Hope to see you swimming in the Blackwater at midnight. Roy Battye, Social Secretary. 'D' Bldg. Basildon. Int. 460 or Chelmsford [redacted]. - SAILING AT THE REGATTA The sailing this year was fantastic. The wind strength varied from force 2 - 5 or was it higher? It certainly seemed so, particularly in the last race when wind against tide produced those terrible waves in the 'narrows'. Although there were many capsizes and some boats were damaged, the Rescue Facilities coped magnificently. Without the splendid and generous assistance we received from our neighbouring clubs with rescue crews and craft, we would probably have been forced to curtail racing on the final day. A full set of sailing results are included elsewhere in this issue, and as you will see the Marconi participants ( 41 in all ) did particularly well, winning or placing well in the Mirror, Enterprise Hornet, Fast and Slow Handicap Classes. The entries were again over the 200 mark — some from as far afield as Wales and Hampshire. The Pennant Races, in aid of the R.N.L.I. appeal, were also well supported (83 entries) and we shall be able to send £35 to the Institution. Reception and Race Organisation worked successfully once again, due largely to our wives - 'Bless them' and to Robbie Sims, our stalwet R.O. On behalf of all the competitors, "Thank you for a terrific weekend". Ron Greygoose, Regatta Secretary. CADET NEWS The second Cadet Race held on Sunday June 8th produced 6 starters and Stephen Perkins crewed by Malcolm Hutchins their first win, with Colin Harper crewed by Simon Durrant second place. Timothy Foreman decided he'd give Angela, his crew, capsize drill just before the start and dampened his ardour somewhat. Nigel Metheringham is another cadet whose recently experienced the egstatic joy of a wetting when crewing for the Cadet Captain. I had planned to introduce capsize procedure later in the year but as is evident, we tend to rush things somewhat. It's very encouraging to see the number of Cadets who regularly crew in the points races and further crews are required on a regular basis. Any Cadet willing to crew, please contact me. The next tuition will be Saturday June 14th and we expect nearly 30 cadets to turn up. We will split up into 3 groups of advanced Cadets, those who know the basics and a group for beginners, together with cadets crewing on the rescue boat. Rick Anstey, Cadet Captain.

4. SOUTH SEA SAGA —- Part 2 Sunday March 16th. We woke up to a nice, bright morning, but it was still fresh - the seagulls were shrieking at an even higher pitch. We had to make an early start in an attempt to beat the tide turning at the narrows between the Isle of Wight and the mainland. Also to beat the Harbour Master collecting the mooring fees. Mood on board a bit subdued. Was it because it was the last day, or because Rick was at last on board? More likely the after affects of the beverage taken the previous evening. Had breakfast and left moorings about 09.00 hours, motoring out of Poole Harbour in the deep channel. We gave friendly waves to the natives on the chain ferry and received waves back with clenched fists ( were they the taxi drivers we had blessed with our patronage?) It was to be a beat back to Lymington in a steady force 4-5 N.N.E. wind. Offshore there was quite a chop, which was quite exhilarating, the bow digging in and sending spray over our heads to land on two of the most "subdued" members of the crew ( sitting across the stern seat) who were couwmiserating with one another, swaying side to side in their brightly coloured sailing smocks, with greenish faces, they looked like "Bill and Ben" in a storm. Our skipper decided that we were carrying too much canvas because the gunwales were 2 ft. under and ordered two of the crew forward to reef the main. For the uninitiated, the roller reefing arrangement consisted of a handle on the front of the mast connected via a shaft and universal joint to the boom. This had to be turned in conjunction with the mainsail winch handle on the side of the mast, which lowered the sails. At the same time the other crew member had to feed the sail out of the mast sail track. This operation was likened to standing in a 45 inclined bath full of freezing water, under the shower, trying to rub one's tummy with one hand whilst patting one's head with the other hand. Naturally, wearing a life-line in case one slipped down the wastepipe. After all this exertion, and one of the crew nearly losing fingers in the winch, the crew collapsed into the cockpit, only to hear that the boat had developed bad lea helm and the reef had to be taken out again ( thank goodness we don't have that probelm on Mirrors.) A strange phenomenon had occurred to-day, unheard of in the history of the Mirror Fleet, when the words, "Who wants a drink" were uttered, there was not a single reply. As we approached the narrows, it was apparent we hadn't beaten the tide and had to revert to the engine to make headway. The swirling motion of the waters looked decidedly ominous during this part of the trip. Once the calmer waters of the Solent were reached, the remaining crumbs of food were devoured, together with "tea or coffee" creating strange menus such as "fried egg and cake", On entering the creek which lead to the marina sails were taken down. Heads were bowed in reverence as for the last time we passed "Harper's Post Having moored up, came the discharging of cargo and tidying up the boat. The latter carried out so well ( wives, please note) that the owner commented "Well, Bill, as Osea) it has been returned in an immaculate state". We also received our deposit back which, . truth were told, no-one expected to see again. The two cars having loaded, farewells were exchanged. Bill, having been responsible for six lunatics for the weekend, was in such a state of mental exhaustion, he had to be chauffeured to London whilst he had a sleep. To me, the most funniest "repeatable" happening of the weekend, was the sight of three "happy" crew members, about 1 o'clock in the morning, for the first time trying to convert the table into a bed - it took them approx. 30 minutes. It was a very enjoyable "long" weekend saga, and our thanks go to Bill and Gloria for arranging everything. LOST AT SBANSGATE: 151b Meon type anchor. CRUISER CHAT Russell Fuller has encountered some rather nasty old mooring gear on the sea bed around his Dauntless, With the increasing number of wooden boats in the club, it is an idea to check the sea bed around your mooring for odd bits of iron, concrete etc. Ray and Maureen Ball had an unforgettable first night aboard "Coppelia". They were awoken at 4.0am on a wild night to find that Mike Sisson's "Duet" had broken her mooring and was trying to make friends with the end of the groyne. As Coppelia was not afloat (she was launched the following morning) they dressed , got in their dinghy and amidst rain and thunder rowed out towing Duet and put her back on her mooring. A very commendable effort. On the same night, Ken Stevens and John Smith set out to deliver "Carasou" plus new owner to Ramsgate. Navigating by the illumination from the lightning flashes, they found their way out to the Wallet, Here Ken went below to answer the call of nature, and John for & mathematical exercise deduced that the rise and fall of persons in the vicinity of the Head was about 12'. The sea was abit steep and choppy and the shipping forecast was diabolical, So agreeing that discretion is the better part of valour they ran for Brightlingsea. Xen has now become the proud owner of a beautiful Sea King.

EDITORIAL You may notice that a few of our regular contributors to Navigans are missing from this issue, they are too busy sailing.. Our social events have been very successful. Open Day went well, although many visitors were disappointed at having toforego boat trips due to the strong winds. The following weekend the strong winds again diminshed the cruiser contingency from Marconi - Elliott, Rochester only one boat was able to come around from the Medway. However, eight \dinghies were trailed to Stansgate and a good day's racing was enjoyed by their crews, with a pleasant evening in the clubhouse at it's conclusion. The barbecue went extremely well despite the rather damp conditions and the midnight swimmers are ever increasing in numbers. It's sad to see the final going of the old clubhouse and with it a great many happy memories. We hope that it's new owners will enjoy it as much as we have, and our treasurer is grateful for their contribution to our club funds. A couple of reminders. The committee would like to remind parents of the dangers of small children swimming off the hard with lilo's. Apart from the risk of them being blown off shore, there is the additional hazard of not being seen by dinghies returning to the hard and being run over or knocked off the lilo into deep water. People trailing boats are warned that contact with overhead power cables is very quickly fatal and not recommended Apparently, a dozen people a year are killed this way and it is left to the sailing clubs to warn their members of the danger. So when trailing a boat keep the mast down low.. The pile of lost property in the clubhouse is mounting. Everyone must think we are all a very honest lot, the way things are left lying around; but the clubhouse secretary is thinking of sending a lorry load of goodies to Oxfam, so if you have lost anything please contact the 0.0.D. who will check if it has been picked up and stored away. Well I think that's the lot. One last item, a column in a New Zealand sailing nagazine must bring back memories of the Mirror Fleet I.0.W. cruise, it's title, - "You can't go about yet, I haven't finished my gin". Brenda Tate. 2. MIRROR FLEET NEWS Once again Mirrors from the Marconi Sailing Club were in winning form at the Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championships at Stone on Sunday 6th July. The weather was ideal for both sailors and spectators - sunny and breezy. The first three places were taken by :~- John Weedon (ist), Ray Hampson (2nd) and Roy Battye (3rd). Not forgotten, of course, their sons who crew so ably for them. There were 15 Mirrors entered - 9 of these were from the M.S.C. The fleet continues to increase in numbers, the last count was 61 boats, with another one or two in the building stage. Stan Oaker, Mirror Fleet Captain. HORNET HAPPENINGS Several changes have been taking place in the Hornet fleet over the past few weeks, with people and boats coming and going. Mike and Angie have now gone to America for a year, but we hope Paul will still be sailing their boat during that time. It has been good to see Geoff White sailing with Jennifer lately. Although, Geoff has sold his boat, I believe he is thinking of getting another. Alan Pratt has added another Hornet out racing and Murray Todd has brought Blackjacs: down again > After much hard work, Gary Constable and Steve Hepple have now completed their boat, Ethelred the Unready, and began sailing with it. John Weedon, Sailing Secretary. SAILING NOTES Handicaps When different classes of sailing dinghies and cruisers race against each other, most clubs use the R.Y.A. yardstick system of handicapping. All the popular classes have published handicaps which are reviewed annually, using information gathered from member clubs. On the Blackwater there is a committee which can recommend variations to the R.Y.A. figures for local events and currently the only changes are the Snipe and Squib at 99. The handicap numbers are proportional to the time an average boat of it's class would take to sail the course. Therefore, to work out the corrested time, one has to “divide the elapsed time for each boat by its handicap. The more usual method is to express this in seconds, taking at boat of 100 handicap as the scratch figure, this makes the calculation:— Corrected time = elapsed time in seconds x 100 handicap To avoid long calculations there are handicap tables available for working out the sums, the ones used by the club being "Langstone Tables". To use these, the elapsed time in hours and minutes which is checked against the handicap column giving the corrected time in seconds to which is added the odd elapsed seconds uncorrected. 4. CRUISER CHAT The cruiser fleet enjoyed a pleasant evening at the General's Arms the other week, when the general topic of conversation was the forthcoming cruise to Holland. We were pleased to hear that the South Knock Buoy is now lit although some of the light ships maybe out of service for their summer refit. Eric Youngs took Snodronning over in a comfortable 20hrs and will be returning the week before the main party leave on the 26th. weather permitting, of course. John Hooper had a sniff at the other side during the spring bank holiday reaching Calais, but had to leave Davolos 11 for a time in Ramsgate because of bad weather. Two other boats made more extended cruises during that holiday. Andy Dixon exploring the Crouch, and Jill and Peter taking Jestabel up the Thames as far as Tower Bridge. It's nice to see Sirius back in the club although what Terry would have to say about some of Bill Penkman's escapade's I dread to think. Cliff Clarke and his wife have sold Topaz and are now the owners of an Islander 23. Our cruiser captain has his boat based at Woodbridge at the moment where he says the week rates are very reasonable. We were pleased to hear that Dick Weaver's operation was successful and he is now on the road to recovery and we send all our best wishes and hope to see him back on the water soon.

EDITORIAL Well, by the time you read this I should be on my way home from cruising in Holland. We have managed a holiday issue of Navigan's, thanks to a kind offer of help from Mick Gray. "ric Youngs and his "Mirror" crew did very well in reaching Veere and then coming home via Calais, clearing Customs at Stansgate. “So we should have plenty of entries for the Mamgu Trophy this year. John Weedon had bought a new boat, a 420 named "Blackbird". It seems that the question of a new dinghy class is resolving it's self naturally. The club now has five 420's and several Mirror fleet members are considering buying one; following John's example and passing on their ldirror's to up and coming Cadet sons. Commodores Notes Last month a report from me failed to appear but as Brenda said sailing and other Club duties prevented me from meeting the printing schedules, I was not at the Club last weekend for the first time for several months and it seems I missed all the excitement including a visit from & whale who must have heard the glowing reports about Our new clubhouse and popped in like so many others to see for himself; I understand he did not ask for an application form. On Monday I received a telephone call from a Mr. Purnell thanking the Club for recovering his dinghy which had been left at anchor near Standsgate during the Old Gaffers Race and had drifted off. He was very appreciative of our part in helping him to recover it. I also learned of the problem experienced with the gate during the same weekend and although repairs are in hand it is probably worth mentioning that contributory factors leading to the premature failure of a small part could be that the gate becomes temporarily misaligned when people swing on it and it suffers severe shock when it slams shut under its own weight. Wie are looking at methods of strengthening the part that failed but in the meantime would you please discourage. people from swinging on it and try to avoid slamming it. We are now in the period of the Club's maximum use with the children on holiday and members using the facilities most days of the week. This puts an extra burden on our Caretaker, Claude Emerson, who does such magnificent work in keeping the place always looking so clean and tidy. He is finding it quite a handful compared with the old clubhouse and it would be much appreciated if members could tidy up as much as possible after them and help to keep the extra load to a minimun. Emptying ashtrays, and giving surfaces a Wipe down before leaving would make all the difference. I would also remind you that in the old Clubhouse we had a rule Stating that cooking of private meals in the Galley was not allowed and the same rule still applies to the new Clubhouse although there is no notice to this effect at present. At the recent BACSPA (Blackwater and Colne Sailing Protection Association) Annual General Meeting, the Chairman and Secretary retired and I am very pleased tell you that our nominees, Stan Allerton as Chairman and Frank Savill as Secretary/Treasurer, were successful in the election. As most of you know both have served the Marconi Sailing Club well for a number of years in the past and have held office during some of the most demanding years in the Club's history. I am sure BACSPA will benefit from their experience and continuing interest in the river 4s a whole, and I would like to thank them for accepting nomination and congratulate them on behalf of the Club on the outcome of the election. i am now about to depart on holiday as are most of the Committee and many members and I would like to wish you all a happy holiday whether it be sailing or just sitting in the sun, and I hope that this year the weather holds for the whole season and everyone gets their fair share of sun. Commodore. r.S. We are again being embarrassed by the amount of waste water being created at Stansgate. Earlier in the year we made an appeal for conservation as too much waste causes the cesspool to overflow. The trouble this time appears to be caused by excessive use of the showers particularly after swimming when it appears that several showers are taken by the same people during a day. If it is 4 rinse between swims that is required please use the hosepipe on the hard which does not drain back into the main drainage system. I think this plea particularly applies to child-en who do not appreciate the amount of water they are using and some parental guidance is required please.

3 Subscriptions 1976 At the last A.G.M, we were warned that a rise in subscriptions would be necessary this year, and since then the inflation rate has increased further. Excluding all capital costs associated with the new clubhouse, last years operating profit of £370 is expected to turn into a loss of around 1200 - a figure which would have been considerably worse if we had not had a substantial increase in both membership and boats. Unfortunately we cannot bank on such increases in the future, and inflation will undoubtedly increase our costs significantly during the coming year. We are now in a position of being responsible for substantial capital assits in the form of the clubhouse and rescue boats, and must expect substantial expenditure in future years if standards are to be maintained or improved, The clubhouse fitting out has cost nearly £3000, and to replace our two outboards would now cost over £600 (excluding the VAT which we reclaim). Even if we assume an optimistic average lifetime of 10 years for all these items, we snould be putting aside at least £400 in 1976 for their eventual replacement. Our payments to the MASC for 1976 and subsequent years have not been settled, and our cl-shouse running cost estimates are somewhat tentative since they are based only on the fi. .¢ two months of full use. Present indications are that next years fees should be around £5 ordinary subscription, £9-50 associate subscription and £10 hard fee, including car parking but excluding VAT (compared with current fees of £3-50, £6-50, and £8 respectively + \reater percentage increase in membership fees than hard fees appears appropriate now the new clubhouse is open. ‘The alternatives are, of course, to reduce expenditure or find new sources of income, The basic costs of running the site (i.e. rent, rates, electricity, water, gas, sewerage, telephone and caretaker's wages) now amound to well over £8 per member, Any Significant reduction in this area could only be made by drastically cutting facilities available to members. The next largest single item of major expenditure is Navigans, costing £1 per member to produce and soon to cost a further £1 to send out to associates and other members without Marconi postal addresses. A number of ways of increasing income have been suggested, including the following: extra charges for boats laid up at Stansgate in winter, visitors charge of perhaps 25p per person per day, re-introduction of race fees, or charges for hot showers. The problems with most suggestions are those of enforcement, additional work for club officers in collectio or “ifficulty in devising fair scales of fees for the widely different requirements of our r"@n ers. The present system does have the great virtue of simplicity, which is essential for a totally voluntary organisation. Your comments are invited - please contact myself, any committee member or write to Navigans. Would you like different membership/hard fee ratios? Should wives pay an extra fee? Now is the time to guide your committee so that they can prepare firm proposals well before the A.G,I, E.M.d .cBarnes, D Block. 7, [redacted]enue, Baddow Int. 797. [redacted], Ext. 729.

2. COMMODORES NOTES With the holidays over all the familiar faces are reappearing at Stansgate, although it is not always too easy to recognise them under this deep tan. It is only now that one realises that the summer is nearly over and that we must start thinking about things like Laying Up, Laying - Up Suppers and Annual General Meetings. The Committee met on Sept. ist. for the monthly meeting and discussed many of these topics; and elsewhere in Navigans you will find a note on arrangements we are proposing to try this year to avoid if possible cruisers becoming bogged down in the dinghy park during the winter. This scheme requires both short and long term rearrangement of the dinghy park and we hope to do this with as little inconvenience to members as possible. At this point I would remind you that vehicles must not be taken into the dinghy park and last year much damage was done to the surface by people disregarding this by-law. One particular piece of news that the committee were very sorry to hear was that after many years of providing the club with an excellent Galley Service, Margaret Cottam feels that the time has come to retire as our regular Victualler at the end of the season. We are very grateful to you, Margaret, for the years of support you have given us and ~—. feel you are entitled to a well earned rest. This means that next year we shall have to make new arrangements and there are two alternatives open to us. The first is to find another Margaret or group of Margarets who would take on the running of the Galley as a sideline, and would keep a stock and run it as a business proposition. If we are not able to make arrangements of this sort then the second alternative is to revert to the arrangement we had before Margaret came on the scene, when the Galley was run on a rota basis, and to do this effectively we would have to form a Ladies Committee. If there are any members who are interested in running the Galley, I or any other committee member would be pleased to discuss it with them and we would welcome any other suggestions members may have. R.Y.A. Affiliation. One of the propositions which may have to be put at the A.G.M. concerns our type of future membership to the R.Y.A. As many of you will know the R.Y.A. revised the whole membership situation at their A.G.M. in March this year and the new structure takes effect from Jan ist. 1976. A summary of the situation is that there are now two types of membership open to individuals, which are either Personal Member or Affiliated Member and two types of membership open to Clubs, either Fully Affiliated or Affiliated. Last autumn the R.Y.A. sent all Personal Members and Clubs a full brief on their proposals and definition of membership and here I have tried to summerise the situation. \ Full Personal Member as previous member but at an increased fee, on account of inflatic of £5. Receives benefits which include free booklets to value of £2.75, discounts on other books, direct access to R.Y.A. for advice and measurement certificate at a reduced fee. Will also receive personally the R.Y.A. mailings. Affiliated Personal Member Only available to members of Fully Affiliated Clubs and annual subscription of £1 is collected through club, which includes appropriate fee on renewal of club fees. Limited benefits are available to individuals enrolled in this manner which include free booklets to the value of £1, discounts on other books, free advice if applied for through club and measurement certificate at a reduced fee. Provision has been made by the R.Y.A. to ensure that Personal members do not pay twice. Pully Affiliated Club is one which collects £1 per head from its agreed sailing member— ship, which it could be agreed must be boat owners only, and passes this on to the R.Y.A. Members would then receive through the Club a membership card and be entitled to the benefits of R.Y.A. membership described under Affiliated Personal Member. Affiliated Club The Club has the same benefits as a Fully Affiliated Club but members do not have any individual benefits. The fee the Club pays the R.Y.A. for this is 4% of subscription income with a maximum of £300. The cost to the club for next year is anticipated at approx. £100.

3. The World Authority on Sailing is the International Yacht Racing Union and in this country the R.Y.A. acts as the National Authority. In order for us to organise sailing and be a recognised club it is necessary for us to be in the R.Y.A. and it is also necessary for our members sailing away at open meetings and visiting other sailing clubs to belong to a R.Y.A. recognised club. So we cannot opt out completely. To summarise, the situation is this, if you want to be a Personal Member of the R.Y.A. then what the club opts to do will not affect you. If, however, you feel you want to become an Affiliated Member of the R.Y.A. then the club must become a Fully Affiliated Club. My personal view is that there are some advantages in belonging to the R.Y.A., which I have done since I became a boat owner, but it is difficult to quantify the advantages in terms of hard cash. Fully Affiliated Club Membership seems a good way to keep the majority of active sailors in touch with sailing and would enable them to play an active part in the R.Y.A. affairs as the Club would have voting powers on their behalf to the tune of 1 vote per paid up member. The choice at the A.G.M. will be yours, but if in the meantime you have any views on this, I, or any committee member would be pleased to hear them and if you feel that you want to go into print, there is always Navigans. Looking back on that decision it now seems more justified than ever since we would be hard pressed to offer tickets for a Laying Up Supper at the Cahncellor Hall at £5.00 per head compared with our price of £3.75. Taking these iteme in the reverse order, I will outline briefly the committee's position. 6. A visit to the "Graduate Nationals". Never having the opportunity to race in a fleet of Graduates, Peter and yours truly decided to jump in with both feet and entered for the Graduate Nationals at Saundersfoot in Pembrokeshire. So at 2.00am on a fine Saturday morning we set off with "Zulu" on a trailer and a tent on the roof of the car. 7 hours and some 270 miles later we arrived on site in company with a 100 or so other Grads from many parts of the country, including a strong contingent from Scotland. Saundersfoot Sailing Club were acting as hosts, made everyone welcome and conducted the whole week's racing programme superbly. Many "Nationals" have been held at this club and anyone who has attended will readily understand why it is so popular. After our arrival, tired from the journey and setting up the tent, we were able to relax by going for a sail in the bay and getting to know a few of the other visitors. Our first race was scheduled for Sunday morning, when we joined what seemed like hundreds of Grads preparing to leave the beach and get to the start line. Unfortunately the wind was virtually nil and it became necessary to paddle in order to reach the start about a mile off shore in time. Inevitably the race was postponed and after drifting around for about 14 hours in blistering sunshine, it was decided to try and make a start in the afternoon, so we all paddled back to the shore again to slake our thirst. The afternoon was more encouraging with a very light breeze. The gate start was a new experience but after reading the race instructions it all made good sense and we managed without any probelms. We were obviously not the only one's new to this, as some crews could be seen reading their instructions as the start progressed. In this first race we were pleased to find that our boat was reasonably competitive and although there were only four boats older than our 20 year old, we were able to show the way home to much newer and lighter glass fibre boats. After 4 reasonable start we rounded the windward mark about halfway down the fleet. Successive wind changes altered positions a great deal and the "windward" leg of the course up to a shortened finishing line turned into 4 run with all the boats bunched together. All the 100 or so boats crossed the line in the space of a few minutes literally jammed together with minor bumps and curses all along the line. The poor race officer gave up the impossible task of sorting out the finish order and declared the race abandoned. It was a very useful practice race for us newcomers. There were more race officer headaches on Monday with light winds and another paddle to the start. It was decided to use a fixed line start. Despite a " five minute rule” applying so many boats were over the line at the gun there was a general recall. This was repeated twice more before a near despairing race officer was finally satisfied with the fourth start. We were quite pleased with our position of 55th that day. Tuesday was more reasonable with a gate start and a fair breeze. Nothing exciting but very pleasant racing. We were by now quite at home on the Olympic course and finished about halfway down the field. Wednesday morning saw us paddling once again to the committee boat stationed about a mile off shore. The start was scheduled for 11.00 and then postponed for shour. When the new starting time was nearly upon us the wind veered through 180° to blow from the opposite direction. Another postponement while all the race marks were repositioned to suit the new conditions and the Scots contingent amused themselves and us, by having a singsong after hauling on board the "liquid refreshment" they had been trailing on lines in the water. Thursday brought better conditions with a forecast of winds up to force 6 later in the day. We had the normal scheduled race in the morning while in the afternoon Sunday's abandoned race was re-run. The wind really did get up and there were many capsiges and retirements, not us fortunately, although we were very tired when we finally crossed the finish line somewhere about 60th place. Friday bought very light winds again and when we did get started the race was quite uneventful with us once again in the middle of the fleet. This was our last day at Saundersfoot and we left for home at about 6.00pm.

Te All in all a wonderful week, we never saw a cloud, and Saundersfoot Bay is just perfect for sailing. The comadeshipamong the competitors was really good and we learned a fair bit about sailing Graduates. Roll on next year's National's. Tony Drury, Handicap Fleet Captain. HORNET HALLAM TROPHY Despite the very heavy rain and force 8 winds on Saturday, the Hornet Hallam Trophy attracted 27 entries, and provided some very interesting racing. Saturday morning's practice race was held in a force 2-3 wind with very heavy rain showers but unfortunately for RicB&rd and Mike Barnes from Stone, who crossed the line first, the race was abandoned, as no one started on the long line. The first Points Race on Saturday afternoon made many crews think twice about their boats and gear and stay on shore, as the wind increased to gusts of force 8-9. However, some 9 boats started and 5 finished after some very hair raising sailing, when at times not one boat stayed upright. *ter all the capsizes the "racing" remained very close, first was, "Dark side of the Moon", uelteeve from B.S.C. and second was D.Nicholson also from B.S.C. Sunday morning brought sun and light wind as a complete contrast to Saturday. The mnings race was again very close with places changing in the light and variable winds. uae Nicholson brothers crossed the line first, but had to wait for confirmation on the result becuuse of a protest over the start line. C.Stodel of B.S.C. was second and S.Heppell M.S.C. was third. The final points race also in light winds proved to be ideal conditions for one of our own fleet, Steve Heppell and Gary Constable, in their new boat.As they romped home with a commanding lead, the rest of the race became something of a procession with the tide making the rules. The Nicholson's were second and Tom Sheldon from the Nedway S.C. was third. The Hornet Fleet give their thanks to the Mirror Fleet and Club Officials and all other helpers who made the meeting a success for all those who turned up. But the meeting must have been disappointing for Peter Clayton (Fleet Captain) who after putting alot of effort into the meeting, could not sail owing to an accident at the Furopean Championships, when he did a great deal of damage to his boat, and the turn- out from the Marconi Fleet was very poor, only two boats. He must be feeling very let down. Let's hope we get more support next year. SOCIAL SCREED As this is the final issue of Navigans for 1975 I'd like to wish all a Happy Christmas and hope that the social functions are as well supported next year, as they have been this year. I would also like to take the opportunity to thank all those who have helped at the various functions through the year because its only through efforts of this small willing band of volunteers that events like the Barbecue, Regatta etc meet with the success they do. About 40 children attended their party on Saturday 6th December and very effectively demolished the food, pop, ice cream, sweets etc., a mixture calculated to turn most adult stomachs, but not the kids apparently. They wereentertainedby a magician, and Vic brought along a projector for a short film show, in addition to the games. The kids had a fine time I'm sure with a good start to their Christmas. There are still some tickets for sale from:- Pat Harper, Vic Tate - Baddow John Needon - New Street Tom Gaskell - Badiow/Cromptons Albert Fuller - E.x.V. This will be on Tuesday the 13th January starting at 7.45pm. So far I have two films:- Single handed in a Wayfarer across the North Sea and Performance Afloat. I am also hoping to persuade one or two members tc show their own films. Any offers? Roy Battye, Social Secretary. MIRROR PLAT NewS We held our first winter meeting on Monday 17 Noventer. About a dozen members turned up, but none of those ijirror Chimpanzees that Brenda mentioned in last month's editorial, perhaps they only attend Laying-Up Suppers? For those who didn't come to the meeting and were keeping their fingers crossed hoping for 4& change of fleet captain, you can uncross them now because you are stuck with me for another year. We decided that the 1976 Nationals are out for most of us, as it will be held the f° +t week in September, which is the week the children go back to school, after the holidays. Some of us may go to West Mersea Sailing Week again next year. Two liirrors from our club went there this year, and had a very enjoyable week. We had perfect weather, a private camp site, and some prizes to bring home, which, after all, is what we race for. The highlight of the week is the “Round Mersea Race", and is well worth while taking part in. About 140 boats entered, and each is allowed to choose their own starting time which they state on their entry form, this is to allow each competitor to make his own judgement of the tide depending on the speed of his boat, also you can go either way round the island, the choice also has to be stated on the entry form. You get a start signal at your stated time and a signal when you finish, it is a handicap race for all classes. The best part I thought was when we arrived at the Strood or bridge, we picked up our boats and carried them still rigged across the road, ( there were plenty of helpers and the rule of outside aid doesn't apply for that part), while a policeman held up the traffic. To get all the boats overtakes quite a time, although they didn't all arrive at once. So it's a case of even motor cars givine way to sail. Incidently, Mersea Week is open to all classes and is not exclusively for Mirrors. But before it all happens again there is for most of us decorating - gardening and in my case a greenhouse to build for Vera, I must have made that promise whilst under the influence of sailing. So good luck with all your winter chores and a Happy Christmas. Stan Oaker, Pleet Captain.

5. COMMODORES REPORT My first year of Office is now over and it seems no time since the last A.G.M. The year has been an exciting and eventful one for the Club with the opening and commission- ing of our new Clubhouse. As it was indicated it would be by Dennis Byatt last year, the Clubhouse was handed over shortly after the 1974 A.G.M. and the winter months were spent fitting out the clubhouse in time for the start of the season. As a result of the monsoon conditions that prevailed throughoit the winter, we were almost forced to change the name to the Island Sailing Club. To overcome the problems of access on the seaward side of the clubhouse, we were forced to spend additional capital on installing land drains and a hardcore and gravel drive to the North and “Last of the building. After the rain stopped we were prevented from completing the levelling and grassing on the South due to the baked condition of the ground and the desire, as it should be, by members to sail. It is now hoped that this can be completed in the Spring. The formal opening of the clubhouse took place a week before the Regatta, and at this the Club was congratulated on the design, standard of finish and facilities available. I feel that with the opening of our first permanent home on land on which we have the free- hold in our 25th year a major milestone in the history of the club was achieved. As well as ~““ymissioning the clubhouse we also installed and switched on the photo electrically ¢_.utrolled Hallam Light - a permanent memorial to Terry Hallam - and a welcome navigation aid for all users of the Blackwater. It has the added advantage of providing light for members using the club after dark and acts as a deterent to the undesirable. During the year we have had our teething problems as with any new building but these have been overcome by the efforts of Committee Members, Members, Claud Emerson and the sustained interest of Mick Taylor our builder. Our biggest disappointment came at the Regatta, when once again we were in trouble with the Cesspool but subsequently we sought permission to install a soakaway and this was granted by the Anglian Water Authority and the work has now been completed. We are hopeful that our problems are now really over. During the year the Committee took several decisions which we felt would be in the long term interest of the club. The most significant of these being to use a large amount of our reserve fund to equip the clubhouse with new furniture etc., throughout as with rising costs the outlay would only become larger if left. We tried to choose furniture which would be both functional and attractive and would stand up to use by sailors in dripping wet suits etc, I think the furniture has shown itself capable of this type of use, as has the floor, even though at times it would appear there is more of the Blackwater inside than out. The excellent summer and the new facilities have contributed to raising our membership an all time high of 450. In the early part of the year the new members came complete with boats, but as time progressed things changed and there were less boat owners among the new members. We hope that many of these will feel the call of the wind and spray and will soon join the ranks of our regular sailors. One of the minor disappointments expressed by the Committee almost universally has been the state that members have left the club in after use. Keeping the clubhouse clean and tidy was always a Problem with the old building, but it is now magnified many times. It is only by the efforts of Claud tmerson assisted from time to time by his wife Ivy, that we have had a clean building to come to the next week and I feel that only by a little extra thought on the part of all the members will he be able to maintain the standard. I would, therefore, ask you all next year to make avery effort to leave the saloon and changing rooms after use as you would like to find them. Despite the ever rising costs and the considerable expenditure on which we have embarked our Treasurer has kept us out of trouble and with the aid of a windfall or two we have been able to end the year with a small surplus. As you have been advised and will see from the proposal to be considered later in the meeting the Committee have reluctantly been forced to recommend increasing subscriptions to keep pace with inflation and we hope this proposal will be given your support. As reported in Navigans we have agreed in principle with the M.A.S.C. terms for the use of the site for a period of 6 years from January 1976 at £2,000 p.a. Under this revised agreement we undertake to pay the rates which we estimate at over £900 for 1976. As discussed at last year's A.G.M. we arranged to fit Magnetic Locks to both the Clubhouse door and the gate. We experienced some teething problems with them initially but, unless anything has happenedinthe last few days, they are now working satisfactorily. You may recall that the object in fitting them was to protect major items of members and club

6. property and to prevent the use of the site by unauthorised people. We believe we have been very successful on both these counts as we have not heard of vanishing dinghies this year, and certainly the number of vehicles stranded outside our gate at almost any time of the week or weekend has confirmed the value as a deterent. This has been confirmed by Harry Holt who has gain helped to regulate the comings and goings. Thank you, Harry. As we said last year Security is a major concern and although we think we have been reasonably successful, there have been occasions when the Clubhouse has not been fully secured and we would ask you all to be vigilant on this matter and to ensure that you do not open doors and windows unnecessarily and always lock up after you. The Club, after enjoying about 7 years of excellent Galley service from Margaret Cottam, to whom we are very grateful, is going to have to re-organise the service. I raised this subject in Navigans earlier in the year and asked for anyone interested in taking over the galley to come and discuss any ideas they have. I know a number of ladies have expressed willingness to help and I would be pleased, after the meeting, to talk further with any that are present tonight so that we can explore these ideas further. Before Margaret left for her Australian holiday she was presented on behalf of the Club, with a Travelling Case in appreciation of the service she has given us, and I am sure you will agree with me that her smiling presence every Sunday morning will be sadly missed. Sailing activities this year have thrived and although I do not want to encroach on the Sailing Secretaries preserve, I feel I must congratulate all who have contributed to .ne sailing success of the Club, be it on the water or on the shore. Our Social calendar this year has been a great success and here again I would thank all who have been concerned in the organisation and running of the events. At the A.G.M. of B.A.C.S.P.A. the Marconi Sailing Club took over the Chairmanship and Secretaryship and our congratulations and thanks go to Stan Allerton and Frank Savill who took over the respective offices. This is not an annually elected office and they will remain there until such time as they find it no longer possible for them to continue. I would like at this time to thank the members of the committee for their unfailing support during the year and particularly for the late hours they have kept on occasions, when far reaching topics have been under discussion and it has been important to obtain the views of all. I was very pleased to find when we came to discussing nominations for 1976 that the majority of the members were willing to offer themselves for re-election and if I may take this as a vote of confidence then I would say thank you. To the two retiring members, Clare Urry and Jack Reeve, I would also extend my gratitude for their support, both this year and in years gone by. I extend further thanks to Jack and Joyce for their regular service behind the bar, and Jack says he will still be there next year to pull the odd pint or two. Navigans, much admired by those outside the Club privileged to read it, has contin to appear regularly due to the efforts of Brenda Tate and Mick Gray. I am sure it is one of the strengths of the Club and, if, like me, you still have back numbers to hand provides an invaluable reference document. I am sure you will agree that brenda deserves your support and I know she welcomesarticles from anyone and particularly more Fleet and other news about the Club and its members. There could be a tendency for it to become heavy if it relies too much on my own and other officers notes. Thank you, Brenda, for your continued effort - she has agreed to carry on for another year — and to all of you when you hear of anything you think might be of interest to the Club, please spare a thought for Navigans. Tonight you have the opportunity to reflect on the last 12 months and to make your observations on the past year and your recommendations for consideration by the Committee for the coming year, and I will not spend any further time on details as you will be given ample opportunity later in the meeting to discuss any topics you like. In conclusion I would like to thank all of you who have contributed to the running of the Club and taken part in the activities, this year as without you, the members, and your support we would not be able to function as a Club. Thank you. John Witter, Commodore.

T- TREASURERS RurORT FOR 1975 You should have before you the estimated account for 1975; together with the final account for 1974. You will see that a new breakdown has been introduced for 1975 which I hope will give a clearer picture of the club's finanaces. The previous breakdown has been in use for at least five years, during which time the expenditure under the "general" heading has increased to the point where this year it would have exceeded the net subscription income. The estimated surplus on the revenue account for this year is £91, mainly due to the profit from last year's social events. The major reasons for increased expenditure has been the general rise in prices-and the additional costs of running the new clubhouse. The latter is estimated to be of the order of £6-700. Fortunately these have been partially offset by subscriptions from new members, particularly since the proportion of boat owners has been more than maintained. The main feature of the past year has been the expenditure on the new clubhouse and its surrounds totalling nearly £3,000. Major items have included:- Tables and chairs £845, Drainage and hardcore for surrounds £511, Magnetic locks £490, and Changing room furniture £241. This expenditure has been partially offset, however, by the sale of the old clubhouse : boat-shed. iWe have also received an electricity refund (due to incorrect meter installatic and expect further sums to result from rating and V.A.T. appeals. BEW SUBSCRIPTIONS In the August edition of Navigans we explained that an increase in subscriptions would be necessary, if the club is to maintain its present standard of services. Since then agreement has been reached with the M.A.S.C. concerning the rent for the site. While this represents a very satisfactory agreement in the long term, it does represent an increase of £350 over this year. This figure taken together with the effects of inflation and our responsibility for a considerable amount of expensive equipment has led to the need to raise the order of £1,000 next year from increased subscriptions. Considerable thought has been given by the committee to the proposals presented tonight. The opportunity has been taken to clarify the hard fees for families with more than one boat, particularly in the case of cruiser tenders. The postal element of the associate fees has been separated to enccurage the use of relatives with internal post addresses, and to allow us to charge family members without such addresses. Some members have susgested that we should cherge for hot showers, but this has not been considered worthwhile, at the present time, since water heating costs have only been about 10p per member this year. The appeal in Navigans showed no enthusiasm for other ways of raising money, and, therefore, the basic fee structure remains unchanged. The car park fee has been absorbed into the membership “pe very few members did not pay this fee. Now that the new clubhouse is in operation, it is felt that the membership fess should have a greater percentage rise than hard fees. Taking the pessimistic view that our membership wili drop to 400 next year, it is estimated that these proposals will increase our net subscription by £900. It is hoped, however, that the membership will continue to grow, and inflation rates moderate so that the proposed rates will suifice for several years. Ted Barnes, Hon. Treasurer. In all some 1,000 man hours of work was put in during the working parties and had we not been able to undertake the work when we did it would without doubt,,have been a very different story. The committee wish most sincerely to thank all those who helped in any way with the repair work and to say how encouraged we are to find a spirit existing in the Club which can rally the members in such an unselfish way at a time of need.
