Log of the "Barbara Star" from 15.8.75 — 25.8.75. Friday 15.8.75. 21.00 hrs. Finds us in the dinghy motoring to the "Barbara Starr", clad *n all our wet weather gear, I even have my umbrella up. The rain is pouring down as though ‘ishing us for the sins of our forefathers. This, after months of dry weather, when the avast godly of us have been praying for rain for our gardens. But why now? Just as we are about to go aboard. The devil's way of looking after his own I suppose. There was some consolation in the thought of the runner beans at home lapping up this lovely rain water. Later we discovered that Braintree hadn't had a drop. Saturday 16.8.75. 09.29 hrs. Lovely sunny morning. Quietly we slip our mooring at an unusually deserted looking Stansgate. The Hollanders are still at sea. Running on a port tack with the wind a moderate W.S.W. On to Thirslet beacon with just a lonely cormorant flying low over the water keeping us company. Last night's wet clothes strewn around the cockpit drying out. Umbrella put away for a rainy day. The swell is high, but not, as yet uncomfortably so. Visibility good. St. Osyth trees quite easily discernible. Another addition to the layed up ships anchored at Bradwell. This one of british registration, namely "Salter's Gate" London. What a state the shipping world must be in with all these boats lying idle. Barrier wall alongside. Not much traffic about. Everyone's having a lay in. Being a nervous inexperienced sailor I'm getting the wind up. "Where's my life jacket?". Bench Head coming up. Interesting to see the new Radar reflector atop it. The boat is rolling, so is my tummy, but Cliff is enjoying it. It's all right for him, he can swin. Still good visibility as we pass the N.W.knoll and Bar buoys. The radar masts at Foulness are quite clearly seen. Invaded by a huge bee in the cabin. I do wish it was in my garden pollinating the marrows or something.

Fighting the battle with the bee has upset my battle with the bulge. Some light refreshment is called for. Its very difficult though in these weather conditions wish I had another pair of hands to go with my two left feet. With one eye I spot the Knoll buoy in the distance and with the other I can see Clacton. No, I am not cross eyed. Just very observant. Walton looks pretty with the sun shining on it, but then so does everywhere when the sun's upon it. Tolling its message to all men andwomen of the sea we pass the Wallet Spitway, followed by the Swin Spitway buoy. Its just like being called to prayers with all these bells ringing. "Please God will you make the seas calmer". We are now doing 6 knots which is supposed to be the potential of the “Barbara Starr”, but she will do a little more going down hill. Midday and we are in the East Swin channel on a close reach with a fort looming in sight to the south. West Hook Middle looking very colourful in mid ocean. We are riding high on a wave and catch the first glimpse of the Kentish coastline, and then tacked in sight of the Barrow Beacon. Log stopped working probably due to weed. If it doesn't clear Cliff will be over the side in snorkel and flippers as soon as we anchor. That's always good for a laugh. To starboard, Whittaker Beacon. Log cleared itself, what a shame. S.W.Middle, huge swell on. Apples and oranges rolling around the cabin floor. Bad housekeeping. I have alot to learm if I survive this battering? Even the dinghy is trying to jump aboard. Overtaken by motor cruiser "Pepitor". Battling on between Maplin sands and edge buoys. Seas getting rougher, and I'm scared to death. Going to retire to my boudoir with a fit of the vapours for a while. Tacked all the way up the Thames to Sheerness, avoiding the wreck of the old ammunition ship "Richard Montgomery", which has been laying near the entrance to the Medway since 1944. Rumour has it, that if it did blow up, half of Sheerness would go with it. Still forging ahead, all hands on deck. Passing Garrison Point. The roughest trip I've ever made. I'm seriously thinking of hitch hiking back. At last. Nicely anchored at Queenborough, Isle of Sheppy. Battered and bruised I quietly say a prayer for our safe arrival. Sunday 17.8.75. 0O7.30hrs. Rudely awakened by the raucous voices of two anchored boat owners shouting to each other across the water. They are re-enacting Treasure Island. Robert Newton surely gave that story the kiss of life when the film was made. For my part I wished "Me earties" had left me in peace for another hour. We have a nice quiet days sailing locally with my sister and brother-in-law, who, (God help them) live on Sheppey. They ate all my home made scones and splits too Splite is the Cornish name for bread rolls, for the uninitiated. Naturally, to get the best flavour from them you smother them with home made jam amd Cornish Green. ~ It was nice to see me sister after two years. We'll call on them one day and eat thr out of house and home. Monday 18.8.75. 11.10 hrs. As we leave Queenborough the wind is N.Hasterly. It's high water and lovely warm sunshine. Heading eastwards towards the Swin, tacking all the way. 11.32. Garrison Point on one side, the Isle of Grain on the other. Seastoo rough to make coffee. The Holland ferry is in the docks at Sheerness preparing for their trip to Flushing, which they do in seven hours. We passed under the bows of the cargo ship "Framcop" anchored at the Nore, and steadily forced our way through the rough seas until we reached Brightlingsea. (19.00) It was a very boisterous and "Moisterous" trip from Queenborough during which the decks were well washed with spray. I feel like a battered wife. Tuesday 19.8.75 12.10 hrs The Harbour Master slipped up here, as we slipped away without paying. Unintentionally. It must have been his day off. Wind S.W. force 5. Seas again very choppy. Very few sailing vessels out. To be continued,

2s COMMITTEE NOTES Our Editor made an appeal to the last Committee meeting for the contributions to Navigans to be positive and encouraging, but as we progressed through the meeting we became aware that the things we needed to draw to your attention tended to appear restrictive. Unfortunately they must be said, so my notes this month are headed Committee notes. A number of incidents have been reported this season which have included infringements of the Club Rules and are therefore, of a serious nature. Rules have two main purposes, to provide guide lines for the Administration of the Club and to impose some discipline which is for the benefit of all. In the second case it is often also to protect members from themselves, as is the case with insurance. What people may not always remember is that, although they are Prepared to take risks with their property, in the event of an accident somebody could be seriously injured and if not adequately insured the party to blame could have a life long debt both financially and of guilt. We annually ask all boat owners to sign an undertaking that their boat is adequately insured before bringing it to Stansgate and this should not be done without being absolutely sure that there will be cover before bringing the boat. Members are also reminded that the Club is there for the benefit of the members and — it has been observed that there have been a considerable number of non-members both visit. on shore and sailing and there appears to have been a marked reluctance for these guest's names to be entered in the visitor's book. Under the present rules there are two slightly different versions of rules relating to guests depending on the circumstances. To clarify the situation the Committee passed the following bye law. "The names of all adult guests brought to the site shall be entered in the Visitor's Book by the introducing member". Members are requested to observe this bye—law and to ensure that their friends only visit the site when properly accompanied. We have already heard of anumber of items of members property disappearing since the start of the season. This we find both disturbing and distasteful. As you are aware a public footpath runs through the Club and members are urged to be careful with their property and not put temptation in the way of others. The Club cannot in any way be responsible for the safety of member's property. SAILING SECRETARY'S NOTES SAFETY IN DINGHIES A few notes about this subject are appropriate at this time of year when conditions can be cold and windy and most people are out of practice. First of all pay attention to your equipment. The boat should be checked over to ensure that it is in a sound condition, worn halliards, fittings etc. should be replaced and the buoyancy verified. Clothing also is important and if conditions are such that a capsize is likely then a wet suit is recommended, especially with children who lose body heat quickly when immersed. A good fitting life jacket or buoyancy aid is essential, which must be worn at all times when afloat. (This is a club rule where under 18 year olds are concerned). When you do get into trouble however, keep calm and do not waste unnecessary energy but keep with the boat and try to recover the situation. If all else fails summon help. The universal distress signal of waving your arms up and down by your side may be useful. When there is a strong wind or tide an anchor should be used to prevent you drifting out of sight until help arrives. Last but not least it is up to each person to decide whether they are capable of coping with the prevailing conditions, if in doubt ask and when the answer is "NO" —- don't go. Of course, if you are practiced at recovering from a capsize and have well found equipment, this will extend the range of conditions when the boat can be used safely. John Weedon. The Log of the "Barbara Starr" continued. Our boat, a 23' Islander which we have just acquired is certainly being put to the test and so far coming up trumps. All that afternoon we sailed through heavy seas and high winds and arrived at Walton. 5.00pm. After rounding Pye-End buoy and tacking into Walton creek, 21 miles of sailing. Had a nice walk along the sea wall and found a fish and chip shop at the end of it. What ever would we do without this delectable meal? Got chatting to a family who were holidaying in @ caravan, very pleasant people, walking back we saw scores of sea cadets hurrying .« towards the town, couldn't get there fast enough to spend their money. Wednesday 20.8.75. 9.50am. Raised anchor earlier than planned. We were getting uncomfortably close to the boat next to us. Set off down the Walton channel, jib only. S.W.wind. 11.30am. Harwich harbour and the Guard buoy. To portside several red lightships are anchored. Tug XX12 passing. B.R. cross channel steamer leaving Parkeston Quay for the Hook of Holland. The tug "Egerton" crossing our stern and H.M.S.Ganges at Shotley is Sighted. Passing the Shotley Spit buoy to enter the river Orwell. Seas very rough as we pass the mouth of the Stow. The Ipswich Pioneer II car ferry is on its way to Rotterdam. ~Sontinue on our way to Collimer buoy with Suffolk Yacht Harbour to starboard. -OOpm. In very calm waters we anchored at Pin Mill. Cliff went ashore for water, bread, etc, and I with an unusual spurt of energy did some cleaning up. A strange boat came in and used someone else's mooring, expecting to stay there all night. Later the owner returned asked him to move, and in doing so got himself tangled up with the buoys, with the other boat going round in circles watching every move and the squatter getting more and more tangled. Eventually, very red faced he managed to free himself. Motto, "Don't use other people's moorings without permission". Later we spent a convivial couple of hours in the Butt and Oyster talking to an old salt (and soak) who had, at one time worked the barges. I do wish he had worn his teeth, I couldn't quite grasp all he was saying. On second thoughts I don't think he understood what I was talking about either. That's why we got on so well. Slept very soundly after a few gins and a jar of cockles. 10 miles sailing today. Thursday 21.8.75. 08.30am. Still in bed I am viewing the panorama through the open hatch. As yet no-one astir, except Cliff who is making a cup of tea, and a few squawking seagulls overhead. To port the smoking chimney of Ipswich power station dimly showing above the trees in the distance, with a line of colourful boats moored in the foreground, or foresea, or foreshore, or whatever. I'd be content to stay here all day, but Cliff has chy flippers, so I discard my night clothes for my day wear, which is less bulky, and we vontinue our way up the Orwell passing the Harwich Yacht Club en route. Winds very light. The Ipswich Pioneer II has returned during the night and is now on its way back again to Rotterdam. No time wasted there. (I bet they make a profit). Turn within sight of Cliff Quay Ipswich to take the tide down the Orwell. 16.47. Sailing past Felixstowe docks on our way to the mouth of the Deben. A beautiful evening with the sun brightly shining upon Felixstowe on our portside. Suddenly and dramatically everything changes. The sky darkens, the heavens open and it rains cats and dogs. The thunder rumbles in the distance, our sails fill to bursting point. All this after a cloudless sunny day, very little wind, and within half an hours sailing time to the mouth of the river. Cliff loWered the mainsail, changed genoa for working jib and started the motor, and myself, knees quaking, at the tiller. In pouring rain, thunder and lightning bad visibility and everything else the heavens could throw at us we entered the mouth of the Deben safely, due entirely to Cliff's navigation. With rain on my spectacles I couldn't see a thing, I should have used my umbrella. Finally we found a safe anchorage opposite the Bawdsey Radar Station, which is, I believe, well known to Radar pioneers such as our own President, Sir Eric Eastwood and others. Friday 22.8.75. 10.20am. Wind N.W. Lovely sunny morning. All craft anchored around us have last night's wet clothing drying out on deck. Numerous boats moored outside the Ramsholt Arms. Very pretty, set in tall fir trees with fully ripe corn fields on either side. Convenient for the men who do the thirsty work of cutting the corn.

6. Tacking quietly between the many boats moored at Waldrinfield, we were without warning assailed by an agressive pseudo Oxford accent coming from behind, "Get that bloody thing out of my way". Drawing myself up like a very large figurehead I called back in my broadest Cornish accent, "Have you read your little book about courtesy on the water". We then noticed that this individual was having a private race with one other yacht, so we unofficially joined in and led the way until just before reaching Woodbridge, when they overtook us, but they were bigger than us anyway, and also we were looking for a place to anchor. After anchoring in this very picturesque harbour with the town sitting amongst the trees, and St Mary's Church tower just showing itself above, we explored the town, purchased a few vittals and then sailed back to Shottisham woods and anchored for the night. Eventually four other boats joined us and , as usual in this particular spot a couple of families went ashore and had a barbecue. It was a lovely evening with the water as calm as as a lake. We did just 12 miles sailing that day. Saturday 23.8.75. 8.30am. Found us up anchor and leaving with some regret this very peaceful and pleasant haven, with our neighbours cheerfully waving us on our way. A bright and sunny morning. Wind westerly. Temperature cooler. 10.45am. The coast line of Felixstowe abeam with its long row of beach huts. Viewed —> from here they look like colourful tombstones standing on end. Sailed through Harwich harbour to the river Stour as far as Wrabness. Decided it was too rough for anchorage so we turned tail and anchored on the sheltered side of Shotley in the river Orwell. The wind had dropped on us. Sh... had to use the motor to get there. We left a line out over- night and found a hook gone in the morning, so we'll never know how big the one that got away was. Sunday 24.8.75. 9.45am. Sailed from here on a fine morning but clouds were gathering from the N.W. The wind is S.W. Intrigued by the old Harwich lighthouse which is surrounded by scaffolding. Presumably under repair. Also spot the old black shed where the ancient tread mill operated crane is preserved. We had a look at it some time ago. Apparently it was used in Nelson's time. It being Sunday, we clearly hear the church bells ringing their come hither message from the town centre. 12.15.pm. Sailing; past Walton-on-the-Naze with its cluster of beach huts, a feeling of nostalgia overcomes me for my native Cornish coastline. Its beautiful golden sands, and overhanging cliffs, and caves for shelter when the rains come, which they do, all too frequently. 21.00 It was a long sail and at last we reached Burnham on the river Crouch. It was getting dimitty, as we say in Cornwall, so we put the navigation lights on, after fighting the tide. "The strong man", the locals call it. For our last night afloat we moored at . Wallasea. We had done 34 sailing miles, 5 motoring. Although feeling very tired, we go ashore dressed in our usual shabby way and visit the Ward Room. “Ah, special dinner on tonight. &2 per head. Just what we need", and on entering the restaurant we spot an empty table. "Can we have this table"? I asked the lady in charge. With a withering up and down examination she answered, "Sorry madam, all tables are booked". Which, of course, could have been quite true, but I can't help feeling that if Cliff had taken his faded peaked cap off and I had worn my diamond tiara we would have managed to get our dinner. However, not to be out done we ordered an ‘open samdwich' at the bar, one of their culinary specialities, which consisted of a slice of toast, with & lump of grilled steak on the top and a salad. All for 55p. Fully recommended by us. After which we had a few drinks, a nice sing song, with a gentleman playing an organ like instrument and then made our unsoberly way back to our boat, along those bobbing pontoons. We slept like logs that night. Monday 25.60.75. 8.14am. Up and away early. Unfortunately had to motor down the Spitway against the tide. "We were getting nowhere fast". Plagued by flying ants as we left the mouth of the Crouch, and they stayed with us until we reached Bradwell. Became becalmed after passing the Bench Head so reluctantly we used the motor for a while. Called in the Bradwell Marina for petrol, after which we had a marvellous sail to Stansgate, where we moored up after a quietly satisfying exploration of water rather than land for ten wonderful unforgettable days. Hileen M. Clarke.

Many members whose yachts have plastic hulls will be distressed to find that their »psides, specially just above the waterline are becoming stained. Polishing has little effect, despite the maker's claims and some are resorting to painting. These stains can however, be easily removed by painting with a solution of oxalic acid in water by brush. The drips which will inevitably run down on to the anti-fouling, do not appear to have any ill effect on the T.B.T. which was used in the case tested, although it is advisable to sponge off continually during application. The stain is removed like magic and after a good wash, it can be polished normally. The powdered oxalic acid can be bought from the chemist for 10 pence which is enough for several hulls. BNTJRPRISE FLEET NWS (or Underwater Exploration part 3135) The Regatta provided a good turnout for the Enterprises and again we were the largest fleet there, though only a few Marconi boats competed. We all seemed to enjoy the weekend, but next year I want to see more of you participating. You never know, if you sail enough this season and get in practice even YOU might win a prize next time. Some people have been saying that this column is almost amusing and they look forward to hearing of my adventures afloat, as well as my adventures when actually in a boat. Yes, I did capsize at the regatta, twice, though I would like to believe that only one was really my fault. So for those of you who think this article is going to be funny too (especially young Weedons) here is an introductory discussion on Fluid Dynamics to help you understand the theory behind sailing. In the 19th century a chap called Bernoulli investigated the phenomenon of fluid flow past an aerofoil section and proved that, within limits, the faster the fluid over the top surface moves the lower the pressure and hence the greater the lift force on the aerofoil. In a simple mathematical form, assuming partial (dv/dt)=0 Bernoulli derived the following 3rd dimensioral vectorial equation;- curl v x v = grad (ve /2 +h +Q) where Q is a potential function, h is the enthalpy and grad is not a boat but a vector operator. By considering streamlines and using very simple maths, the equation can be written in its well known form of 3s- intergral of ( “P/r + v°/2+Q)=C where p=pressure, r = density, and C is salty (or a constant). You all with me so far? No, well then I will talk about the next fleet party instead. It will be held on Thursday 24th June at the General's Arms and I am asking anyone who wants to go to, or think they will be asked to go to, the Area Team Championships on July 3rd, to come along - and bring crew/wife etc. If you have not already heard, we did make a profit at the last party and everyone thought it was so good that we must have another. See you down at Stansgate. Rob Swale, Fleet Captain. Tel:— Work New Street Int. 9379 Kixt. 736 = Home Chelmsford [redacted]. CADET NEWS The Cadet week we held immediately after the Regatta was very successful. Out of 23 Cadets taking the Elementary Day Boat Certificate 15 passed and will be presented with certificates pasted in each Cadets log book. What is more encouraging is the fact that each Cadet took their practical test in very severe weather. Force 5 winds, heavy seas and very cold. A true test indeed. Of the 15 Cadets, 4 were ladies, I would add that I was one of the men. We will be arranging a day at Stansgate probably a Saturday so that Cadets who have to take certain tests a second time can have a further opportunity. I would like to take this opportunity to formally thank Colin Leveridge for his patient and persistent tuition and the time and trouble needed to secure success which was very evident. If Colin and I can fit in the first of the Saturday tuition days in during June, I will ring everybody up in good time. I am sure everybody thoroughly enjoyed the Cadet week and hopefully we can repeat it again next year. Rick Anstey, Cadet Captain. 41, [redacted], Chelmsford. Telt— Chelmsford [redacted].

6. TEANK-YOU Jill Savill thanks all the ladies who worked so hard and ran the galley during the Regatta; and a special thank you to all the children who ran the sweet table so well. CRUISER FLEET NEWS Entrophy, Tijo, Jappa and Vanillus enjoyed a week's cruise up the Thames during the Spring Bank holiday, due to engine failure Jappa had to sail all the way up, a very hairy beat. They stayed three nights at St. Katherine's Yacht Haven within the shadow of Tower Bridge, very cheap accomadation for the centre of London at £3 a night. Margaret Campbell said that the atmosphere at the Marina was very friendly, almost like a village, with many people equiping boats for long distance voyages. They met up with Tony and Judy Porter who have spent the winter there getting ready for a summer in the Med. Avril and Ken are still living it up at Burnham, and at the time of writing 10 Marconi members are "batchelor thrashing" off the coast of France in Bettine and Entrophy. Lovely to see Geroge and Bobbie Charlton down at the club enjoying the sunshine. John Hooper really spoilt Vic and I went he took us out on Davolas for a day and we came home and said we must get a boat that sails; we are very lucky for Tony Cherry has offered us Ace for our summer holiday's so we are off to Holland with Nick and Daphne Tovey for a fortnight at the end of July. Brenda Tate.

COMMODORE 'S NOTES Mid season and the holiday period is on us and with this prolonged spell of fine weather the Club has again come into it's own with members enjoying it to the full. I wish you all very happy sailing there and wherever your sailing takes you during the couple of month's school holidays.The increased use of the Clubhouse and the very hot weather brings with it the attendant problem of adequate security since to make the lounge and changin: rooms bearable it is often necessary to open windows. I would therefore, ask you all on behalf? of the Committee to ensure that all windows and doors are secured as you leave the vicinty of the Clubhouse, please do not leave it to the member at the bottom of the dinghy park as he may leave without visiting it, and he should have his own key if he wants to go into the Clubhouse. John Witter, Commodore. FIRE RISKS In the past hot dry years we have reminded members of the risk of fire and we endorse here the warnings already given in the local and national press. Please, therefore, be extra careful about putting out cigarettes and matches at all times and particularly on ‘ site and along the approach road as the verges are very dry and there are valuable crups and stock in the vicinéty. One stray spark could cause a major disaster. MILK BOTTLES Please note that there is no milk delivery or collection from the Club and if you‘do bring milk down with you please take the bottles home again. They belong to your milkman. FIRST AID It is proposed to publish a list of names of members who have knowledge of first aid. This season we have had some rather awkward problems to deal with and it is felt that positive help from trained persons would be beneficial. Would volunteers please contact the undersigned. D.C.Harper, Clubhouse and Precincts Sec. Home Telt— Chelmsford [redacted]. Office New Street Int. 593. CADET NEWS Colin and I had hoped to begin the summer tuition series this month but unfortunately holidays are in the way. The earliest date will be late August. Those Cadets wishing to take some of the Elementary Certificate Scheme tests will have the opportunity in either late August or early September before the water cools. However, on Barbecue Day (Saturday July 17th.) I will be at Stansgate from 14.00hours to give the younger cadets actual sailing experience. For the more ambitious, I hope to persuade Peter Clayton to make a couple of Hornets available in order that some of the more experienced cadets can graduate to the more exciting and faster dinghies. I suggest all those interested in sailing a Hornet phone me first (Chelmsford [redacted]) before going down. The Cadet Series is wide open, 3 different winners to date and promises to be a hard fought series. My thanks to all those parents who are encouraging their cadets to sail and providing the enthusiasm necessary for a strong Cadet Fleet. Rick Anstey, Cadet Captain.

3. ENTERPRISE FLEET NEWS (or "Starship Enterprise" - boldly going where no-one has boldly gone before boldly, Star Date 82118°1). This month's article is going to be short and sweet - just like me - as it appears that many of you did not understand the simple maths I quoted last month. My attempt to be different and serious and make you think that-I was not just a comic capsizer appears to have had an effect though. You all think I have got water on the brain, or something. Oh well, back to the frivolities. I was disappointed with the even smaller turnout at last month's get-together as only the people involved with the Team Championship, and one other person, turned up. I realise that some of you were on holiday or busy elsewhere, but it does not seem worthwhile to continue with them, at least until the Autumn, with the present sort of response — unless YOU think otherwise. So please TELL ME if you disagree. I am pleased to see the Commodore on the water at last, and in fact I think he has won one race. (We had to let him, really, otherwise he would have given us extra duties to do ) Several of us, namely: Ron and Louise Greygoose, Geoff Josey and Chris Weedon, Dave Suster and myself went off to King George S.C. on July 3rd. to represent the club tn the sterprise Area Team Championships. Although we just missed out on the Finals (by 5.25 ints after 5 races) and being bitten by several of the millions of ladybirds, we all seemed to enjoy the day. We lost the first two races because we were not quite "in gear", but we won the next three. I personally enjoyed the last race as on the first beat we had a really good fight with someone from Ardleigh 5.C. — eventually getting the better of him of course - to finish second to Ron who had slowed down to watch. My thanks to Dave for Crewing for me and getting me and the boat there and back safely, and I hope changing the water pump was not too difficult, (in joke). That's all for this month, see you* on/under/in the water. Rob Swale, Fleet Captain. * Delete as necessary. Tel:— Home Chelmsford [redacted]. Work New St. 736 or Int. 9379. P.S. Thanks mainly to 2 Club members (Mr Fuller who donated a Cheetah catamaran to the Club and Mr Lingwood who was willing to exchange this for his Mirror "Hotpot") we now have another dinghy for the Club member's benefit. Any Club member wishing to borrow Hotpot should apply to the Officer of the Day, but it is expected that those using it have had some sailing experience and handle itcarefully as a Mirror is not all that robust. A log book is kept in the Clubhouse entrance hall to record each loan. Normally the period of the loan would be one hour or the duration of a race, Cadets and members of non-boat owning families being given preference. John Weedon, Sailing Secretary. COMMODORE 'S NOTES The end of the season is approaching faster than any of us would wish and with it the Laying Up Supper. Elsewhere Roy Battye has outlined the evening's programme so that you have good notice of the event. It is again at the M.A.S5.C. and as with other events during the year I am looking forward to a good turn out of members at our premier social function which sets the seal on a successful sailing season. I do hope lots of you will be able to come. Within a month of the Laying Up Supper we have the A.G.M. at which the new Committee is elected and as always there is room for an infusion of new blood into the body which reulates the life of the Club. Members who feel they would like to find out more about the Cogmittee should not hesitate to discuss it with any officer or Committee member. Next month we shall be asking for final nominations but in the meantime why not give some consideration to standing for election yourself. During the last year a sub-committee has been meeting to review the Club's Constitution and Rules which were in need of updating to bring them in line with custom and practise and the changed situation resulting from the purchase of the land and the opening of the new clubhouse. The work of this comnsittee is almost complete and if we are not able to inclu¢s copies of the preposed rules with this Navigans we certainly will with the October issue — Fundamentally there are no major changes from the previous rules but for many of you it w: be the first oppotunity to see a copy as the old ones have been out of print for some time. Adoption of these revised rules will be an item on the Agenda at the A.G.M. and to ensure that there are no misunderstandings at that time the Committee would ask you to read then through as quickly as possible after you receive them and to raise any queries with any Committee member at the earliest opportunity. The Committee have also been giving some consideration to the state of the road and have obtained some estimates for the cost of essential repairs, which will have to be undertaken during the next few weeks if we are to avoid the risk of further deterioration over the winter. The cost is estimated at eround £250 and this together with other large expenditure on the Hard (£400), replacement of the workboat engine (£450) and repairs to the Crecent engine (£100) will absorb more than the budgeted surplus for the year. We considered asking for volunteers to repair the road but concluded that, as at the time of year it needed to be done menbers would prefer to sail and professional equipment was required, we would have to pay for the work this time. On two occasions since the major repair and resurfacing exercise some 9 years ago at a cost of £1,000 of which £450 was recovered from member's donations, minor repairs have been conducted witb voluntary help. John Witter, Commodore. CRUIS#R FLEsT NEWS We have a change of Fleet Captain to report this month; Russ Fuller takes over from John Smith and we all thank John and his wife,Ann most sincerely for all the work they've put in on our behalf. I hear that Jack and Jill Bates have a new Sea King on the way, having recently sold Pelican to a new owner at Mersea. The Blackwater will soon be full of Sea Kings. We are hoping to arrange for a supply of fairly up to date Yachting magazines to be available at Stansgate for those extended dinner breaks during winter refits etc. Please find and return them at the bookcase - not the galley or the bar counters - that gets abit unpopular. Best wishes to George Charlton for a speedy recovery after his recent visit to hospital. It was nice to see him and Bobby at Stansgate during the summer, Bobby often showing us how to make the most of the Stansgate water and George giving a crafty eye to all that went on. Well done. At the September meeting at the General's Arms we heard various exploits of summer cruises and saw some very interesting slides. Amazing how John Hooper pops up everywhere. Hope we have more members there next month on the first Thursday when we shall again have a show of holiday slides. Please bring some of yours — Vic is itching to demonstrate his electric pointer. Russell Fuller, Cruiser Fleet Captain.

TOM PATTERSON It was brought to the attention of the Kditor that a long standing member of the Sailing Club, Tom Patterson, Senior Froduction engineer, Marconi, Basildon, was retiring on September 30th after 23 years with the company. To "celebrate" this event Bruce Lony has magnificently illustrated our inside cover this month, and we received the following from John Taylor at Basildon. I would be pleased if a mention of this laconic,cryptic, camera mad, boat "cat" mad otherwise agreeable Scot could be made in your September issue of Navigans. I don't know if this Scottish evolution business has anything to do with his leaving, but we have always maintained that had Hadrian's wall been another thirty feet higher Tom would not have suffered the ignominy of having his 'Supercat MK1 towed to a mud flat on Osea Island by a Mirror dinghy ably handled by Bruce Leggett and ddie Groves who, loath to adminster the ‘kiss of life" brought Tom and Tony l’ssex back to life with a hot drink. For a 'foreigner' say his associates he wasn't a bad ‘un. I have very pleasant memories of his performance on a fiddle with Sweet Georgia Brown. His performance wasn't with Sweet ( ‘rgia - he played the tune at our annual Christmas Party and Dinner at the iiasonic Hall Shenfield - his supporting cast, or backing being a bottle of CLAYVA or Drambuie. We shall certainly miss Tom whose all round knowledge of Electronic engineering techniques, "stickos", "goos", araldites, resins etc was invaluable —- especially when he was awake. MERSKA WEsK AND THe MARCONI SAILORS At about 09.00hrs on Monday 9th August. 1976 about twelve people from Marconi Saili. Club descended on Mersea Island. They took with them three Mirrors, one 420 followed by Frank Savill plus family plus Solo on Thursday and Friday. Not forgetting all the camping equipment. Apart from mud, mosquitoes and lack of wind at start times we all had an enjoyable week. The mud showed itself at low tide, (most days we launched at low tide), in the form of grey-black ooze, about a foot deep that spread everywhere. Feet sank in it, ropes trailed in it, sailing suits were covered in it, and launching trollies almost disappeared beneath it. By the time the race was over each day the tide was up and the mud was covered. The mud which had got into the boats was usually washed off during the race and disappeared through the self~bailers. The mosquitoes came out at dusk in their thousands. They must have been a special breed, they could sting even threwth thick clothing. Also they obviously enjoyed the finer things in life because they only seemed to bite the ladies. There were some very attractive ( and painful) pink and white mottled patterns on feminine legs the following mornings. : The wind wasabit late in getting up some mornin,s and on Thursday, Friday and Saturday the start line was out at the Nass Beacon, which meant paddling the boats for about a mile ( the blisters have almost healed now). Most days the wind did get up for start time and we had some good sailing. On Saturday we launched extra early to allow plenty of time to get to the start, but the wind also came up early and we arrived at the start line about an hour early. Well one can't be right everytime, can one? On the lighter side of the week, we had good weather, we won prizes, and had pleasant social gatherings in the evenings. One funny incident happened on Monday night, or was it the early hours of Tuesday morning, Pat? Pat was outside my tent calling, "Stan, something is wrong with my cooker".

Mersea Weekend the Marconi Sailors cont. I still don't know what she was doing with her cooker at one o'clock in the morning - or what was wrong with it ( but Pat, I award you full marks for being original). A word of thanks to all our crews(especially Katie) and to the wives who got us all to the starts on time, cheered us from the beach - fed us all, and were pleasant and attractive company in the evenings. THE MAwGU TROPHY The MAMGU Trophy is a 12' to 1" model of Mamgu presented by Mr and Mrs A.M.Adams to the Marconi Sailing Club for two purposes:- First, to commemorate the’ ship which for five vital years of the Club's growth served as our Clubhouse. Second, to promote a wider interest in the sea and seamanship by encouraging members to go cruising and to share their experiences for the benifit of others. The Trophy is to be awarded annually, and held by the winner for one year, for the best log and account of a cruise made in the preceding 12 months. The cruise must be in a sailing or auxiliary yacht or dinghy, and should be generally of at “rast three day's duration, though a shorter passage of particular interest may be consiusved. Use of engine, if any, must be stated. The log may usefully include details of the yacht and any other interesting and relevant matter. The author of the yacht must be a member or associate member of the Club; he/she must have taken an active part in sailing the yacht, but need not have been the owner, charterer or skipper. A small panel shall be appointed by the Committee to judge the entries, the decisic— of the panel shall be final. The panel need not consist entirely of club members. Logs are to be judged on their interest and value for others who may attempt similar cruises, and on the seamanship and enterprise implied by the whole undertaking. Thus riding out a gale or @ passage in heavy weather, conducted in a safe and proper manner and described well enough to assist another mariner in a like situation, should score highly, whereas a colourful account of escapades arising out of gross ignorance or neglect of seamanlike prudence or out of sheer foolhardiness, may be placed lower than a cruise in which hazardous conditions were avoided by good planning. A copy of each log entered for the MAWGU shall be presented to the Club if the judges deem it worthy, to be kept for members to read, and to be published, if required in "Navigans". The award of the WAMGU Trophy may he withheld in any year if the judges consider that no entries of sufficient merit have been received; but only after giving notice in "Navigans" at least two weeks before the closing date. CRUISING PRIZES Prizes will be awarded for member's first cruise, in the following categories:- (a) For a cruise to a neighbouring estuary. (>) For a week's cruise away from home waters. (c) For a cruise abroad. For (a) a cruise to a neighbouring estuary, it must be a complete out and return trip in one's own boat, sleeping on board, or camping, using only gear that has been carried in the boat. (The neighbouring estuary to the Blackwater does NOT include the Colne, i.e. the Blackwater and Colne are regarded as one estuary). For (b), a week's cruise away from home waters, the extremities of the cruise must be 40 miles apart, on a sea voyage. A chartered boat may be used as long as the entrant has complete charge of it. For (c), @ cruise abroad, the boat can be one's own or a chartered one. A brief written description will be required for all cruises, and these should be submitted to the Sailing Secretary. It should be noted that anyone receiving outside assistance while sailing will not be eligible for a prize. All these rules are flexible and each cruise submitted will be judged on its own merits and with regard to the circumstances under which it was made. HH KHME R HHH KH EK HH EH Are You Suffering From the "Itch" There ure, I understand, a number of people within the sailing club who have the "Itch". It is a condition which appears to affect members of all classes. The cause is hard to define, some of the afflicted claim that it is brought about by spending too much time in a trapeze belt, others claim thet the conditions experienced in a amall two person dinghy on a hot windless summer day are certain to bring on an attack. Then again, conversely, I hear thut otrers sufferers claim a few hours spent each week strapped into a trapeze belt would solve their problem — and single hunded sailors sometimes see a small two person bo:it as an instant panacea. So as you can see one persons salvation is another persons itch. I do not believe there is an easy solution to the problem but there may be one gleam of hope — group therapye Why not? It works for alcoholics, battered wives and compulsive flashers so why not for the poor oli itch sufferer. A friend of mine

i SGGee Gare belongs to a therapy group - for nervous twitchers - they meet at a "therapy centre" called the Blue Lion. After an evening spent imbiding quantities of elixier and en- gaging in heart to heart talks my friend and his associates often find that thier nerves are so steady thut they can't move from their chairs let alone exhibit 4 nervous twitch, which demonstrates just how effective these groups are. Anyway, I digress - back to the itch. Now this itch to change class ~- buy another boat -— or even build one is a dilema fucinz 4 number of us. Should we change to a class already existing in the club” or should we start a new one? I have made a few enquiries among the afflicted and after a bit of scratching around have come up with the qualities thought to be most desirable in 4 new class racing boat at the Marconi Sailing Club. She should be constructed from G.R.P. and be about 13' to 14' long, she must carry 4 spinnaker, be well represented locally and an established class nationally and should rate somewhere between 96 and 19°, Cost and durability are also important. Now there must be lots of boats which would fall into that loose description - one of which must fulfill all our require- ments. This is where the "group therapy" comes in. I suggest that all we who are seeking a new boat should meet at one of the local health centres to see if the spirit moves us — who knows we may 411 end up us part owners of a quarter tonner! Telephone me at either of the numbers below and I will add your name to the list to ensure you a place in the first session. Patrick Black, Chelmsford [redacted] Bilericay 22654, Ext 41. COMMODORES REPORT 1976 1976 has, as I have seen it, been a year of consolidation for the Club during which we have been learning tolive with, and take advantage of, the splendid facilities we now have at Stansgate. The incredibly fine sunner brought members to the club by the hundreds and I would venture that more members enjoyed more hours at their club than in any previous year. During the year a number of major repairs and improvements were undertaken and again a considerable amount of money has been invested for the future of the Club. Undoubtedly the major task of the year was the repair to the Hard last Christmas when many hundreds of hours of voluntary work were put in and with the generous help of friends of the Club, who provided machinery and plant, we were able to protect the launching facilities of the Club for the future. More recently we arranged for the repair of the road which provides our access to the site. Our work last year to alter the drainage system was not so successful as we had hoped, due to the uncertain level of the water table on the site. To take advantage of the soak-away system we had installed, we were foced to introduce, during last spring an extra man hole and by purchasing a pump we have been able to pump over from the col- lection tank to the: dispersal system and in this way we have been able to cope with the continually increasing volume of largely fresh water waste created on the site. The pumping is normally carried out at times when there is little activity at the Club. We have been fortunate again this year in having the continued services of Claud Emerson to look after our Clubhouse and its surrounds. He is often helped by his wife and between them they have done a magnificent job in keeping the Clubhouse in an almost continuous state of readiness for us. It would appear that the observations made last year on the general cleanliness of the Club did not go unheeded but we newer cease to be amazed by the amount of unclaimed lost property that accumulates and much of it not inexpensive clothing. Financially we seem to be solvent still despite considerable expenses during the year and our Treasurer, Ted Barnes, has kept a close eye on our budgets, I am pleased to report that our contribution to the MASC for 1977 for the use of the site remains _ unchanged. During the year we experienced a break-in for the first time for 4 number of years but we were fortunate that our losses and cost of damage repairs was only £10. This does however highlight the need for constant vigilance and we are strongly of the opinion that our locked gate provides a major deterrent to the casual unwanted light fingered visitor and offers significant protection to both Club and personal property. While on the subject of g,te locks, many of you will have noticed the number of cars that accumulate outside our boundary and we are in discussion with the Tenant Farmer and the Owners of the adjacent sites on methods of discouraging the unauthorised usgof the approach road which is causing a4,:gravation to all the legitimate users. Our sub-committee and volunteers have again worked extremely hard this year on all theactivities of the Club and many successes have been achieved.There is one area where a apecial mention is deserved and this is the Galley which has provided sustenance to many a cold and wet sailor throughout the year. Our thanks go to Jill Savill, who took this over when Margaret Cottam retired last year, and to her willing, cheerful and hard working band of ladies who have given a marvellous service which has been appreciated by 411 who use the Club, I am pleased to say she has volunteered to continue for another yoar. This year we say farewell to a few Main Committee members but I am pleased to say many others are offering themselves for re-election tonight. To those departing, Hric Royle our secretary for the last three years, Roger Durrant, Tony Cherry, Gerry Bamford

a and Brenda Tate, Navigans Editor for the last three years, 1 would like to express my sincere thanks for the support they have given to me, to the Club and to past Officers during the time they have served the Club. You may have noticed that one name has been left off the list. After 4 long and difficult search without much success among the members for a replacement Sailing Secretury John Weedon, who has already served four years and does not want to see the sailing activities decline in the Club, has offered to see us through another year. I am sure you will all want to thank him as I do for this act of generosity. I would add that in reaching this decision, I believe John was influenced by the willingness of a fairly new member to the Club Mike Vaughan, who accepted nominetion for the main Committee with the express purpose of assisting John as Sailing Secretary, Thank you both for helping to solve what was becoming a very difficult situation. There are also a number of new names on the nominations list who will be readily welcomed together with the appointed Officers onto the Committees for the coming year. During the year a lot of work has gone into bringing the Club rules up to date and later we have the formal proposition to adopt these revised rules. In parallel with thi>, we have been redefining the function of the Club Officers and sub-committees. The need for both these activities arises out for the growth of the Club and its f,cilities and hence the work and it is being done so that more work can be carried out at Sub-committee level and thus the amount of detailed work done by the Main Committee can be reduced. The terms of reference are not finalised but the first drafts are available and the refined versions will evolve as experience is gained by using them. We are hopeful that these changes will do something to reduce the load on some of the Committee members by spreading it more evenly and that we may be able to shorten sume of the meetings that can become bogged down in detail. Time will tell. This report would be incomplete without mentioning our cadets, their skipper, Rick Anstey, and Colin Leveridge who together have achieved such success with their sailing, their tuition and their examinations for the RYA Elementary Day Boat Certificate. Con- gratulations to all who have been successful this year and good luck to all those going on into next year. Perhaps we should all remember that a strong and active cadet section today represents an insurance for the future of the Club and be thankful that this side of our membership is being revitalised. In this report I have said very little about the sailing side of our activities as that will be covered by our Sailing Secretary in his report. I would however like to pay tribute to the hard working members of the Club who have provided the racing facilities by manning the Race box and Rescue launcles each weekend during the season and without whose help there would be no organised sailing. A number of our social events have not been supported so well this year which is obviously a dissapointment to both our Social Secretary and your committee. A lot of hard work goes into the programme and without a feedback it is difficult to know what is required. We are always open to suggestions on the sort of thing wanted and extra help with the organisation is always welcome. This year brought the tenth anniversary of our licenced bar at Stansgate.e. It is very difficult to keep track of a commitment ten years in the future if you were not there in the beginning and thoser that were are not around at the unexpected anniversay. Hence your committees severe embarrassment when quite by chance it was discovered that our Club Registration had expired. Immediate action was taken to renew the Registration and I am pleased to report that there were no objections to it being renewed so we must have been thought to be keeping an orderly house and we can continue to drink with confidence for another ten years. A great deal of work goes into organising and stocking our bar for the benefit of Members and our thanks are due to all those who contributed to provide this welcome facility. I do not feel I can conclude this report without mentioning the Navigans Production

team who have sent regularly to all members 4 copy of our monthly publication. This team has worked extremely hard and well and our new Editor is preparing for the coming year. Thank you Brenda and Vic Tate and Mick Gray, the backroom boy, our Registrar, who collates addresses and dispatchs some 450 copies each month. In conclusion I would like to thank 4ll the members of the various committees, who have spent so many hours on the business of the Club for the support given both to me and the Club. I would also like to thank all of you, the members and friends, who have helped with the day to day activities of the Club and who have provided the vital services that are a necessary part of the life of the Club. Thank You. John Witter, Commodore. SOCIAL SCREED We should all be just about recovered from the Christmas and New Year festivities by now I guess. The new social sub-committee had it's first meeting in December, the main item being the social programme for 1977. This has been agreed by the main committee and will be published the Year Book to be issued shortly. My hope for 1977 is that we have better support for the social events during this year. Support for some events during 1976 was disappointing with about 170 turning up for the Christmas Dance and only 150 adults for the Laying-Up Supper - rather poor for a club boasting a member- ship of around 400. Having held the Laying-Up supper for two years ut the M.A.5.C., your committee has decided after considerable thought, argument and taking account of the general feeling of the membership, to hold the event this year at the Lion and Lamb. We hope this may encourage more along and halt the gradual decline in attendance - more about this later in the year. As I announced in the December Navigans , the first winter neeting will be held at the M.A.S.C., Beehive Lane, on Wednesday 26th January. This will take the form of 4 discussion forum and will be in two parts. The first part will be concerned with the rules of racing, with Roger Hance leading the field as usual and giving us the benefit of his knowledge and experience. The second part will be concerned with the choice of dinghys, and should be of interest to those contemplating changing class, new members and may help to reinforce existing fleets, or resolve the issue of a new class within the club. I hope the fleets will be represented in strength if only to look after their own interests. The second winter meeting is scheduled for the 23rd February (Wednesday), and it is hoped to show a film and have an experienced sailor along tu tulk about cruising in the Greek Islands. This will be confirmed in the next issue. Roy Batty’ soil Secretary.

My thanks to those Parents who bring the Cadets every time. Januery's meetings are as follows:- Elementary - Wednesday January 12 — 7.30. Committee Room Intermediate - Wednesday January 19 - 7.30. " Elementary evening is to cover 1. Recovery of man overboard. 2. Safty afloat. (items three and four in the Log Book) Intermediate evening is to cover 1. Sailing a given course. 2. Basic knowledge of sea terms. The February issue of Navigans will be devoted to Cadets as the January 1976 issue. > Would as many of you as possible write an article about any subject associated with sailing and send to Shirley Wood by the end of week ending February 5th 1977. Rick Anstey, Cadet Captain. Mona's Cup I wonder how many of our present members know the origin of Mona's Cup? In the early fifties, when our headquarters were situated at Heybridge Basin, we made frequent visits to the Jolly Sailor whose proprietoress was Miss Mona Clarke, who inherited it from her parents. As she was a very friendly soul, and took a special interest in our sailing ac- tivities, she kindly presented us with a fine challenge cup to be awarded to the winner ~, of an annual all-in race, and this is still included in our programme. TM* On one occasion, Mona actually came aboard Mamgu and fired the gun starting this race. In later years, this has rather tended to be supported by dinghies from our present premises at Stansgate but in future, more cruisers should be en€ouraged to participate and it is suggested that Mona should be invited to be present for the occusion. On one occasion when this race was sailed from Stansgate the first mark of the eourse was up river, and the Southey Spit Buoy had to be rounded but as the tide was falling some cruisers found there was insufficient water to make it! Mons has now retired but still lives at Heybridge and The Jolly Saigdor is now run by Eric Priestly, incidentally an ex Marconi man. Incidentally, our first laying-up supper was held at The Jolly Sailor in October 19575 we hired the large inner room and ate our sausages and mince pies standing up, and went through to the bar for our drinks$ there was no music to drown our exchanges of events during the past sailing season, and it was a thoroughly enjoyable evening. Amongst our guests was Douglas Thompson, Commodore of the The Blackwater Sailing Club and Sam Poulton from The Maldon Little Ship Club. The price of the tickets was 4/- or 6/6 including the price of the coach which brought us.

-i4- Our first formal laying-—up supper was held at the New Street canteen, which we were pleased to call The Palm Court, on Friday, November 1, 1958; most of the Commodore's of the clubs on the Blackwater were present as was Bill Hillman, Commodore of the B.B.C. Ariel Club, whoses premis’es are on the Thames at Teddington. The price of the tickets was 9/— including the band, but not the drinks! We used to race against the Ariel Club at Teddington and in return, they came to Heybridge the following year, but eventually it was dropped largely because of the distance and absence of boats available. However, a trophy consisting of our respective burgees mounted on q plinth still exists, but as the Ariel S.C. were the last to win it, they are retaining it. SATLMAKER Adrian White of 30 Basin Road, Heybridge has retired from a well-known firm of sailmakers, largely due to ill health, but he is available for all work to do with sails, covers and tarpaulins, which he undertakes at his home. I have given him several jobs ) during the last season, which he has executed very satisfactorily and at most reasonable prices and he slways makes a point of keeping his delivery dates, so give him a try. "420's RULE — 0.K.3" I was motivated by Patrick Black's most sensible suggestion in the December issue of Navigans to co-ordinate and direct the search several members are embarking upon to satisfy their "itch" to change class of boats for the coming season. I am quite sure that the success of a racing season largely depends on 4 sound competitive spirit in well balanced dinghy classes. Reading the trepidution that clearly exists among those members who wish to change classes, may I quite publicly and loyally attempt to remove any indecision and firmly suggest the 420 class which admirably satisfies Patrick's specification for the ideal racing class at our club. Any new class would have 4a solid foundation in the existing few, regularly raced boats and I am confident th:t we have the nucleus of a flourishing class which could become of the club's most successful fleets yet. May I echo Mike Hart's comments of last year by expounding the virtues of the 420? Length - 13'9", GRP construction, Spinnaker, weight - 220lbs, handicap — 96. Continuing THE LOG OF "ACI OF DIAMONDS" 1976 HOLLAND CRUISE Saturday 24th July 06.33 Shipping Forecast. Tyne/Humber/Thames/Dover NW veering northerly 3-4. Galloper N3, visibility 11 miles pressure 1023 steady Vic bought two gallons of petrol as we had used more than anticipated yesterday. We now carried enough fuel for 19 hours motoring at full throttle. (Ace's consumption being 1 gallon per hour at full throttle.) 09-00 Slipped lines at Lavington. Little wind but what there was came from the east, genoa and main set goose-winged down to Harwich but the engine went on to get us down river and off Harwich by 10.00. The sky was cloudy but plenty of sunshine. G, 45 Clear of Harwich, off engine. Course set 115°C for Rough's Tower. Main and genoa sete 10.35 Engine on again 4s we are not making enough way for passage making. Genoa down as it was just flogging, log streamed. 11.40 Rough's Tower abeam, course altered to 100°C to allow for tidal set. Plenty of Portuguese Man-of+War jelly fish and large clumps of weed around must be all the hot weather. The wind began to freshen slightly and we could see rain approaching from the north west. 12.20 Rain arrived, Robert on the helm in oilskins. 12230 Lose sight of land, rain died away. 1235 Sunk Light vessel abeam. 17° 80 Engine off, sailing about 3kts. I went below to prepare a lunch of chicken sandwiches, cake, coffee and squash. It made me feel so bad I missed the Shipping Forecast aguin. 14.00 Engine on. 16.30 Galloper Light Ship abeam. Course altered to 110°C for North Hinder, the really long leg of the trip. Wind beginning to freshen. 18.00 Vic asleep below, so was Robert, at the helm. I took the tiller while he got his head down, it was going to be a long night. 19.00 Unfortunately had to wake Vie and ask if the engine could be switched off. We were clipping along the time and a nasty quartering sea caused the gunwales to go under occasionally. Vic returned to his pit, Mary and I on helm. 21.00 Sighted North Hinder Light vessel. 22 200 North Hinder abeam, and in the very lust of the daylight we sorted out the bout for the night. Genoa down, No. 1 up, Navigation lights on, all went gmoothly apart. frc Robert and Mary beiNé seasick but this they did with the

03.00 = 06.00 Robert on helm. Life jackets and life lines were always worn at night. 04.00 — 06.00 Vic asleep. Our course for closing the Dutch Coast north of Zeebrugge kept us out of the shipping lanes but we crossed over the Thornton and Raan Banks. This resulted in a very short, confussed, lumpy sea. The next eight hours I recall very hazily as I felt decidedly "bad" and retired to my bunk. The wind had freshened and was blowing a fitful 4-5. I awoke about midnight and grabbed the washing up bowl quick. Once that was over I felt almost human aguin, but I had to perform one-handed gymnastics to get myself plus the bowl out into the cockpit avoiding Robert who was fast asleep on the floor cuddling the genoa. Outside in the fresh air things started to improve even more despite my husband's remarks about,"Do you wonder why you joined." I sat down on the thwart and looked around. Over our stern were the con- stantly changing navigational lights of Vanellus and Natasha as they rode over the waves about two miles away. There was no moon to be seen but thousands of glittering stars above an inky black sea. Ace was tpamping on like a good'un through wave crests laced with tiny gleams of phosphorsce. There were ship's lights everywhere. Vic counted 14 on the edge of the bank. I returned to my bunk and dozed until around 03.00 when Vic awoke Robert to take his turn on the tiller. Vic was relieved as although he had seem the loom er: Ostende and Zeebrugge and the lights of the ferries going into the harbour he was glad to get below, muke a hot drink and check his chart calculations, which had been worked out about a week before we hud set out to sea. Our E.T.A. for Breskens wus 08.00, and we were about an hour ahead of schedule, which gave us the problem of having to punch a foul tide. Between 03.00 and 04.00 everyone seemed to be scratching around even Mary woke up and sat transfixed on the companion way steps gazing with eyes as hig as saucers. 04.00 All quiet again, Robert on the helm, Vic on the floor (his 3 star hotel he called it) and Mary and I on the leeward bunks. Wind blowing harder now. 06.30 Woke up, so I must have slept although it didn't feel like it. Breskens ~ harbour entrance ahead. Log in, engine on, sails down, crept quietly alongside a large ketch moored on the visitors berth. 06.45 We were there. Sunday 25th July 09 .00 The wind was blowing well now, Force 6, even behind the shelter of the marina wall. We breakfasted on fresh mackerel and decided that a passage across the Westerschelde would be very choppy and thut it was worth staying the night and see how things were in the morning; because of this, the Harbour Master allocated us another berth to keep the visitors pontoons clear. Engine on, Robert on the helm, we moved away from the ketch out and across to the opposite line of pontoon. We found our place and Robert began to manoeuvre Ace in between two boats so that she would be lying bow onto the pontoon. I was standing by the pulpit on deck with a bow line ready. Vie shouted to Robert to throw the gear lever into reverse, but horror of horrors the cones did not disengage and Ace stayed ahead. She hit the pontoon with an almighty wallop, her bow rearing up out of the water and then sliding down again. As luck would have it the pontoom was a curved

wooden one, floating about a foot out of the water. We inspected the damage and found it was not as bad as we feared, The puint had been chipped away and the wood bruised in two places on the stem, well above the water line, but this would be repairable without too much difficulty. All we had was explain to Tony!! and handle the clutch with more care. Bresken's Marina is large accommodating approx. 700 boats. The pontoons are excellent with water stand pipes every 30 yards. Petrol and diesel are available. The only disappointing feature were the sh wers and loos housed in portable units at the top of the marina wall. The showers were a guilder a time. The Yatch Club is situated along the main road into Breskens about 1/4 of a mile away. The town itself, with shops and supermarkets is about 1/2 mile from the marina. In the early evening Vic and I strolled around the town and on the way back stopped to look at the Fishing fleet which was in the harbour. Vast nets were spread out to dry and hanging from derricks on the deck were huge "tickler" chains used for dragging the sea bed. While cleaning my teeth in the lady's loos, I looked up and a vaguely familiar face said, "Hello". I suddenly realised that it was the lady who sometimes sails on Eric Young's boat Snedronning. It was lovely to pave a chat, they were now on thejr way home having been up as far as Middelburg. Monday 26th July 09.00 Up and away, destination Middleburg. As we had hoped the weather improved visibility was good, plenty of cloud but the sun was shinning. Fresh northerly wind. Genoa and mainsail set, once we were clear of the marina. Ace beat across the Westerschelde, we kept well down to avoid the large sand bank that lies to tie East. We turned to starboard once near tre northern shore and suiled up towards the lock entrance. Engine on and sails down, we didn't have to wait long dodging the ferries before we were in the lock. There were no difficulties with lines, we went alons the wall. Brian brought Natasha alongside us. It wasn't very crowded. The lock at Flushing was the largest th.t we encountered during our cruise, as it is the enctrance to the canal system of Zeeland, it is used extensively by commercial tratfic. The general procedure when entering any lock in Holland is to wait and listen “or the Lock Master's instructions. He will have running bow and stern lines to the rings or bollards which are situated along it. These can then be adjusted as the I water level alters, and can be quickly and easily slipped if required. Never, wver have fixed lines. I have seen the owner of a large, expensive motor launch hacking at his ropes with a carving knife as the water receded at least a foot away from his hull. Once through the lock and into the canal system we made our way up to Middelburg. Brian made a quick dash into the Flushing Yatchhaven to see if twoother Marconi boats, Teal and Jestabel were in residence, without sucess No trouble with the three bridges that crossed the canal butan interesting incident while waiting to go through the last, the mainroad bridge by the railway station in Middelburg. We were gilling around in company with half-a-dozen yachts and a couple of barges, Vic on the helm bent to adjust the throttle and the handle came off in his hand!! Vanellus took alongside while some fast repairs were carried out. Under the bridge we passed with nostalgia the bus stop where the Marconi fleet had moored last year. Turning left off the main canal into the town system we had to wait about 5 minuites for a dainty white painted wrought iron road bridge to be raised. Once through we were delighted to find that this portion of the waterway had been piled and pontooned, there were even portaloo' and a rubbish truck on the quay side. In a few munutes we were safely tied WP da our berth. ddelburg, the county town of Walcheren, is charming, with many buildings

of historical and architectural interest, and on this occasion bursting to the seams with holiday makers. We took the children on the pony bus to see the sights and then retreated back to our peaceful holiday haven. We spent a very pleasant evening, Vic and Robert in a local bar with a gentleman from a Maldon boat "Wigwam", I on Natasha with Brian and Jackie and their neighbours, a couple on "BarbareeLl", out of Bradwell. It's a small world. to be continued... A letter to the editor Dear Editor, I would like to make a somewhat belated comment on the Laying-Up supper. I am sure that many members like myself are not prepared to psy some £4 per ticket for an indifferent formal dinner/com e disco party. SOCIAL SCREED A fair size audience attended the first winter meeting to listen to an interesting and informative talk by Roger Hance on racing rules, with a useful guide to racing tactics thrown in as a bonus. Thanks go to Roger. The discussion on club dinghy classes during the second half of the evening was wel] supported by a number of speakers, who put forward good arguments for their classes. It was perhaps too much to hope that we would finish the evening with a clear idea of which fleets the club aught to be seeking to strengthen in the future. I'm sure this discussion will continue if only on an informal basis, The second winter meeting is scheduled for the 23rd February at the W.A.S.C. start- ing at 7.45 pom. We will be showing a film aboutcruising in the Greek Islands and there will be a speaker from the Yacht Cruising Association, who has sailed these waters. A date for your diaries is Saturday March 26th - this is the date of the Fitting- Out Party to be held at Stansgate starting at 8.00 p.m. There will be 4 group and a4 buffet with tickets on sale soon at £1.00 each. If there is sufficient demand a coach will be run. Further details in the next issue. Roy Battye, Social Secretary. WHY CHOOSE THE 420 DINGHY? Further to the discussions held at a recent social meeting I would like to outline the reasons for promoting the 420 as a possible future fleet at Marconi. When one considers the existing dinghy classes - Hornet, Enterprise, Mirror and recently the GP14, these were all designed as hard chine, plywood skinned and thus suit— able for amateur construction. As many people are how likely to be attracted by the lower maintenance requirements of G.R.R., a boat designed solely for G.P.R. construction would be preferred (it is acknowledged however that the above classes, except the mirror are available in G.R.P. but these are not accepted as competitive ih all circles). The other requirements as far as I was concerned were to have a spinnaker, to be reasonably light and competively sailed locally without being too demanding physically. The 420 I believe fills these requirements. However the main snag encountered wus the limited supply of suituble secondhand boats and as a consequence their cost. Having acquired a 420 after overcoming the above problem I am pleased to report that the boat can be very satisfying to sail especially in a good breeze, being very stable but quick to accelerate in the gusts and comfortable to sail. Beating in light weather is probably one of its weak points but this can still be a challenge. The foregoing is not intended to split the existing fleets but to encourage one or two mirror crews to graduate for which the 420 would be ideal or some of the handicap menagerie to change or even for those who are not yet boat owners to come to a satisfactory decision. Any further information gludly given. John Weedon, Sailing Secretury. Tel. Work, Wuteyphous Lahe, “xt 2177 Home Chelmsford [redacted].

THAT 'ITCK' AGAIN Roy Battye, writing in the January Navigans, suggested that part of the first winter lecture would be concerned with the choice of dinghys, and that the discussion might help to resolve the issue of a new class within the club. Perhaps not surpris- ingly the meeting did not resolve this matter, and the discussion became the usual hard sell by individuals or groups wishing to promote their favourite class. In the end the clock terminated the discussion leaving the merits of some classes unsung. I would like to take this opportunity to continue the discussion on a slightly different tack, but I must stress that this is a personal view and not a club view. I want to consider the question — "Which dinghy classes should be adopted by the club?" But first let us look at the advantages afforded a class after it's adoption by the club. Class racing results are published, and in some cases class trophies provided for the various series sailed. The class is also represented directly on the sailing sub-committee, which obviously imcreases its influence on sailing matters. Also, the club looks favourably at requests for class open meetings and this in turn gives rise to increased interest in the class. So, which classes should be adopted by the club? Surely the simple answer is that the club should adopt any class that can justify fleet status. By this I mean, any class large enough to support the race programme provided for it, and large enough to provie it's share of the effort required to run the race programme, namely Race officers and Rescue Crew. Classes no longer able to satisfy the required conditions must be relegated to the Handicap fleet, and the embryo classes must grow within this same fleet. After all it is still possible for the members of small classes to extract their own class results from the handicap results. Once established within the handi- cap fleet a fully grown class can apply for adoption by the club. So mueh for the club's choice of dinghy class; what about your choice? You must first decide whether to choose a two-man boat or a single-hander. If you have a reg- ular working relationship with another person, a two-man boat will, ih my opinion, provide the greatest satisfaction. Of course, there are some of us who fail to cult- ivate that good working relationship. We have to be satisfied with a single sail, but don't misunderstand me it has the great advantage of independence, and with only _myself to blame it is sometimes easier to analyse my mistakes. The list of possible boats has now been reduced, and if your personal require— ment can be met by an existing club class, your ,roblem is solved. If you choose to sail single-handed there is no suitable club cl.ss a present. Even if you choose to sail with a crew there may be many good reasons why the existing club classes are not suitable to you. You are therefore about to join the handicap fleet. What are the disadvantages of sailing with the handicap fleet? In any single race, even classes having the same handicap number will perform differently and winning is often amatter of luck. It can happen that even a long series of races over one course area will give an advantage to one type of boat due to the prevailing conditions. The handicap numbers will only be correet for along series of races over all types of course on ponds river, estuary and sea conditions with fixed line and co.mittee boat starts. Normél class racing tactics are irrelevant, and in general it is difficult, if not im- possible, to improve your racing performance. Real inprovement can only be achieved by racing against boats of the same class. One more of the sane type will do, but the more there are the better the racing. If you choose a boat class thut will not give you the required competion at the club you will have to go elsewhere for your competition sailing. Indeed, if sailing

Gt is more important to you trun the club, it may be reasonable to move to a club with an adopted class to suit you. There are some advantages for both clubs and the class if this is done. An alternative solution is to choose a class sailed regularly by nearbye clubs, since this will at least enable you to attend thier open meetings, It may help to look at the list of classes sailed at our own regatta. Once you have decided to depart from the existing club classes the choice for you is quite wide because the actual type you bring to the club is not important. However, your choice will be affected by such factors as, do you wish to race, do you wish to improve your performance, are there plenty of local open meetings, price, second-hand market, the choice already made by others and whether your choice is likely to affect the choice of others. The last two factors are quite important since they affect the possible growth of a new class within the club. Finally let me say that I will not be fully satisfied until I am able to sail in a club adopted class, and if , as might well happen, a Moth class is established due to the keeness of our cadet fleet, I might one day be persuaded to join. In the mean- time I have made my choice and I am very satisfied with the sailing it gives me. Now it is up to you to make your choice and then go out and buy that SOLO or Moth or SOLO or 420 or SOLO or Express or SOLO OFfeceereeee Frank Savill, Rm. 1234/1, A Block, Baddow.
