TURNING OUT TIME Would abl of you who store your boats with Alf Cottan please get together with him for their removal on Sunday 27th March after 2.00p.m. What's all this about 4 new dinghy class? I attended a social meeting recently, at the M.A.S.C., held to obtain some tips from Roger Hance on the racing rules and I thought, to discuss the possibility of a new dinghy class for Marconi. Some of the comments made were sufficient to make any discerning class captain turn to sailing model boats and to make me write to Navigans$ This is about the third season discussion has got around to a new dinghy class, how- ever no-one has yet said exactly what is wrong with the present adopted classes. Well, I hope I can start your ink flowing by making these observations :- It seems to me that as the Marconi Club is made up of people with different needs is sailing, such as:— those who are novices or have a young crew, those who re- quire a cruisihg/racing dinghy, those who want a thoroughbred two sail racing dinghy, those who want an exiegiting threesail racing machine, and finally those who want (or need) to sail single handed. In view of this, several complementary classes of dinghy are required to fulfil these varying needs, and I think the Mirror, G.P.14, Enterprise, Hornet and Solo or Lazer do just that. If there were two similar classes the effect woul be to waste potential of both classes. Therefore any new class would have to be com- pletely different, or supersede one of these classes. As an enthusiast who wants the challenge of a three sail racing machine, I believe the Hornet to be the best class on our river to fit the bill. I have written about its virtues before. It has after all been selected over the past 25Yours by many well known helsmen, and hus been used in Poland as an Olympic trainer. I don't intend to go into details about it's attractions, except to say that over the past ten years of sailing Hornets, I have had a lot of enjoyment from them, and made a lot of friends both at our club and around the country, and I would not wish (short of winning the pools) to sail any other dinghy. If you fancy the challenge of a three sail racing machine, why not try a Hornet? Anyone who wants to sail or maybe just crew,can contact Pete Clayton, out fleet captain who will make you very welcome, and may even buy you a beer at one of our Friday social meetings: Mike Turner, Hornet K 1937.

= +0"= THE LOG OF"ACE OF DIAMONDS" 1976 Continuing HOLLAND CRUIS TUESDAY 27th July 09.30 We discovered that the wrought iron bridge was opened on the half hour, so after breakfast we left heading northwards for Veere. The wind was fresh northerly, cloudy sky. Approaching Veere we spotted a familiar boat flying the M.S.C. burgee, Davolas II. A quick tete-a—-tete, or should it be tete- a-Tate, with John, who after a pleasant holiday was homeward bound. He told us that Tealand Jestabel were staying in Goes for a few days. The Veere lock was very crowded, everyone jammed together like sardines in a tin. The Dutch coped in their usual efficent way, despite the help of an Irish gentleman, single-handed in 4 tiny but obviously well travelled boat. Locked out, into Veerse Meer turning to port and through the harbour entrance. 11.00 Tied up by the old town quay, occupying the same position as lust yeur. Veere is beautiful, the town skyline dominated by the vast Groote Kirk und spire of the town hall, although like Middleburg, it was full of holiday makers. The facilities at the Yacht Club, which is situated by the harbour entrance are excellent, meals are aveilable, and their showers were the cheapest that I encountered (25c.). Petrol and diesel can be obtained from the Yaeht haven near the entrance to the lock. The Post Office, shops and bank are literally across the road from the quay. After lunch we set off for Goes. Vic had bought an excellent map of the atfea from the locul chandler's, costing 95c. Studying this we decided to leave the boats behind and take to the Dutch publié transport system. The Tovey's joined us, Brian and Jackie were waiting to meet some Dutch friends. 16.00 The bus journey from Veere to Goes via Middleburg was uneventful. We sat back, relaxed and enjoyed the countryside. 17.15 We arrived at Goes Yacht haven to discover it was my niece’ Fiona's birthday so we joinedthe party and enjoyed 4 magnificent feust on Jestabel. The weather and setting were really superb, the wine flowed freely, and we very reluctantly took our leave just after 21.00 We caught the local train back to Middleburg only to discover that due to someone mis—reading the bus time-table (MZ), we had missed the las6 bus home. It was a very weary party that bundled into taxi's to take us the last 7 kilometers into Veere, but it was all rather fun, I've never ridden ina Mercedes before. WEDNESDAY 28th July The wind had freshened and a good NNW Force 3-4 with the occasional stronger gust was blowing resulting in very choppy conditions in the Meer. Vanellus and Ace left mid- morning leaving Natasha who planned to travel further afield than us. Motored out of the harbour entrance, turned to the north set main and genoa, cut engine. Invigorating sail up to the North Sea dam, keeping a sharp look out for the marker buoys, there's no tide here and going aground here means a lot of trouble. Dropped the hook for lunch and then hitched a lift on Vanellus, who with her bilge keels could go alongside the jetty at the edge of the Meer. We hal a bracing walk ulong the top of the dam, the sea looked very unpleasant for ssiling, but plenty of people were swimming. Ice creams by the rather murky water- side, interesting to note, plenty of portaloos and rubbish bins. Up anchor and sailed back down keeping to the north shore, still Main und genoa. COMMODORES NOTES It is now two months since I contributed to Navigans and during this period I have felt very much akin to a boat in winter with polythene wraps over parts of the house and damp creeping in everywhere while alteration and rebuilding has been goimjon. I am now pleased to say thut with the advent of the brighter weather the work is complete and like most of you I 4m beginning to think about sailing again. It is pleasing to note that even in these hard times our level of membership in renewal this year hus dropped by no more than is normal in any year and may actually have dropped less than usual. It could be that people are inclined to see 1977 as a stay at home year and will be enjoying more of the excellent facilities they have on their own door steps. As was reported last year the Stansgate farms were being offered for sale and we now know that the whole estate has been sold by Gonville and Caius College to a Dutchman who we understand has bought as an agricultural investment and is not aiming to build the projected marina in Ramsey Marshes. We have not as yet had any direct contact with the new owner or his agent but we hope to establish the same fraendly relationship we had with Gonville and Cauis. We also understand that the farms will continue to be farmed by the existing tenant farmer. Some of you may also have seen in the national and local Press suggestions thut there might be a district refuse tip sited at Stansgate but I am pleused to advise you that common sence has prevailed and Maldon is going to keep its own rubbish and enlarge the existing tip. With the Sailing season approaching the question ef who is going to sail which cluss is aguin being asked. I have been following the discussion and cor- respondence with interest as it is a route we huve been before. The main difference is that this time we already have four established classes (Enterprise, Mirror, Hornet and Handicap) and if we made the count a year or so ago five if we include the GP 14. Last time there were two classes (Enterprise aid Handicap) and three if we included the then ailing Fleetwind Cluss. At this time we were, as now, con- sidering what additional classes the Club should adopt. Many suggestions were made and many hobby horses mounted but in the end the new classes adopted, Hornet and GP 14 were determined by the endeavours of the protagonists of their classes overcoming the attempts of others to establish such classes as Snipe, Fireball and Flying Dutch- mane This was achieved without destroying any of the existing classés. In a Club like ours, which is basically a family one open to any employee of the G.F.C. - Marconi Group of Companies, it is not our custom to make membership conditional on ownership of a particular class of dinghy or to stipulate that one must race a certain number of times a year. For these reasons the Committes cannot dictate the classes that will be sailed but can only recognise a trend and endeavour to steer people towards a particulur class which when there is sufficient interest may be adopted. As I see it, and this is a personal view, there is a need to re-establish the GP 14 or to find a suitable alternative such as say the 420 so as to re-introduce the variety of choice of class for those wishing to graduate from Mirrors. There is also a very obvious need to look closely at the Singlehanded situation er, like most other clubs have at sometime or ot’ery we are going through the phase where there is a demand for single handed class sailing. It is now probably too late to adopt a singlehanded Handicap Clauss within the Handicap Class and bears on the sucess of this make some recommendations for next year. In the final analysis however, the choice of classes must be urrived at by examining the track record of those offered. This means that a common end proved desire for a particular class must be demonstrated so if we really do need a new class or two some effective lobbying will be necessary to establish a class that meets the specification re- quired by the majority seeking a charge. This I believe is now beginning to happen

but followers of our existing classes must not be complacent and will need to continue to canvas in order to maintain their existing strength as it is inevitable that in building up another class some converts will come from our already establish- ed classes and we could end up by weakening our competitve sailing and setting back the clock. John Witter, Commodore. CRUISER FLEET NEWS We have sold all available tickets for the Fleet supper evening but I would like to remind you all of the Club's Fitting out Party, also to be held at Stansgate on March 26th. Fitting out must be well under way now and I hope that many of us have acquired new life jackets, learnt more about the use of distress flares, and have invested well in paint. But may I rembnd everyone of two essentials - firstly to care- fully inspect rigging and replace any itme that is in any way doubtful and second- ly ,» to examine mooring equipment for soundness before launching. It is too easy to assume things are O.K. because they were lust year. Many club members are interested in the traditional wooden boat and these people in particular will be sorry to learn that Reg Patten died a few weeks ago after a short illness. Reg spent many years with Dauntless while their business expanded in the early duys after the war, and then about 1958 he set up Sea King in a little shed ih Leigh High Street, He built sixty seven sailing Sea Kings and a few motor cruisers. It must be true that no two of these are identical 4s a policy of continuous improvement was adopted. Any customers ideas were built in and then often became the new standard. The first boats were 23ft and the range extends to just over 30ft, at which size there is no more rom in the shed. Only one set of moulds is used, these fit the 23 footer and planking for the larger boats a misses the moulds by the appropriate amount. A particularly remarkable process since © not one plank in a clinker built boat is straight. When I asked Reg which bilge pump he recommended me to fit in Kalinka his reply was simply " You don't need one", Confidence indeed, but Kalinka has never taken in any water except rain since the moment of launching. Such expertise is getting rare these days but fortunately Keith Patten is continuing the business so you can still have a new craftsman built boat if you want one. The Greek Islands will be our subject for our Aprilmeeting at the Generals Arms. That will be our last programme until Autumn but I hope members will continue to meet through the summer. Our fleet funds are sufficient to pay for the room even allowing for the inevitably reduced numbers during "The SEason". Finally I hope to see you all on the water shortly - may we be blessed with sunny skies and fair winds in the coming s#ason. THY LOG OF "ACH OF DIAMONDS" 1976 Continuin: HOLLAND CRUISE: Saturday 3ist July Up late, still raining. Vic and I spent the morning shopping and looking over 4 Sabre that we had noticed wus for sale. Could this be our next boat? We certainly liked the look of her. 12.30 Left the marina heading up the Veerse Meer, main and genoa set, close hauled wind NNW Force 4. A fierce rain squall blew up after we had been out for 15 min- utes and after 2 little arguing it was decided that the jenny was unsuitable in the adverse weather conditions and some what crowded waterways. We ran under main for a time and then set the No. l. All went well untill we reached the most southerly point near Aarberien Hiland, we now had to beat up towards Veer and this made conditions below somewhat unpleasant. We took down all sail and started the engine and motored on past Veere. We saw "Lady Ann", a boat owned at various times by several members of the Tate family and now kept in the canat at Heybridge, with Mirror tender anchored just north of the harbour entrance. We carried on for another mile and went into Oostwatering. This is an enormous marina still uncompleted and we were the only English boats there. We had a walk roun between rain squalls and then settled down for the night and listened to the wind howling in the shrouds. Sunday lst August Clearer skies today, with the sun doing it's best to shine. I took advantage of the excellent facilities, shower's were a guilder and I washed, spun and tumble-—dried a mach- _ ine load of clothes for a &1. A bit expensive but well worth it. Robert visitéd the wery luxurious chandlers (fitted carpets) and finished up repainting’ the bow damaged in Breskens. Vic cooked the lunch, we had salad$ — In the afternoon we walked along the sea wall or rather Meer wull into Veere, which was more crowded than ever. Nick and Daphne treated us to some splendid ice creams at the quay side cafe, so we sat down in the sunshine watching the people and the boats come and go. We saw several yachts flying the Lawling Cruising Club burgee. 19.00 Left Oostwatering and in the evening sunshine motored back towards Vere and the lock. Vic demanded his camera every few minutes as the light was so fantastic. The lock was almost empty, 1 barge and 3 yachts including us. 21.200 Tied up in Berth 34 at Middleburg. Everyone went to the Yacht Club except me, they sneaked away while I was putting Mary to bed. Monday 2nd August The day was spent shopping in Middleburg and amongst other things large numbers of clogs were purchased. I had hoped to have a good look around the Town Hall, which is Situated in the main Market Square, but a modern art exhibition was being held there with an exorbitant ehtrance fee, so I didn't bother. The Bowsher's came in during the day and we all congregated on "Ace" for the evening I can't remember if that was the night I cooked a beans and sausage supper for everyone or not.

We were now heuding for home so it was agreed that detailed reports of the 06.33 and 17.55 shipping forecasts would be kept. Our route home was to be via Ostende, this made the North Sea Passage a little shorter, and was the best port for picking up duty free. 17-55 Shipping Forecast. Gales in Finistere. Fisher/German Bight W 4-5 veering NW 5-6 Humber/Thames W5, 6 later veering NW.decreasing 4-5 Showers, visibility good. Tuesday 3rd August 06.33 Shipping forecast. Gales in Finisterge, ridge of high pressure filling in Shannon moving across Denmark Straits. Fisher/German Bight NNW 4-5 showers visibibity good. Humber/Thames/Dover NW 4-5 decreasing 3, isolated showers, visibility good. 10.00 Vic and I took the kids to the local swimming pool and then had coffee, ~ on the terrace, pleasant but chilly. We paid up our harbour dues which were 6 guilders per night (about £1.30). 15.30 Out of Middleburg and turned right down the main canal towards Flushing. On this occasion our timeing was bad as we came down to the Flushing road bridge and caught the full flood of the rush hour traffic, 80 we had to stooge around for about an hour, This was rather annoying, as the Yachthaven was almost a stone's throw away through. the bridge tucked away on left going towards tie lock. 1739 Tied up in a cut's cradle of lines, with a lethal access to the pontoons, 17-55 Shipping Forecast. Gales Finisterre. High over Shannon moving westwards Fisher/German bight NW 6-7 in east, showers, visibility good. Humber/ Thames/Dover West veering North West 3-4 showers, visibility govd. We enjoyed a drink in the clubhouse with some rather boisterous German gentlemen and then the Bowsher's joined us on Ace for coffee, crackers and cheese. Wednesday 4th August 06.33 Shipping Forecast. High Shannon moving east to Fastnet. Low céntral Baltic moving east. Low Cape Farewell moving NW and crossing NW sea areas Fisher/German Bight NW 5-6 decreasing to 4 showers, visibility good. Tide H.W. Flushing. 09.900 Departed Flushing Yachthaven destination Ostende. We shared a beer with Wigwam, who lay alongside us while locking out. 09.45 Out into the Westerschelde, blue skies but some rain clouds around. Wind NW but only 1-2, set mainsail and genoa, we ran down parallel to the coast keeping about a mile and a half off shore. Mary and 1 began to have attacks of the queasy tums again so Vic gave us someéhing to do I went on the helm and liary became flag officer taking down the Dutch and hoisting the Belgian colours and the yellow duster. SAFWTY AFLOAT It is the time of year when a reminder concerning the subject of safety is ap- propriate. When sailing on one's own be especially cautious and at other times at the club the following notes are reproduced for guidance:-— 1) Officer of the Day a) Responsible in the vicinity of the Club. b) Ensure that the Rescue crew have access to their equipment and are ferried to the boat(s). c) Maintain radio contact with the boat. (This responsibility may be delegated to the Race Officer. 2) Race Officer a) Check off the competitors at the start and as many tims as is pracical during the race. Report any missing boats to the rescue crew, b) Ensure that any boat not completing the course has returned to safety. 3) Rescue Crew a) Check the boats sailing as often as is practical and if any are missing confirm their wheresbouts. b) When the racing has got under way take up station neur the gybe mark in heavy weather or downtide in very light weather. In medium conditions a central position can be chosen. 4) Members a) Ensure personal equipment and boat is adequate for the conditions. If the weather is such thut you will not be able to cope do not venture out, ask if in doubt. b) If, however you do require assistance on the water, stay with the bout and wave both arms up and down. Do not use more energy than can be helped and drop anchor if in danger of drifting away. c) If racing sign off immediately afterwards, this is most importamt when retiring. FALLING IN THE WATER Compared with the high accident rate of road users, sdiling is 4 relatively safe pastime. However accidents do occur, und when they do are usually more serious as often rescue is either a long way away or more difficult to obtain. It is therefore more important to take precautions and also to know what to do when an accident does occur. Why do people die when they fall in the water? Other than a n attack by sharks or mechanical injury them are three main causes of death. 1. Hypothermia, i.e. lowering of body temperature due to the cold environment. 2. Drowning i.e. thexukwekxnfxwatar filling of the lungs with water, and 3. Vaso - vagal shock, i.e. the shock of water entering the lower pharynx or upper respiratory passages causing a nervous reflex which stops the heart. To deal with these in turn, the first is by far the commonest cause of death due to immersion. 5 It has been shown that few people survive for more than seven hours in water at 59 F., muchhigher than British sea temperatures, and the survival time in water at 32°F. is only a few minutes. As on land, the best way of keeping warm in the water is to wear warm clothing. Intom this category come ‘wet-suits' of whichthey should be best of all. If you can get out of the water and sit on your dinghy, so much the better as unless the wind is particularly cold your heat loss is slower. Contrary to what might be expected, movement in the water accelerates heat loss as the extra heat generated by muscular effort is more than offset by the removal of the warmer layer of water around, and heated by the body. Therefore unless it is to swim a short distance to a rescue boat or the shore it is much better to lie still as possible in the water supported by a life-jacket. As the time of immersion is obviously an important factor, one should stay as near as pos— sible to the point where rescue might by expected. This is usually near the boat. There is no evidence to show that alcohol in normal quantities accelerates heat loss, which may be of comfort to those of us who indulge. The quickest method of warming someone is a warm bath - tempera tue 97°F - 100°F, but this is only of use if they can be bathed within 20 minutes and is seldom feasable. A warm atmosphere, hot water bottles, the close proximity of another human body and warm blankets after removal of the cold wet clothing are the usual methods. So, if you cannot rescue yourself, wear warm clothing, keep still and make it as easy as possible for your rescuers by staying near the boat or where they expect you to be. To pass onto the last two headings, prevention is — wear a good life jacket and hold your breath as you go in. Once a person has ceased to breath irreversible brain damage occurs with 3 -5 minutes so that any attempt to revive them must be made immediately. If drowning is complicated by hypothermia the chance of successful revival is very small.

- )- Before considering how to revive a person let us consider briefly what happens when lungs fill with water. The water may be fresh or sea water. In the former case the osmatic pressure of the blood causes a rapid absoption of water from the lungs into the blood stream which so lowers the osmatic pressure of the blood that the red cells burst, releasing a large amount of potassium whcih the heart can not tolerate and it stops. This tukes place vepy rapidly, as roughly speaking the minute sacs in the lungs if all were spread out would cover ia tennis court and they are designed specially to absorb. In the latter case the r-verse occurs as the osmatic pressure of sea water is higher than that of the blood and this causes an outflow of fluid from theblood stream, flood- ing the lungs and preventing oxygen getting into the blood.. The heart can keep beat-— ing for a few minutes after this occurs, so the chances of successful revival are much higher. The treatment of drowning and also of vaso — vagal shock is the same, namely - artificial respiration. I am sure thut the simplest and most effective method is mouth to mouth respiration perhaps better known and the kiss of life. As with all unconcious people, including unconciousness due to hypothermia, the first essential is to maintain a clear airway. This is done by hooking the forefingers of euch hand behand the angle of the jaw of the rescued and lifting the jaw, and there- by the tonge, forward. If possible the lower teeth can be hooked over the upper teeth. It ig a waste of precious time attempting to empty water from the lunzs of the rescued. It is much better to attempt to inflate that part of the lung which is not filled with water -— usually a considerable proportion. If you kneel facing the feet it is possible to lift the jaw forward, hold the lips together in an airtight joint and breathe gently down the nose. In this position one can watch the chest to see it inflate. Remarkably little effort is required and adequate time should be allowed for the chest to deflate, about three times as long as the inflation period. If the airway is cleur i.e. the tonge is not blocking the back of the throat, the movement of the chest should be gentle and easy. I don't know how long one should continue this as it is mainly a moral question. If one considers thut the brain is dead after five minutes and quadruples this time I think this is reasonable and is the criterion I have taken on the few occassions I have It is important to realise thut if the rescued is breathing it is positively danger- ous to give artificial respiration. This will only hinder theri own respiratory efforts and possibly inflate the stomach, blowing vomit into their air passages and killing them. It is only necessary to keep a clear airway and keep them warm. One last point which I must mention is the question of vomiting. In a concious person they will get rid of their own vomit but in an unconscious person they may well inhale it with fatal results. Turn them on their side with the head lower than their waist and no fluid can possible enter the lungs. This article has turned out to be much longer than I anticipated but even so is only an outline of what ha»pens when one "falls in the water". Greater pens than mine have suid "prevention is better than cure" and it is never more true than of sailing accidents. A. Doctor.

COMMODORES NOTES Half way through May and we seem to have slipped from a wet winter to a wet winter to a wet spring without noticing the start of the Sailing Season and the im- provement in the weather which we expect to accompany it. The club is however coming alive with the moorings filling up and the dinghy park sprouting masts of varying lengths as Members' winter deliberation turn into reality and the fresh boats arrive at the Club. The Committee and particularly the Regatta Organisers have become very conscious of the approacl:ing Spring bank Holiday and are considering the detailed preparation for what promises to be a bumper Regatta again. Some volunteers have already come forward to help with the work during the holiday weekend but as always we shall be pleased to hear from other members who are willing to lend a hand on the day. In particular Jill Savill will be pleased to hear from anyone willing to help in the Galley, Ron Greygoose from anyone who likes being behind the bar and John Weedon from people who like watch- ing the sailing from the race box where there is a constant demand for spotters. Vol- unteers are asked to contact the above as soon as possible. So as to prepure the site to welcome cur visitors we are holding our usual] pre- regatta working parties when we shall be cutting grass, trimming hedyes, disposing of rubbish, clearing the hard and generally tidying up all the facilities. The Working Parties are being held on Saturday May 28th from 10.30 and Wednesday June 1st from 6.00 when we would ask as many members as possible to put in an appearance and help to prove the old proverb "Many hands make light work". Please bring with you a good selection of tools including shovels, forks, brooms, rakes, hammers, saws, shears etc., and any members with rotary grass cutters or flymos would be particularly welcome. Many of you will have heard by now that the Club was broken into on the night of May 1st/2ndwhen a certain amount of damage was caused and property taken. Although at the time the gate was shut and all doors and windows secured it would seem an ap- propriate tune to remind all of you of the need to ensure that everything is se¢ure when you leave the Club and to be vigilant for your own and Club Property and not to put temptation in the way of the casual unwanted visitor. It also appears that there is still a mar-et for inflatible dinghies and even lucking them down is not an entirely effective deterrent. Please when using the Club keep your eyes open for the unusual and advise any Committee Member of any suspicious circumstances that may come to your notice. John Witter, Commodore. As she closed in I bore away to give her plenty of room to windward, but she kept coming: on an almost collision course. She passed about 20 yards to port and a weury looking helmsman shouted, "Which place is this’” fie told him. 15.00 After a peucefulsail down, arrived off the Ostende pier heads. We followed a Dutch yacht in, but were surprised when on reaching the dog leg of the pier, he suddenly swung the helm and came out at full chat. So did we when we saw the Townsend Ferry coming straight for us. Tied up in Ostende without incident, 7 boats out on the middle trot. With a very spick and span, new Dutch Bast next door, I cringed at the thought of the sand that would get onto the children's shoes and then be deposited on the deck. A leisurely drink in the clubhouse, ordered duty free and changed our currency. 17.55 Shipping Forecust. Low Denmark straits moving Ni. High 4600 Miles west off Land's “nd moving westerly. Gales: Bailey, Faeroes, Si Icelund. Fisher/Germ.n Bight NW 4-5, 6 luter, showers, visibility good. Humber/Thames/Dover N 2-3, 4 later, showers then fair, visibility good. There to our surprise was 4 forlorn looking Jestubel, 411 tied up and nowhere to go. What had happened? Thursday 5th August As the forecast was reusonable, we decided to stay one more day and enjoy all the sunshine. After heuring the forecast, we woved the boats buckwards away from the main trot onto the outside pontoon, which would wake life a lot eusier when we slipped out in the early hours of the morning. 05.45 Woke as the dawn was comif up, took over the helm while Vic took photo's of Natasha. Plenty of shipping around. 06.10 West Hinder abeam, Natasher very close, Vanellus about *# mile behind. Tyne /Dogger/German Bight WNW 3-4. Humber/Thames/Dover variable NW3. Vic asleep, Robert on the helm, and naviguting. We saw the Sunk Head Tower and in the far distance the Old Light House on the Gunfleet Sand. We reckoned thut we were at the top of King's Channel and altered course to 270°C to take us doen towurds the Sin Spitway, all sails down. 16.00 A few murky bumps on the horizon and then we could just make out the shape of the Naze Tower at Walton through the Huze. 16.05 Rassed Wallet No. 2 Nasty shock, wrong side of Gunfleet. On studying the the churt, we realised that the tide had been much stronger than anticipated and set us right across the top of the East Swin. Instead of travelling diagonally we had moved sideways. Woke Vic up and told him the glad tidings. Although the shore was hazy, it was not difficult to make our way down the Wallet to Colne Point and Brightlingsea. 1645 Tied up along side John Roger's Macwester in Brightlingsea Harbour. Who should be on the same trot, "Wigwam". This time they gave us not beer, but a very welcome cup of tea. No evidence of custom's officers around.

Saturday 7th August H.W. Stansgate 11.08 08.45 <A very weary officer returning from a spell of night duty at Colchester cleared us for customs. 13.00 The crew's of all three boats hud an excellent lunch in the Jolly Sailor restaurant. 16.30 Left Brightlingsea, tide just beginning to flvuod, wind easterly. Motored out to the Colne but we had to give way to racing dinghies gybing around the channel marker buoy, which reéulted in us just touching the mad. Luckily, we came off almost at once, Vic putting her hard asterm. 18.30 Back to the mooring at Stansgate. References s- Admiralty charts, North Sea Harbours and Pilotage, Calais to Den Helder, by E. Delm-r Morgan. Veerse Meer en omgeving available from Fa L Meijers, Veere. I have used the Dutch spelling for all places except Flushing. Although our log was streamed on both crossings it was found to be erroneous, so I have not recorded these beadings. In fourt.en days we travelled 300 miles. The passage from Lavington to Breskens was 105 miles, Ostend to brightlingsgea 90 miles. NORTH SUA PASSAGE This is the story of the delivery of 'Victoria', a new 48ft. Motor Sailor from Maldon to Flushing in Holland, and the problems which were overcome during the North Sea Passaze, on the lst of September 1976. Some Sailing Club members muy have seen the boat, either at Dun Webb & Feeseys Yard or at anchor off the Club (Sat/Sun 28th/29th August) the weekend before we left. She wus moulded by Tylers and fitted out by Dan Webb and measured 48 ft LOA, 36ft. LUL, 13ft 5 Beam. 6ft 6 draft. Her power plant was a prototype heavy vehicle Volvo engine of 120 Horse Power. Her working sail area 1,190 sq. ft. The crew were as followsi— Capt. & Owner — Jim, because it wus easier to say but real name - Thage Bergrenn, from Sweden. Navizitor:— Bill Basson, the one urmed ex bomber Pailot, Grand Prix Rac r, come Deep Sea Sailor (Age 65+) John Swinton of Dan Webb & Feeseys, Jane John's 16 year old daughter. Stan Cumpbell the writer ‘ , I think that it could be said that the Grew Campbell his 1 Jimmyold 8 were-easonably experienced sailors, though

ae not seasoned ones. Navigational Gear We had all the charts thit were needed, hand bearing compass, radar, and radio direction finding equpment. We were,one could say, amply equipped for such a passage. Time of Departure and Proposed Passage. We were to leave Maldon at high water (6.20) p.m. On Wednesday lst September and our passage was to be made in roughly four tides (24 hr. approx.) The route was to be via the Spitway buoys off Brightlingsea, north up the Hast Swin to the Sunk Sand Towers und across to Longsand Head (off Harwich) thence via the Galloper Light Vessel between the North and South Hinder Light Vessels and then direct to Flushing, which was an overall journey of 120 odd miles. The coastal Weather Forecast for 6.00 p.m. Thames and Humber was fairly good - Northerly 4 - 5 backihg North Westerly later. Gales forecast from Heligoland, Dogger and area North, but a high was approaching from the South West. Departure This was made between 6.00 and 6.30 and before long we had settled down to what should have been a pleasant und straightforward trip. To our surprise we were showing 8 knots on the log although the Skipper had his doubts, chart checks confirmed this. We agreed to have a hot cooked meal before we cleared the river, so Jane provided a meal of stew and dumplings (or were they golf balls?) followed by fruit and hot coffee. This ultimately proved to have been a very wise decision because our next meal was some sixteen hours later for reasons which will soon become obvious. The first major problem came at nightfall when it was patently obvious that steering by compass was going to prove very difficult, if not almost impossible, as it was too small and mounted too far away from the wheelto be readab'e. All crew members tried with varying degrees of success, which did prove that it wus not the crewmembers eyesight and that it had to be accepted and lived with. However, the Benchhead and Knoll were passed, tye Spitway Buoys negotiated and then North up the East Swin. At 00.30 we listened to the Shipping Forecast, which was as follows :- Thames, Humber N.W. 4 — 5 Gales in the area North still and a cold front moving South. Jim (th Skipper) asked how long a fromt took to pass and I said that it could be days or hours, but at this time of the year it should not prove a problem, So we de@ided to press on. Galloper gave 4, but we thought it ought to be 5 and made 4 remark at the time. We were still in sight of Harwich and Felixstowe and Sunk Sand Tower Light. Not:-— To sailors coming up the East Swin, remeber the light is on the north side of the Towers for the use of shipping out of Harwich. The Towers looked big and menacing in the dark and were passed quite a while before the light protecting them was left behind. To be continuedeccecce

COMMODOR"S NOTES Another Regatta has come and gone although this time the elements were less favourably inclined towards us with most of the period challenging sailing during the races we were able to hold. It was disappointing for those who had worked hard to provide a good sailing weekend and for the competitors who were not able to enjoy a4 full racing programme. The joint Jubilee Challenge Cups arranged between Stone S.C. and ourselves due to take place on Tuesday also had to be postponed. As with any event catering for large numbers of enthusiats, be it sailing or any other sport, the resources, both in terms of volunteers and facilities were stretched. I would like to express tke thanks of the organisers to all those who helped, both before and during the event, to make the weekend a sucess. In particular we should thank those who managed the reception area and the race box and the spotters who braved the elements at the race box to record the starters and finishers, the crews providing refreshments, both liquid and solid, who were at their posts to offer a cheery smile and a plate or glass of something nourishing throughout most of the period and the members of both our Club and visiting Clubs providing rescue craft and crews who this year were pressed in to almust continuous service. John Witter, Commodore. MARCONI REGATTA 1977 <- a view from the roof The regatta is now over and by any standards is spite of the weather, can be judged a success. At what cost thouzh’ to the few members who actually did the hardwork — before during and after.Their numbers get less every year and each year we have an ever in- creasing plague of people. The Bank Holdiay is meant to be a break and more and more members and officials conclude that it is a good thing to be elsewhere during this holdiday. The bar took a profit - in terms of man hours spent it was probably a comercial loss except for the cash in lieu of wages donuted by the workers, in some cases say Ron Greygoose and John Witter probably in the hundreds of pounds, Whether people wish to continue this type of donation is, of course, a matter for individuals and there is evidence that there is a decreasing number. The committee for next year will have to consider whether it can staff such an Open increasing committment. Our resources are inadequate — 3 Ladies loos and 2 gents for nearly 1,000 people. The drainage is inadequate and the memory lingers on — the biz ditch will be foul for the rest of the season. I am firmly of the opinion that the club can no longer stage an open regatta in the waythat it had developed, and I doubt whether the majority of the members want it to. Many complaints were heard and it may be significant that there were no thanks voiced at the prizegiving. To be constructive - There is no need to abandon a spring jamboree, Mardi Gras, festival regatta, Stansgate week or W.H.Y. but lets make it a closed event. yWembers

and guest by invitation. Open races can be staged throughout the year to return hospitality but spread out and interleaved with normal racing. The particular fleets looking ——— their own. We could still have our own events with the cruisers ie ing in with the dinghy men, instead of abandoning the site to the hourds, en mass. Lets have a regatta of our own and then we can enjoy it without the nagging feeling you ought to be serving beer, washing glasses, hading out cotton wool, working ing the galley, spotting boasts und heaving trollies for this vast throng of people who can't communicate with above the din of the disco. No, we can't cope with these numbers —- lets have some sanity even if it means putting the subs up £1.50 or so- at least the effort will be shared equally that way. Perhaps we could have sume other views and maybe aim them at our A.G.M. this year. Tom Gaskel. SOCIAL SCRihD The weather could have been kinder for the regatta and the succeeding cadets week, Nevertheless the campers and curavaners made the best of things and the social highlights of the cadet week must have been the bonfire, firworks and the wine and cheese party on Jubilee day, and the darts match on the wednesdywere forgotten. There are two events coming alony in July. The first on July 16th is the Annual Barbecue at Stansgate, starting 8.00 p.m. There will be a disco and the usual barbecue food - chicken portions, sausages and rolls. Akl the help possible would be welcome for the big job uf setting-up on Saturday and dismantling on Sunday morning. Cost of tickets will be 90p including food, obtainable from the agents listed below. On Saturday July 30th, starting at 2.00 pam. we ure holding a "Fun Day" , and ope thut we see a bumper turn out of members families, and their friends are welcome. ./r this occasion we plan to organise whit we hope will be an entertaining day with competitions for all on the water und land, designed we hope to give a lot of fun and entice a general involvement. We'll be holding a beach purty in theevening with a bonfire and beefburgers with rolls (at cost) cooked in the open’. Come along and make it a family day out. Poor Jimmy had to look, for his Dad was at the wheel and looking ahead and he was looking for lights and timing them wit) a stop watch, for which he deserved a medal. Things may not be in chronological order from now on nor may they ever, but lets get back to why we hud trouble getting the mainsail down. The situation was as follows:- The Genoa was thrashing haifway up the Mast, but still acting as a steadying sail, the Main was down, but the engine was running, 80 we could'relax', review the situation calmly and decide our next move. There was a unanimous decision to re-establish our position, which isn't samprising since for a couple of hours we had been at the mercy of wind and sea. It must be pointed out that we knew we had plenty of sea room to leeward so at no time had we been in danger of running ashore. That is why we were concerned out Mast, Rigging and Sails primarily. I think that the method of confirming our position is well worth bearing in mind for the Navigator never left his chart table. It might be worth noting here that conditions were such thut all crewmembers had life jackets or buoyancy aids on (lifejackets being blown up) and all were secured by some means or other to the boat. This was mainly because of the darkness and the atmos- phere which noise. movement, spray, torrential rain and general uncertainty created. At times there was considerable confusion, but at no time was there panic. Back to positioning ourselves, We knew that we were somewhere in the vicinity of the North and West Hinder so the helmsman (myself) steered as straight a course as possible, Jimmy had the stopwatch and the Navigator was st his chart table below, Most lights even if different colours, normally flash 'X' number of times in so many seconds. Jimmy's job was to look for lights, start the watch on the first flashof the next sequencg, let it go through its sequence and stop the watch duwnxtkexkatekxand on the first flash of the next sequence. He then handed the watch down the hatch and said '4 reds every "that"! or '3 whites every "that"' - the "that" being the time that he couldn't see bat the Navigutor down below could. I added "fine on the port Bow" or "on the starboard beam" whichever wus appropriute. Within twenty minutes we had a light and two light vessels looms to look at, but the waves were biz enough and we were small enough to blank out whole sequences fur quite long periods. We did however know that the two light vessels should have been the NOrth West Hinder which were about twenty miles off the belgium Coast, and ubout 8 to 10 miles from us. %: TB Yet another amusing contribution from the amusing Rob Swale... There were these two Flying Dutchman sailors who went out one day in their boat, and the weather was very rough. Well, they capsized and both of them drowned, so Being dinghy suilors they naturally went to heaven. When St. Peter found out they were just in time for the "Next World" Championships and that a brand new boat with all the latest goodies was waiting for them. So off they went in their perfectly rigged and tuned boat, and with it being held in heaven, naturally the wind was a steady Force 3-4, the tide was non- existent and the sun was shinning. COMMODORES NOTES As is invariably the case following the Annual Regatta many views are expressed and at the first combittee meeting a review of the event is undertaken and this year we had the added benefit of Tom Gaskell's observation which naturally stimulated lively discussion. At our meeting we analysed at length the various facilities required for an event of the nature of our Regatta and the following are brief summaries of the feel- ings of those directly responsible for the various crews of organisation. Sailing - Well covered with good distribution of help. Minor problems with spotting due to inclement weather. Rescue facilities stretched but coped despite the Club being without a permaneant coxon at presetn. Galley — Geod preparation and supply of food etc., Some people spent more time in Galley than ideally we would like but this is ofter at individuals own insistance. — Good service given by Brewers. Bar Generous sup.ort behind bar during peak periods but in general too much on one person outside peak periods. Some spells of duty particularly during Saturday evening party became stretched and mere advance com mitment required to spread load. Clubhouse Facilities - This is the area in which we are most stretched to meet the demand. There are however problems with providing extra facilities but these are under consideration. Despite this shortcoming mapy people return each year knowing what to expect. This deficiency must therefore have its compensations. No conclusions on the future of the Regatta were reached as the views expressed so far have been of an organisational nature and generally about people who have not in themselves taken such a pessimistic view.Before reaching any final decision the Committee also needs to hear the views of the Sailors on whether this sort of Open Competition is what they want during the Spring Bank Holiday where there is an op= portunity to stage an event of at leust two days duration. The question of Regattas is clearly an emotional one and unless some of these who enjoy it and want it continue say so the view will be one sided and it will surely die. It should also be borne in mind that the problem of getting voluntary help to do things at the Club is not unique to the Regatta but is present throughout the year and is a older problem to which we have to find a solution if the Club Officiers and Committee are not to become disillusioned. I would emphasi@e that the remainder of my notes reflect my own thoughts which are not necessatily shared by all the Committee. Tom's saiania/okwa sen tions published in last months Navigans are well intentioned and containa considerable amount of fact but I question the conclusions he has drawn in a number of cases and I think we have to consider that the Regatta seeks to achieve. The main objectives as I see them ares a) to provide good competitive sailing and an opportunity for ou members to sail against members of other clubs on our home waters. (1/6 of the total entry of 225 came from within the club and were represented in 9 fleets.) b) to offer an opportunity to sail from our unique and much admired facilities to members of mainly local Clubs on the river and in Essex and thereby reciprocate the facilties availablecto our members at other Clubs. c) to limit the disruption of Club life to a minimum of weekends in the year and to avoid openening the G1ub to all on too many weekends in a year. This was in defference to the wishes of the members who are not competitive dailors and who like to enjoy the privacy the Club can offer for the majority of the year. I do not consider making a profit from the Regatta as a main objective, although naturally a successful one does make a substantial pfofit and if this were the prime motive TI would not be prepared to spend the time supporting the event. An analysis of the entries and those who were committed to helping with the event

shows that the majority of help came from the entrants and their families with addit- jonal support provided from the fleets on a rota. to The question of size and how to limit it and still offer open sailing is oned about were equally worrie which there appears to be no easy solution but 12 years ago wes with size when we had 80 boats and since then we have held Regatta more entries than this year's without the benefits of our present Clubjo use. Genera lly there has been a The main differ ences think tendency over the years for the entries to level off. people under canvas thanI previo now really arise from our ability to accommodate more usly and not from the sailing organisation, I cannot support Tom's view that the emphasis of the weekend should be on having a closed jamboree rather than an open sailing meeting. If sailin the prime g were not purpose for holding the weekend with the social aspect s being our means of entertaining our guests there would be little need for any specia l social activi ties at all during the weekend judging by the general low attenda nce of member s at recent informal social events. I am firmly of the opinion, and I am not alone in this, that to drastically curtail this as a sailing event is not in the interest or traditi on of the Marconi “Sailing Club and that it would be @ receipe for disaster for the compet itive sailing interest of the Club. alternative The suggestion of holding several open meetings during the year is ofan organi a great deal but I am not convinced it is an answer as it still requires ave club racing with an sation and commitment and it would be extremely difficult to interle our facilties would be open event as without rescue launch support from other Clubs jnadequate for the number of boats on the water at any one time. not a The idea of our cruiser members sailing in races with the dinghies is quickly new one aS it was one of the prin¢iples of the early Regatta s and died very . Our present experience shows the Barnacle races to be almost non existant , entries in the B.J.S.C. Cruiser races are very limited and we seem to be having difficulty in raising a Club team for the inter club cruiser team race. The idea is a non starter still I think. I do not expect my personal view to be supported un animously by the Members or the Committee, but the Club consists of a lot of minorit y interest s making up the whole and one of the jobs of the Committee is to try to cater for all these interests over a Neriod of time and a balance has to be struck. If this sort offoropen cometition is still required then the Spring Bank Holiday is a very suitabl e time it as it is still relatively early in the season and the large pottering section of the members hip has not been brought out by the sun and warmer water temperature. In condasion I would say I have no regrets about the many hours spent on the are and visitors Regattas since they first started and my reward is knowing our members welcome enjoying good sailing. I would not pretend that more help would not be to it is there if it was realised it spread the load in all areas but unlike Tom I belive the Regatta has a very was needed. I am also strongly of the opinion that high reputa- tion in the Sailing World and is something the CLUB should be proud of and should continue to strive to run. John Witter, Commodore. LETTERS TO THis EDITOR Marconi Regatta - 1977 Like many others I removed my cruiser from Stansgate the week before the Regatta to give the racing enthusiasts more room at the start line. Because of the inclimate weather I returned to Stansgate on the Monday to find crowds of strangers, a drunk at the bottom of the ditch and to crown it all my ;oor old banger with its paint work deeply scored fore and aft plus.a flat tyre. I know, that like myself, the old bus has other scars and they can be patched with a dab of paint but next to me was a shiny 'R' registration which might have got the same treatment if it had not been for the vigilance of two Marconi members who chused these visiting 'children' away, a possible expensive prank. May I second the views of Tom Gaskel, if necessary, let us increase our subs to make up for any monies lost, let the individual fleets have their open meetings spread out during the season but more imp rtant let us have our own Regatta, con- sisting of Marconi members and friends, a mini Cowes weekend where dinghy sailors can crew or helm cruisers in short course fun races, they could teach potterers like me how to get more out of my boat, young Stephen Perkins did exactly that in 1976. Some of the more aged cruiser owners might even be allowed to crew in a fun race in dinghies and of course interleaved with all this the more serious races could be held. If the weather is fair let the cruisers take some of the dinghy wives and younger children on a circumnavigation of Osea with dad sailing in Convey, a chance to take photos? To conclude, ‘et it be a weekend of family fun where we can unite as a club and get to know each other more and engender a real club spirit. Freddie Hurrison. Mirror Sail no. 32069 Newly painted and varnished with all equipment - includin. sea avhor 2 adult and 1 child buoyancyaids and new boom up cover. Offers around £200 to Richard Bowman on Chelmsford [redacted], after August Ist. —— eee ae Se — —-——- _—--— — — - —_—-—- Continuing North Sea Passa,e The Skipper went right up into the bows when we found «a point of steering which seemed to be most stable and after .n inspection he called for the knife, John took this for- ward and when the necessary rope was cut, the sail dropped low enough to be got at and wen eventually stowed. This is an over simplification for the job took almost an hour under the impossible conditions. No words can describe the boats movement, the noise of the wind and rain, the we cold hands which together with tiredness had to do what had to be done | we could not have entered hirbour. I at the helm gave u hearty cheer, but even that was carried downwind and away, This then was our first bit of luck in a night of stbacks. With our large (pennant) down, which hud acted in some ways as a steadying sail, we began to roll violently. Rrightaning noises below subsequently proved themselves to be tool boxes and provisions. A throrough inspection below showed thut we had made water, but nothing serious. The c'ue was a very wet curpet up forward outside the toilet compartment. It was condirmed later that tie water had spi’led out several times w}en we were heeled ore were tossed about. To prevent further noise and damage we decided to put the mizzen up as a steadying Sail. One had to experience the chunge to appreciate the difference a very small sail can make. Notet- Whenever fuced with a situation such as we were experiencing, always get some sail on, no matter how insignificant, for it can be the difference between acute discomfort und danger to bi.dy and limb, as opposed to a damped sideways movement which is fur m@re bearable and much kinder to ship and crew, After an hour or so we had come inside the shouls off Ostende und we were comparatively sheltered. All hands came on deck and with great relief 1 am sure , watched as ‘yours truly' (becaus: he had been on the helm most olf the time) was given the sreat privilige of taking 'Victoria' through Ostende breakwater to muke her first landfall. That was one of the most satisfying mom- ents of my lire. Within an hour we were tied up and asleep.

On waking we inspected the boat and tidied up prior to going ashore for 'big eats’. The inspection showed the following:— 1) The Genoa wis only slightly torn and damage marginal to one seam and the eyelet were the sheets were attached. 2) There were two deck leuks, one caused be the struin put on the handrail protecting the steering console and one round tie forehatch. 3) A starboard side stunchion was bent us wus the guardrail running from it. It's base screws had also gone and tha angle plite strengthening damaged. It was where t e end of my lifeline was attached wehen I was flung across the cockpit:! Other than the above, no damage was found. On finding that we were still seuworthy and having hud «a sleep, we were ready for a night passage north to Holland. The coastguard however, informed us that the gales would continue for at least 48 hours so we decided to stay put. We walked out on the mole to the Harbour bntrance to see what the seas looked like and deceded that we did not want a repetition of the night before. The follow- ing morning we went to.Zebruwge and took the Ferry home to Felixstowe in absolute comfort —Even if for the firsttwo hours we were in heavy seus. As we neared the English Coast the seas subsided and off Felixstowe we saw the familiar lights of Walton and Harwich. In retrospect it is very difficult to know how some of te problems could have been avoided as it is easy hindsight to hold a post mortem. I would rather say that it added to our overall experience and showed thxut both young and old can co-operate as a team and face serious situations equally as well when the chips are down. Again in ret- rospect I feel that nor wiaiden Voyage should have had such bad luck. However, it proved the boat for the Owner and proved the Crew to themselves. The following advise could be given as guidance should somebody wish to make a similar passaygee 1) Do mat a short nivht sail peior to the crossinz to see that the compuss is adequate. 2) At the same time fumiliarise the crew with working on deck in the dark for sail chan jing and any other necessary activities. 3) Have an alternative destination well planned should the original not prove feasible. 4) If there is a chance of seasickness tuke all the precautions for avoidance well in advance. 5) Remember that cold fronts invariably mean foul weather, 80 don't be afraind of ~ them, but be prepared for 4 change of plans and some very uncomfortable sailing. 6) If it is ever intended to cook of even boil water on the passage, a fiddle rail and gimbals on the cooker are most essential even if only for safety. 7) idake sure th.t some of the crew hu@e enough experience to take care of the boat under any conditions that might be experienced on passage. I think apart from the compass, which was vit.l and the cooker which wasn't, Victoria's crew fulfilled all such requirements and a successful passage was mude even if the origin- al destination had to be changed. Would I do it again tomorrow? - Of course I would —---

There was a vicar who was also involved in the running of the ocal marriage guidance council. One day he was asked to gige a lecture on sex to some couples experiencing marital problems. He reluctantly agreed but as the day of the lecture approached he began to have second thoughts. He talked to his wife about the sub- ject many times for advise and she encouraged hime to give the talk. However, when he walked into the lecture room to give his talk his courage left him and so he decided to give a talk about the couple of times he had been sailing ( at the Marconi S.C. of course}) . He didn't tell his wife of this as he didn't want her to think he was a prude or coward. Several days later the vicar's wife bumped into a marriage guidance counsellor who had heard the vicar's talk and he told her how much he had enjoyed it. "Yes", he said, "I didn't know he hid only done it twice. Your husband said the first time he did it he was sick and the second time his hat blew offii" Guess Who? F.S. COMMODORES NOTES September; tre evenings drawing in, holidays over and ohe wonders where the summer has gone and with it all the enjoyable sailing in the longer days. With the comig of Autumn your Committee's thoughts turn to the events of the winter and the Club's future. Now is the time to start actively thinking about the Laying-Up Supper which is only about 6 weeks away. There have been good turnouts for the sailing act- ivities this year and we hope that you will all Mayo a special effort to come to the Laying-Up Supper to put the seal on the season and to sample the cuisine at this year's venue - The Lion and Lamb - where we succeeded in getting a booking after a large body of opinion expressed a preference for a venue away from the M.A.S.C. We look forward to seeing you and any guests you may like to bring on November 4th. For those who find it difficult to meet the cost of tickets in one go, an "easy payment" scheme has been devised. To take advantage of this all you have to dois to purchase vouchers with your drinks over the bar in the Club or see one of the members of the Social Committee. Following swiftly in the wake of the Laying-Up Supper is the Annual General Meeting at which the Committee for the ensueing year is elected. This year several of the existing Committee come to the end of the period they can serve an office and a number want to retire after giving many years of service to the Club. There will therefore be a number of officiers or positions on the General Com- mittee to be filled and it would be good for the Club to have some new faces with new ideas grafted into the Committee. If you are interested in helping to run your Club please do not hesitate to have a word with any Committee Member to find out more about the job and if you agree they will make sure that you are nominated. Next month we will be detailing the Committees proposals and advising you who are willing to offer themselves for election, but in the meantime why not find out more about how you can help run your Club. HORNET FLENT NEWS Six Hornets from the Club travelled to Cramond Boat Club for the European Championships. The club is situated on a small tributary to the Firth of Forth just outside Edinburgh invery picturesque surroundings. We travelled up on the Friday, leaving early in the morning to arrive in time to pitch our tents. The practice race on the Saturday set the patten for the week by blowing force 5/6. Only two club boats were ready in time for this race. J. Tillotson and M. Turner who acheived their best position of llth and E. Richmond aid M. Strong. The wind increased for the first race and had to be abandoned after the first heat. We ull managed to return to the club without serious mishap although Mike's store of spares was seriously eroded on Sunday evening. Monday's race had to also be postponed due to the strength of wind which was fortunate for those of us who needed to repair our boats. The rest of the week went well with one race on Tuesday, two on Wednesday and one on Thursday when the wind increased again to gale force. Socially the week was very good which perhaps reflects our poor showing in the results. Mike and John did best with a 22nd overall. We travelled back in time for the Hallam Trophy. For Saturday's racing it blew force 5 for a change, but at least it wasn't raining. Unfortunately the first race of the series had to be ubandoned due to lack of water round F mark and other administritive problems but Saturday evening was enjoyed by all and Sunday dawned bright and sunny. Mike and John won the 2nd race easily in ideal conditions. The 3rd race was much harder work for them and they finished 2nd but this was enough for a win overall. Don't forget the Fleet meeting this month. Peter Clayton, Hornet Fleet Captain. COMMODORES REPORT During 1977 members have continued to enjoy the facilities of Stansgate with a wide variety of sailing activities and good social fellowship. Membership has stayed much the same as for the last few years and we seem to have settled down to a level which is about the maximum size that can be coped with on a mainly voluntary basis. This year we have not needed to call many working parties to assist with the general maintenance of the Club but the one held towards the end of October was very well supported and demonstrated a good spirit of co-operation and enthusiasm. If we can count on this sort of turn out when required we should be able to continue to operate with a minimum of paid help and thereby maintain our fees at a reasonable level. As you will have seen from the agenda, there is no proposal to increase any of the fees this year which I am sure you will all welcome. Although financially all looks very healthy at present we did discuss the possibility of needing to raise fees by 4 small amount to keep pace with inflation. Your Committee decided, however,that if it was possible to delay this for a year we should try, as financially the year has been hard enough for everyone without adding to the burden. Since last year's AGM no progress has been made with finding suitable alternative locks for the Clubhouse and gate but apart from the gate lock being rendered unservicable at the time of the break-in in May they have proved to be reliable. We shall continue to look for an alternative for when it is needed. While on the subject of locks, one of the causes of serious concern to your Officers and Committee is the apparent lack of concern by Members for the security of the Clubhouse and site. During the year there have been many instances logged where the Clubhouse has beenfound to be insecure and the gate left open. We are also aware of many occasions that have not been logged. It would appear that we are not succeeding in getting the message over to Members that the Clubhouse must be locked when there is no OOD present even though you may be remaining on the site. In making it possible for all members to have access to the Clubhouse we rely on you, the Members, to protect your property by ensuring that you always secure the premises immediately after use. These instance have increased this year and we must remind you all that with Stansgate being so remotely situated it is not possible for a daily checking procedure to be established and I therefore appeal to you all to be extra careful to secure the Club after use. The Committee, Sub-Comittees and volunteers have again worked hard in the service of the Club to provide Members with the facilities they have come to expect, including a galley, a bar, a well maintained Clubhouse, Dinghy Park & Moorings and busy Sailing & Social programmes. To all those who have helped to organise and provide these facilities may I say thank you on behalf of the Club and myself. It is perhaps an appropriate point to stress that these services are provided by voluntary help and that the same people cannot go on for ever and new helpers are always required and welcomed so as to spread the load during the year and across the years. Claud Emerson has again served the the club exceedingly well during the past year and we must all be grateful to him fa the excellent state in which he maintains the Club and the Precincts.

This year there will be many changes on the Main Committee as a number of members have decided it is time to take a rest and let some new faces take a turn. At this point I would like to mention a few of the retiring members who I have been pleased to serve alongside and who will be taking a rest. These are Jill Savill, who after 2 years representing the ladies and running the Galley deserves a rest, Vic Tate who is stepping down to take a well earned rest from active office after championing the Cruiser's interests for many years. Ted Barnes, who has been keeper of the Coffers for the last 3 years, is recharging his calculator. Roy Battye, who after 3 years as Social Secretary, during which time not everything has gone his way, would now like to rest on his laurels after a highly successful Laying-Up-—Supper. The other retiring members Les Mendoza and Rob Swale have had less specific jobs but have nevertheless been valuable members of the Committee. The remainder of last year's Committee are offering themselves for re-election, To all of last year's Committee I express my grateful thanks for your support and service to the Club and to those carrying on "Good Luck". Sailing highlights will be covered by our Sailing Secretary in his report but it would be remiss of me, as your Commodore, not to draw your attention to the contribution made by those members and friends in the race’ box and Rescue boats who make the racing possible each week and express our gratitude. Also the cadets, who have sailed so enthusiastically again this year, and under the shippership of Rick Anstey and Colin Leveridge have worked on their Elementany and Intermediate Day Boat Certificatesto achieve a high level of sucess, are to be congratulated. In making my report this year I must refer to the Annual Regatta of the Marconi Sailing Club. Many of you may not realise that I was Sailing and Regatta Secretary at the time the first one was put on some 12 years ago at the request of a number of the local Clubs who, because the date of the Bank Holiday was at that time fixed by the moon, and not the Government rarely had any water for sailing during the weekend. During my years in Office I have seen this event grow to what it is today; the most popular event on the Blackwater and probably in the East Coast Area. It has always had its problems, even from the first year it was run, but a true test of its popularity is the fact that sailors return each year for this one event. I sincerely believe it is an event which the Club should be proud to present and should make every effort to improve for the benefit of all keen racing sailors as open competition on our own waters offers unique opportunities to our members. An analysis of the classes sailed during the weekend shows that we have our own members sailing in about 80% of the classes. Since all the discussion in the summer, the Committee have considered the various shades of opinion and have concluded that there is a very strong body of opinion among the active racing members, whose families, incidently provide the majority .of the help, that the event should continue. We hear from neighbouring Clubs that there would be great disappointment if we did not offer our hospitality during this one weekend in the year and all those enquiring have been advised that the Committee believes there will be a Regatta in 1978. During the year there has been a growing demand for Cruiser moorings and particularly for winter storage. Your committee recommended revised arrangements for this year, which will just about cope with the demand for 1977/78 winter, and have passed forward a recommendation to the new committee to review the situation for futue years during the early part of 1978.

-7- Finally, as I retire from office I would like to say that I have been proud to be the Commodore of what must be classed as a very successful Club and to thank all with whom I have worked during my term of Office. I know you have spent many hours on the business of the Club during this time and we must all be grateful for this time voluntarily given to an activity which we all enjoy and in which we have a common interest. To you all I express my own and the Clubs appreciation. After tonight you will have a new Commodore and I would ask you to give him your support and help so that he can undertake effectively the job for which he has volunteered to accept nomination, Ron you will certainly have my support and I wish you good luck and I hope you will enjoy your term of office as much as I have mine. Thank you John Witter. A CAUTIONARY TALE A few weeks ago there was a lot of news concerning small fishing boats which were lost in mist and fog off the East Coasts and stretched the services of rescue facilities. The following story relates to a works colleague of mine. Having gone out for the day with a friend who keeps his boat in Walton Backwaters a day's fishing was completed somewhere near the Medusa Buoy off Walton. The boat carried a compass and torch but not a lot more. The return passage, under outboard power was commenced in conditions of slight mist. The ownerimew the vacinity pretty well. Pye End Buoy cume up through the mist, then No. 2 Buoy appeared. Stearing mainly by Compass due to the mist. At this point buoys are closely spaced - everything should be fine. Compass bearing O.K. -— where is the next buoy? Time passes - open sea — more time passes - and more — fuel running low. Friend says we can't keep on like this - drop anchor. Kept warm in small cabin - 2 adults - 2 young boys. A shore rescue service noticed parked truilor and sturted searching. Through mist my friend identifies Medusa buoy flashing. Darkness fall - good torch curried, several pussing ships signalled — not seen. Eventually boat passed close — flush S.0.5. —- its the lifeb.at - rescue. Marvellous attention from the lifebout crew, eventually everyone home safe and well. Several days later small boy seen playing with magnets. Yes they were in his pocket that day. Do some tests, boy moves across cabin — compass swings about 120°. Have your chidren got any magnets? R. Fuller. "GRAFTER" -— 23' Twin bilge keel, 4 berth GRP sailing Cruiser. -4@9 LIFEBOAT RESCUE AT STANSGATE - MAY 1977 The article below is reprinted fron’ THS LIPTMBOAT journal. We happened to be at Stansgate that afternoon, finishing our fitting-out, and watched the whole affair, It was eerie, and nerhaps a little sobering, to see red flares coming from Goldhanger Spit which is the sight of such innocent pursuits as our Mud Race. The rescued yachtsmen took advantage of our clubhouse for a ‘warm-up! and a cup of tea before going their own way, Perhaps this is a good reminder that any of us may need the R.N.L.I. no matter how modest our voyaging. "Rradwell Coastguard Mobile was in the vicinity of Stansgate on the afternoon of Friday, May 20, keeping watch over a number of yachts off Osea Island, when, at 1723, a yacht was seen to be heading for the sand spit at the eastern end of the island and a red flare was sighted. Life- boat attendance was requested and the honorary secretary of West Mersea ILB station immediately gave authority for maroons to be fired. Meanwhile, it appeared that a second yacht was altering course to go to the aid of the first, she also ran aground on the spit, at the north-eastern edge. The wind was north east, strong force 6 gusting to gale force 8, and, with a strong ebb tide, the seas were heavy and short. Predicted high water at Rradwell was 1548. The weather was fine with fair visibility. At 1732 West Mersea Atlantic 21 ILB launched on service, Once clear of the West Mersea approaches she had to reduce speed in the heavy seas, but she reached the 23' sloop"Contessa", the second grounding, at 1752. Approach to the casualty was difficult in the shallow water as the two streams of ebb tide around Osea Island, reaching a rate of 3 knots, were meeting and causing very heavy confused seas of up to 6 feet against the gale force north-easterily wind, One crew member boarded "Contessa" and an anchor was run into deep water by the IIB. Roth this yacht and the first casualty, the 25' sloop "Lionheart", were chartered from Maldon, The two men in "Contessa's" crew of four were loath to leave until told of the continuing bad forecast and an estimated re- floating time at 0100, All four of the crew were then taken aboard the ILB and landed at Marconi Yacht (sic) Club, Stansgate, where the Coastguard mobile awaited them, The Atlantic 21 then went on to "Lionheart", reaching her at 1807, After the ILB had run an anchor away for them, the yacht's four crew members were taken off, the transfer, once again, requiring careful manoeuvring: the four people were landed at Stansgate at 1830. Before returning to station the ILB continued westward to warn other yachts to remain west of Osea Island. The 6-mile passage back eastwards was again made at reduced speed with the ILB leaving the water frequently in the heavy seas. She was refuelled and ready for service at 1922, For this service a letter of appreciation signed by Captain Nigel Dixon, RN, Director of the Institution, was sent to helmsman James Clarke, Letters of thanks signed by Commander Bruce Cairns, Chief of Operations, were sent to Crew Members Graham Knott and David Mills.” Ray and Maureen Ball

Safety Afloat cont. 2) Race Officer a) Check off the competitors at the start and as many times as is practical during the race, Reprt any boats missing to the Rescue crew. b) Snsure that any boat not completing the course has returned to safety. 3) Rescue Crew a) Check the boats sailing as often as is practical and if any are missing confirm threar whereabouts. b) When the racing has got under way take up station near the gybe mark in heavy weather or downtide in very light weather. In medium conditions a central position may be chosen, 4) Members a) Ensure personal equipment and bout is adequate for the conditions. If the weather is such that you will not be able to cope do not venture out, ask if in doubt. b) If, however you do require assistance on the water, stay with the boat and wave both urms up and down. A cruise across the North Sea to Holland or Calais - yes, but a thrash round the sticks - not really. Nevertheless, the Club do organise a few cruiser races including one series - the "Barnacle Points". This year, the agregate of four races count, three are individual races, open to other clubs and participation may or may not be chosen to contribute to "The Barnacle". The one dedicated contribution is a simple run to Herring Point (Maldon) and back and should have been held on Saturday 24th June, Unfortunately only two boats entered -— insufficient for a race = mainly because of a number of problems affecting other entrenis. My boat was still "Soms Mast" but I had an exciting trip to Herring Point and back in Bill Buchanon's "E Boat" -— hotly pursued by Ken Beavins. We would like to run this race now on Saturday i9th August at 13.30hrs., to Herring Point. How about turning out a "flotilla" — you might leam something new about sailing. Dennis Byatt, .
