Continuing the log of ‘Ace of Diamonds’, Summer Cruise 1977 Tuesday 26th Julye Wind still N.W. Force 5 which is making the anchorage uncomfortable. Wendy took Rachel and Philip ashore whilst Andrew had his morning sleep. At the turm of the tide we motored up to Waldringfield where we found a mooring to pick up, with the advise of the "Fairways attendant", opposite the Waldringfield S.C. Jetty which has a freshwater tap at the top end. The Mirror was rigged after lunch and we spent the afternoon sailing it around. In the evening Rachel, Philip and I took the Even behind the island at Waldringfield and put out our drift net. I had just been asked how we would know if we had caught anything when the floats begin Bobing up and down frantically, hauling in the net we found we had caught five Mullet and one Jobe, all in about five minutes. This beats rod and line for productivity Fishing was stopped then as we had more than enough to eat. Wednesday 27th July. Went on shore to collect stores from the shop at Waldringfield, which is very well stocked, had some liquid sustenance from the Maytree and returmed to the boat for a fish lunch, sailed in the Mirror with the children during the afternoon. We debated whether to go up to Woodbridge on the evening tide but de- cided to do this tomorrow moming, at which point the owner of the mooring rowed by and said that he would like it back in a couple of hourse Decission reversed and we motored up to the marina at Woodbridge arriving about 21.00. Thursday 2Sth July. The day started with an unpleasant drizzle which persisted whilst we went into the town which we find fascinating. The facilities at the Marina have been improved, since our last visit in 1975, with the addition of a toilet block with showers which we found were kept clean and had a good supply of hot water. We met Peter Hammer, his wife and brother-in-law in the afternoon, they were over on holiday from Holland in the boat knepie II which was a Deb 535- They were very enthusiastic ..bout the quality of British:boats and gear but were dismayed at the lack of stock held by chandlers as they were undble to buy several items they wanted. Priday <oth July. We all went to the swimmin:; pool this mornings it t& an excellent pool and for those who don't know, issited just beyond the railway station. The weather is brighter now but the wind is still strong so we will stay a few days more. The chidren are making friends and I ave been varnishing, fitting out has to be done when possible, The evening was spent on Knepie II.

tachel and I took the Mirror out of the marina and sailed up to Wilford Bridge, this is something I have wanted to do for several years but haven't found time before. We met Alan and Vere Jupp, from liersea today. They had brought Pelican, Jack sates last boat, up from Nersea for the first time and were enjoying their journey despite seasickness amongst the crew. Knepie II left gm the tide bound for Holland having obtained a reasonable forcast for the tripe We spent the evening on board ‘Ae! with Alan and Vere. Sunday jist July. I finished some varmmishing and the children were playing with Pelican's crew and Isobelle Deveedt from Palanis II, a Belgian boat belonging to her parents Ian and Hilda. We took a walk in the aftermoon along to the playing field behind Eversons boat yard and then onto a ‘green lane' which led down to the river near Kyson quay and we returned along the sea walle In the evening we went aboard Palanis II, Ian is an architect and he also likes to paint and were show some beautiful water colours of the Woodbridge river area. Monday ist August. The weather had now improved and we left the marina at 12.45 with a gentle S.W. breeze to go back to the rocks where the children went swin- ing and looking for sharks teeth and were lucky enough to find half a dozene Pelican and Palanis II came dowm to join us and in the evening we had an enjoyable barb-que on the beach. We decided that tomorrow we would all go round to Woolvastone on the River Orwell. to be cont/. eee All contributions in for August's Navigans by Saturday August j2tn please.

COMMODORES COLUMN I hope you all enjoyed your holidays as much as we did — you can see more 420's on practically any beach across the channel, than there are in ghe whole of East Anglia’ Whilst the summer lingers and we have a few weeks of sailing ahead of us I would like to remind you that our subscriptions have remained steady over the past 3 years despite inflationary pressures. LEach year we budget to spend some £500 on & major item - this year for example it is the re- decorgtimg of the exterior of the Clubhouse. Your committee believes it is now necessary to propose an increase in subscriptions for the coming year, particularly as there is now a growing number of items in need of attention. These include — Road Repairs, New radio for rescue boat, Workboat improvements, Gate Locks and Keys, Site improvements to name but « few. I hope you all agree that we must maintain the Club Property and equipment at a good state of repair and performance. Alan Goss, our Treasurer will provide details of our proposals, next month. I was all @or beaching mear the club but wiser counsels prevailed. Betty's adwice was good for although we were a long way down towards Stone the starting guns, public address commentary and other noise overspill from the open meetings in progress at our Club were clearly audible to an obtrusive degree. Anyone who has spent nights afloat @m twe Blackwater knows that it is often anything but quiet even in the small hours, and we all know how much din is created by speed boats, but I wonderered last weekend whether it was necessary tm or desirable for us as a responsible club to contribute so readily to the general noise. By the time this appears the 4th Barnacle points/Marconi Cruiser Cup race will have been sailed and shall know whether all that back breaking bottom scrubbing did any good - I can guess! CRUISER FLEET NEWS Yet another sailing season, if not exactly over is at least getting well matured. The more experienced and hardier among us have made their trips to France and Hooland, braving some rather poor Summer weather. Some, like my family, have had anotier look pottering localy and up the East Coast. One advantage of sailing is that plans can be adjusted at the last moment to suit one's mood and the weather. We had every intention of sailing to London but it is said "Gentlemen do not sail to windward" so we didn't either. Walton Backwaters proved very hospitable at a time when it was rather blowy outside. We find that Stone Point for the children to plzy followed by an anchorage off Skippers' Island gives an excellent combination, with the odd dinghy trip to Walton for good measure. We made our first trip into the Debden, with "East Coast Rivers" as our pilot. No problems were encountered but I will endorse the comment that plenty of power is meeded to get out against a rising tide ,t neaps. This does give an easy passage over the bar however. We mxm very much liked the tawn of Woodbridge and enjoyed our stay in the tide mill marina - quite a change from swinging to the anchor which is usual for "Kalinka-on-Tour". Enough of me however, how have you all been fairing? The best way to report is to bring all those holiday slides to "The Generals Arms" on the first Thursday in October. Don't Forget. May I remind everyone as luying up time approaches to check over their trolleys. Good location makes things a lot easier while for keel boats some real strength is vital - there is still time to put things right - do it now! At one time cruisers were always extremely steady and leaving or pick- ing up @ mooring was normally done under sail. Most of our fleet approach this situation and it is excellént that in suitable conditions we should practice handling under sail. However the modern design of cruiser racer is so skittish that it would be unwise to attempt this. At least one collision has already occurred to prove this - not with Kalinka this time I might say. In case of doubt therefore please use your motor until well Clear of other boats - no one wants unneccessary wear and tear whether fair or otherwise. See you all at the Generals Arms. CRUISER FLEET NEWS Now that laying up has more or less finished and many of us have taken @ look at or even taken up our moorings, there is @ good opportunity to check over these vital items of equipment. A word of guidance might be useful regarding what is good practice for moorings. A point often misunderstood with ground tackle is that electrolytic corrosion can be our worst enemy - far worse than abrasion and rust. The worst thing you can possibly do to a mooring chain is to put stainless steel wire onto your shackles. The combination of stainless steel and ordinary steel or iron produces an electrolytic cell which wiil rapidly destroy the shackle. Many an old hand has taken up his maring, found the shackle pins to be floating, held only by the wire and then said to others — "What a good thing I wired it or the pin would have fallen out". Poppycock!: If he hadn't made an electrolytic cell the pin and shackle would have been as sound as any other part of the chain. If you feel you must wire your shackles then the wire must be compatible with the chain and shackle. Galvanised iron wire does no harm but may not last very long. wonel will last forever but will cause just a little corrosion. I suppose belt and braces technique would be to put two shackles at every joint if the chain would accept them - I know which one would be in perfect condition at next inspection - the un- wired one! Finally on moorings - for anyone putting down new chain - the major cause of wear is movement between the links and the best investment is te put down the heaviest chain you can get. It will always move less and so wear less than a lighter chain, and when it has eventually worn a little will shill be strenger and much heavier. However, movement causing abrasion is always more critical than simple rusting so it would be a waste of money to pay the extra for galvanised chain - the zine coating will be removed in the first few weeks. The only exception is if you put a foot or so of chain on deck where you don't want rust marks. When it comes to wire rigging the situation is completely different. One hopes the rigging is not immersed continuously in water and so the electrolytic business is not quite so important though must not be forgotton. On the other hand rigging shakes in the wind and I fvel wiring is most important. Stainless rigginy needs monel shackle wire. For galvanised rigging gal- vanised rigging in a mixture of boiled linseed oil and white spirit, then hang it ap in the garage to dry. It should then last at least as long as stainless, which some people say can be brittle. Finally, if you are still with me, an interesting observation on the above subject. Continuing the log of ‘Ace of Diamonds', Symmer Cruise 1977 (sorry Tony, I left you in Woodbridge in August Navigans:) TUESDAY 2nd August Up early, our baby alarm working to schedule, weather forcast wes good and we were ready to leave as planned at 09.00. We beat down river with tre last cf the ebb and against the start of the flood to arrive out at the entrance about 2 hours after low water. We motored out of the Deben, Wendy throwing a well aimed line to Pelican, as she was having difficulty making over the tide, and we towed her out casting off after we had crossed the bar. Sail was raised again and we had a most enjoyable sail into Harwich Harbour on into the River Orwell to Woolverstone where we found a berth in the marina along with Polaris 11 and Pelican. We spent the evening in the Royal Harwich Y.C. who extended their usual pleasant welcome. WEDNESDAY 3rd August A large group set off this morning to walk along to Pin Mill and Chelmond- iston for stores, then we went into the Butt and Oyster for lunch which we thought was good value for money. In the evening we followed a path along the river as far as Freston Tower then turned inland on footpaths which finally led back to Wolverston. The crew became quieter and quieter the further we went. I would do this more often if I was fit enough. THURSDAY 4th August We had decided to go to Walton backwaters today with Pelican, Polaris 11's crew wanted to stay another dayand then all meet again in Brightlingsea on Friday. Our intended 08.00 start was delayed due to fog until 10.00 which meant we missed the ebb. We motored out of the marina and across the river While Wendy was hoisting the sails and telling me how near the shore was. I thought I knew better and we went aground. Soon off as the tide was now flooding. It took us five hours to reach Stone Point which brought home the lesson about working the tides. The S.W. wind was now increasihg raising doubts about our Coastal passage tomorrow. Over a beer in the evening on ‘Ace’ with Alan and Vera we decided to listen to the 06.30 forecast tomoprow and decide then whether to go or not. FRIDAY 5th August 06.30 forecast S.W. force 4-5 so we decided to go out and have a look. Weighed

anchor at 08.30. Sailed to Pye End Buoy by 09.00 and were abeam of Stone Banks Buoy by 09.35. The seas were rough and with the prospect of a beat down the coast in wind over tide conditions we decided to turn and go back to Pin Mill. Pelican could be seen ahead beating on. (We learnt later that they turned and went back to Walton) Just into Harwich Harbour we met Polaris 11 beating out and they turned around te join us » We picked up adjacent moorings at Pin Mill where we spent the rest of the day laying about. We decided to try again tomorrow. SATURDAY 5th August. 06.30 forecast E to NE 4-5 occasional 6. As the wind was only about force 3 at present we decided to go as with luck we would be getting shelter from the shore further down the coast when we thought the wind would be strongest. Let go the mooring at 09.20 in company with Polaris 11. No.1 jib and main set. Left the Orwell at 16.10, worked the tides right this time!. Once out of Harwich Harbour we realised tthe wind was stronger than anticipated, ‘Ace's’ handiing made it apparen that we must reef. Wendy volunteered, she would rather be on deck than " take the helm, I was unhappy about this as the waves were very steep about 6'-7' high, however in a joint effort we took down five rolls in the main and ‘Ace’ handled well again. The Naze Tower was abeam by 11-15 and as we were now runnin g the jib was taken down to atop it flogging. Clacton pier was abeam at 12.35 and the seas and wind were moderating. Past the Bench Head Buoy at 14.15 and picked up our mooring Buoy at 15.30. Todays trip had been an experience for us as the seas were the worst we had been in and I was please d with the perform Once of ‘Ace’ and her crew. In conclusion we all felt our holiday cruise had been q pleasure, we hadn't covered a great distance but we had met some nice people, which is probably what a cruise is all about. ee yete?Aa At F

COMMODORE'S REPORT — 1976 It seems mo time at all since we met here last year, but during that time many things have happened. Not the least some 300 races have been sailed, excluding our Regatta, and many successful cruisers have been made on waters near and far. When you get wrapped up in the organisation and management of the Club it is easy to forget that we all joined to enjoy ourselves and if your Commodore and Officers always seem to be pleading for help it is because the Committee is trying wry hard to provide you with the club it believes you want. They can only go so far, however, and if help is not sufficiently forthcoming some standards must deciine. J know from your very presence here tonight that those remarks do not apply to you. I certainly do not wish to imply that this year has not been anything other than successful or that the committee have in anyway been remiss. On the contrary they have all done sterling work and deserve the appreciation of us all. I have however, detected a feeling that some of the enjoyment may have gone for that diminishing band of stalwarts who will always offer their services rather than see standards fall. Nol the ladies of the galley are not paid staff‘ Nor do any other helpers have any special privileges. I believe we must all take heed of this warning and share the work and responsibility willingly - it must be enjoyable Yor allt if you have any views on how we could improve our organisation please tell your committee as they do need your support. After that cry from the heart 1 shall confine myself to the huppenings of the year. The lounge and exterior of the Clubhouse have been repainted. The lounge was decorated by our caretaker Claude Emerson who has again maintuined the Club and its surroundings in a clean and tidy condition throughout the year. The lounge has been likened to an Art Gallery rather than a Sailing Club. They are nautical pictures after all but if anybody has any alternatives to offer lets ‘have them'. It is our intention that Claude will complete the decoration of the changing rooms and corridors, this winter. Warly in the year a severe storm damaged the sea wall and the site and the Clubhouse lower ground floor areas were flooded. Fortunately very little damage was caused, although the iver Boards equ. pment made rather a mess of the dinghy park. It was however a reminder of the power or the sea and the fact that the sea wall is only just high enought That is the reason why our newly aquired freezer cabinet is now standing in the lounge. We have had several brushes with officialdomthis year. Following the publishing of the River Blackwater Survey we were approached by the Maldon District Council with a request for a licence fee for siting our concrete hard and scrubbing parts on ithe foreshore. The sum of money involved was quite uodest, but as a number of clubs had received similar requests and most were not satisfied with the terms and conditions of the licence the matter was referred to B.a.C.S.).A. to investigate on everyones behalf. As a result of these investigations a new anc more acceptable licence agreement is being drawn up. Whilst on the subject of B.A.C.S.P.A. I must mention the able work done by Stan Allerton and Frank Savill who have only just relinquishec their positions of Ghairman and Secretary after 35 years -f hardwork. Stan has agreed to continue on the B.A.C.S.P.A. Committee as our representative and Frank has agreed to rejoin our

—- 4 — Committee — a potential Flag Officer if ever I sa one’ In July we received another letter from the Council saying that Stansgate was situated in a zone on the Southof the Blackwater where Camping and Caravaning amongst other things was forbidden without specific Planni ng Permission to do report that we so. Application was immediately made and I am pleased to be ableed,tobut have been granted permission for the 28 days per year we request only for a limited period until December 1941 when it will be necessary for us to re-apply. control our It therefore behoves us to be very circumspect in how we regulate and Camping if we wish to retain this permission in 1982. There were several legal objections to our applications. Our Campin g marsha l Jim Coy, ably assisted by Corrinnehas laid the foundation for good campin g behavi our but next year we will need to be very careful. Our immediute neighbour has complained that members, particu larly on busy camping weekends, trespass on her property. The Club has always enjoye d very good relations with its neighbours and I would ask you all to ensure that none of our members or visitors are allowed onto neighbouring land. The River Blackwater has also become very popular as a potenti al Fishery for Oysters. The Committee have been watching developments very closely but so far nothing is planned which will prejudice our interests. The Regatta is obviously the major event of the season. More races are sailed, more beer is drunk, more people visit the site than prectically for all the rest gave rise to a record of the year put together, and the exceptionally fine weatheronslau attendance. The additional toilet facili ties surviv ed the ght. The Barbecue however saw the other extreme and for the first time in many years the rain came and many people stayed away. ‘This event require s almost as much physical effort from Club members as does the Regatts . The erectio n and removal next day of the Marquee, Bar, disco and barbecue scaffolding, equipment and coversnk isthea mamouth task for a social evening. I am convinced we could well re-thi layout of this event and reduce the work load without detracting from the uniqueness of the occasion. It was heartening to see the Cruiser Fleet and other social events taking place at Stansgate; it has always seemed a pity to me that we do not make greater use of our fine new Clubhouse on other than Sailing days. The Sailing Programme will be reported on by our Sailing Secretary, but 1 shoulding like to take this opportunity to thank hi and all the Sailing team for organis such good sailing throughout the year. The number of dinghy helms attending open meetings and winning glory for the series, Club has diminished considerably of late but support for the houevigorou particularly from our up and coming cadets has resulte d in very s and enthusiastic racing at the club. I chose those words carefull y as 1 believe our knowledge of the racing rules and procedures is a little sketchy at the moment but this I am sure will improve with training and experien ce. It was certainl y most gratifying to see the Cruiser Racing Series really heginning to take off. Our collegues from Marconi Avionics at Rochester visited in force again and came very close to beating us. A significant milestone in the history of the club was reached at the Laying Up Supper when Sir Eric Eastwood resigned from the Presidency of the Club. A small parting gift was made on your behalf as a memento to 25 years in office, and the last act of the retiring Committee was to bestow Honary Life Membership onto Sir Eric and Lady Eastwood and we hope to see both of them at Stansg ate next summer.

ai > Sie Our new president eleci Jack Pateman has made the journey from Kent to be with us tonight and I hope you will make him welcome. Security has continued to be of increasing concern. The Clubhouse doors and windows, and the gateway are frequently left open. Several items of members property have been stolen. We must all take more pride in our Club and make sure that everything is secure before the site is left unattended — security must become a ritual. The gatelock was broken open mid-season and the code key stolen. In view of this and the increasing number of cards lost or not returned, the committee have decided to change the security codes and issue new card keys to all members as they renew next season. ‘The locks will be changed on March lst 1979. As outlined in Navigans the Committee consider that it is now necessary to increase our subscriptions. The subs have remained unchan,:ed for the last 3 seasons and it is intended that the increases proposed will see us through a further 3 years. The major item of expenditure will be the repair and resurfacing of the road. for the past few years we have done the absolute minimum amount of work on the road in case the Marina Project came into being. Whilst this may yet still happen the prospect becomes more and more unlikely as time goes by. The road can be left no longer without running the risk of rapid and serious, ieterioration and astronomical expense. To patch and shingle only the bad areas will cost around £1,500 and to tar and shingle most of the road in about 2 years time will cost a further £2,000 and we have been advised that it would be prudent to consider resurfacing every 5 years or so to retain a waterproof layer on the surface. We must therefore be putting aside some £60 per year just for road maintenance. Whilst we have a reserve capable of funding the initial stages of this work, we believe that we must maintain a reserve of around £2,000 in order to preserve our independance and cope with those unexpected expenses which pop up from time to time. ‘The immediate provision of new radio equipment plus the prospect of an increased rental contribution to the M.A.S.C. make it necessary for us to raise an additional £1,200 per annum over the next 3 years. This is roughly equivalent to £3 per membership — still very good value I believe. I cannot finish without making a special reference to our lady members. Can you imagine the Club without Jill, Margaret and the galley team, without Shirley or Navigans, without Joyce and Pat in the bar, without lady Race Officers, without our Wives and girlfriends to feed us when we return from sailing or load the stores if we are going cruising? I hopenot all of us take you too much for granted. Finally I would like to offer my personal thanks to the retiring committee and to the many members who have helped make my year of office so enjoyable and inparticular to David Lawson and the social committee for the Laying Up Supper arrangements. Frank Savill, Fleet Captain HHH HHH HHH K HH KKH HH HH EHH HH OK KH THE NAUTICAL MILE The length of a nautical mile in relation to navigation When I was young, I looked out of the club windows across the marshes into the far distance and it seemed to me that tre earth was flat. When I went to my first school, I told my teacher that the eurth was flat. "No" she said, "That is not so} it is a sphere." "What does that mean?"”. "It means that it is round like a ball" I wrote that the earth was a sphere and they thought me so clever th t they sent me to Grammar school. I told the geography master that I knew that the earth was a sphere. "No" he said, "It is a spheroid". Wht does that mean?" "It means that it is slightly flattened at the Poles". I wrote down that the earth was a spheroid, and they thought me so clever that they put me in the sixth form. I told the Senior Geography master thut I knew that the earth was a spheroid. "No" he said, "That is not se; it is an oblate spheroid! "What does that mean?" "It means that one Pole is flattened a bit more then the other". I wrote that the earth was an oblate spheroid and they thought me so clever that they sent me to University. I told my Tutor that I knew that the earth was an oblate spheroid. "No," s aid he, "That is not so; it is a geoid". "What does that mean?". "It means, earth shaped," He replied: (Note:- Greek, Geios means "To do with the earth") How does all this affect our navigation? Although there are 360 degrees in a circle, because of the flattening of the earth at the poles, they are not all of the same length. At the equator their length is 1842 metres, while at the poles, they are 1861 metres. However, the Admiratly issued a notice to MarinersNo: 1518 in 1970 announcing that the International nautical mile was precisely 1852 meters, which is, in fact, the length of a sea mile in latitude 45 degrees. When we wish to measure distance on our charts, we place our dividers along the (vertical) latitude snd@le which caters for the variation in length at different latitudes and are therefore quite safe in taking one minute as being the length of a sea-mile for that particular chart. In other words, we huve no need to worry - all this has been thoughtfully provided for on t e charts which we use. Eric Payne.

COMMODORE'S COLUMN First the Good News Ladies you now have your own representative on the Committee. In response to my request last month, Anne Bates has volunteered her services and she attended her first committee meeting on Monday 5th February. June Fuller has agreed to look after the planting and tending of trees at Stansgate. Anybody with trees to offer or who is willing to help with their maintenance should contact Russ who will pass on the message. It is pleasing to see families so committed to serving the Club - Thank you both. Now the Bad News Jill Savill after many years of running and building up our highly success- ful Galley Service, is unabie to continue in this capacity. We all owe a great deal to Jill, Frank and the small herd of helpers. Jill deserves a weél earned break, although I suspect she will often be seen helping in a less onerous capacity - it has been another fine family effort. Now comes the rub! We have built up a service which we are now in danger of loosing. Over the past two years the level of help has been so low that the 'few' have had more and more to do. This state of affairs cannot continue. If we cannot find a Galley Organiser to take Jill's place and more help is not forthcoming the service will not operate this coming season. I cannot believe that we will let this happen if you value or have enjoyed our Galley Service please volunteer now! Ken Beavins It is with deep regret that we have to report the death on Oth February of Ken Beavins. A member of very longstanding, Ken was currently serving on the Committee representing views of our Associate Members. A man never afraid to express his views, often in the face of popular opinion, he has done much to treate the Club we have today. We shall all be poerer for his passing. Mirror, Enterprise, Handicap, Cruisers and unattached can then make themselves useful on the final onslaught. John Weedon, Rear Commodore.

The dinghy series last season saw averag@ entries for the Spring Series ranging from 3 for the Enterprise to 7.5 for the 420 & the Summer Series averaging between 3.5 for the Enterprise to 7.6 for the 420. The most popular races which were sched- uled during the season was the Wednesday Evening Races, these attracted a total number of 156 boats, averaging at 13 per race. The Cruiser Barnacle Series has received anincreased interest last year, with four races scheduled. It is planned that with increased interest this series will be extended to 6 races for the 1979 season. The Mona Cup, Pilots Cup & Mud Race received entries of 29, 17 & 25 respectively the former two racesencompassing part of the Barnacle Series. The two Open Trophy races attracted entries of 35 for the Dinghy Challenge Cup & 24 for the Cruiser Cup. The Dinghy Challenge Cup unfortunately a victimof the English Summeron the scheduled date With the race on the reserved date suffering from entries. The Hornet/Mirror Open meetinghad an entry of 30 Hornets and 24 Mirrors. The Hornet entry attracted one of the largest entries to date. It has been planned a0 arrange additionally a Solo Open Event in 1979. The rescue boat organisation during the past season has seen a great improvement under the auspicies of Norman Kerridge. The number of drivers for this duty was kept small by design & this system has enabled rescue facilities to be manned regularly. Our thanks must soto Norman Kerridge & his team of drivers from all club members, with the knowledge tht they are there if required during racing. The race officer manning unfortunately has hot been in the same position. There has been the regular group of experienced members who covered this duty but more experienced members are required and to hold Race Officer irtruction during one of the forthcoming Winter Meetings with follow up work at Stansgate next spring. Anyone interested will be welcome. Finally thanks to all the Fleet Captains and members of the Sailing Committee for the help during the past year. M.J. Vaughn. GS SPRING SAILING The calender on my kitéhen wall is trying to tell me that Spring isn't far away, while the appearance of paint and anti-foubing colourcharts and the smell of varnish emanating from the lounge shout out the fact that the fitting out has begun. In a few weeks time, amongst a melée of daffodils, Easter eggs, why haven't I washed the sails yet, and where oh where are all the East Coast charts, the sailing season will have begun again. With this in mind, I thought members might welcome a couple of suggestions for trips at the beginning of the cruising season. During April and May, the weather can be a bit nippy and unreliable and a short gail with somewhere to go at the end and back, of it is more appreciated by the family than roaring off to the Bench Head long. when everyone except Dad gets cold, wet and miserable and it all takes too So, where to go, first there's Bradwell. A quick sail down river to the power channel station, turn right and you're there. A couple of points to mention, the and is very tortuous and should be negotiated with care. Follow the witheys makingbuoys, it is very easy to run aground on the mud banks. Excellent practise for a passage using the echo-sounder, 4 useful job for a junior crew member calling out the depth. Moorings are available in the creek and there is usually someone around to ask it it's O.K. to pick one up. There is also the marina, convenient for taking on water and fuel, but it is expensive. For a warm welcome ashore you don't have to go far, just walk up the slipway and stop at the first building on’ the right, The Bradwell Quay Sailinga Club. Here, the majority of members are cruis@zsowners and although they have comprehensive, keen racing fleet, there are plenty of potters to exchange gossip with over a pint or two. We called here during the autumn las$ year, and met Bill Basson, one of the founder members, who due te an injury received in the war, looks like a benevolent Captain Hook when he gives you a wave. We were invited to a "Pirate's Evening" and for a £1 a head, no charge for children, we had an excellent cold supper, and there was draft Abbott and a band as well. All very informal and pleasant. If you ike walking, it's . very pleasant to stroll round the village and if you really like walking you can go to St. Peter's on the Wall, the first church in England. Another easily reached port of call is Heybridge Basin. Just leave the moorings and head up River towards Maldon and stop at the "Jolly Sailor". Here, one can lock into Heybridge Canal, although a few moorings are available on the river. The lock is small, but good practise with fenders and warps, if you are thinking of being adventerous and going foreign later in the season. It is good manners to let the lock-keeper, George Clarke, know you are coming if a few boats intend to go together. Once safely moored up in the canal, and if you can get Dad out of the pub, put the outboard onto the stern of the tender and potter up the canal to Beeleigh. It's well worth the effort. The factories and cottages built by Bentalls at the turn of the century are reminders that Heybridge was then a thriving industrial community and not the rather sleepy backwater we know today. You pass around the back of Maldon alongside the golf course and then up to the first lock at Beeleigh. Here you can wander around the outskirts of the Abbey grounds or along the tiny country lanes edged with oak and horse chestnut trees’tn the meadows, beds of wild watercress grow, dark and green. This trip is more fun in company, and ideal for children, big or amall, when you ¢an play dogems with one another or Trace someone along the tow path. You can even atop off at the shops and buy the odd Mars bar, As I said previously, the idea of these two “excursions” is an hour or two's

tw sailing for Dad, combined with an outing for the family. For all the inform- ation proper required, you should beg, borrow or buy a copy of Jack Coote's "Bast Coast Rivers". Bradwell Sailing Club produce a very useful chart showing the creek and it's entrance with all the relevant marks in full, which is well worth acquiring. This article was written with new cruiser owners also in mind, who are about to discover the delights of sailing the Blackwater. May I wish everyone good sailing in 1979. Brenda Tate. ta So LE SARNTY Just a timely reminder to all members whilst the water conditions are cold and the weather unpredictuble. The following notes are recommendations for all time at the club. 1) Officer of the Day: a) Responsible for safety in the vicinity of the Club. b) Ensure that the Rescue crew have access to their equipment and the Bast(s). Club events shoulda be postponed if the available facilites cannot cope with the prevailing conditions. Maintain radio contact with the rescue boat. (This responsibility may be delegsted to t e Race Officer). 2)Race Officer? a) Check off the competitors at the start and as may times as is practical during the race. Report any missing boats to the rescue crew. b) Ensure that any boat not completing the course has returned safely. 3) Rescue Crew: a) Check the boats sailing as often as is practical and if any are missing confirm their whereabouts. b) When the racing-hasigot. underway take up station near the gybe mark in heavy weat er or downtide in very light weather. In mediun conditions a central position can be chosen. 4) Members: a) Ensure personal equipment and boat is adequate for the conditions. If the weather is such that you will not be able to cope do not venture out; ask if in doubt. b) If, however you do require assistance on the water, stay with the boat and wave arms up and down. Do not use more energy than can be helped and drop anchor if in danger of drifting away. c) If racing sign off immediately afterwards, this is most important when retiring. John Weedon, Rear Commodore. ¢

2 COMMODORE 'S NOTES I can't believe iti! It's snowing as I pen these notes, and the Regatta is only a few weeks away. The bad weather has one compensation in that it delays a little longer, the resurfacing of the road, and so gives us time to finish clearing the road edges. The support for the working party called on Easter Saturday was dismal =— less than 20 people came, and half of those were youngsters. The farmer kept his promise to help by bull-dozing the worst of the overgrowth but the task can only be finished by hand. If everyone who attends the club over the next few weeks brings with them a fork, spade or shovel and spends just 20 to 30 minutes working the job will soon be donee. A job well done now will last for years. For those who are not sure just what is required I will explain. The road, over its' entire length is edged with concrete. Grass and soil have gradually grown over the edge, both narrowing the road and preventing water from draining off the road into the verges and gullies. We need to remove all of this material, to fully expose the concrete road surface and edge. It is hard, but worthwhile work. So please help if you can. The O O D will advise if you are not certain what is needed. The section most in need of attention stretches from the second corner after the Eagle Gates entrance for some 300 yards towards the Rainbow Cottages. I am sorry, but it is all work this month! The Regatta does not run itself; the usual working party has been called for Wednesday evening 23 May, and it is hoped that more members will be able to spend Friday 25 May at Stansgate to help erect the bar, toilets and other outside facilities. A full quota of helpers is of course again required to help with the major tasks during the event iee. Galley Bar, Reception, Marshalling, Maintenance and Racebox. SO PLEASE REMEMBER ROAD AND REGATTA During the Regatta and the following week it is imperative that we demonstrate to our neighbours and the Local Council Officers that we can control all aspects of this event i.e. camping, tresspassing and nuisance, to their complete satisfaction. Our planning consent is subject to renewal in 1981 so please be warned. These notes should have been entitled "Ron's Road Show" or possibly "Regatta Round Up". Never mind, the snow has stopped, things are looking up. Finally, please spare a thought for Jill Saville who has just spent a week in hospital. "Jill, we all wish you a speedy return to good health and look forward to seeing you with that old sparkle back in your eye". Ron Greygoose Commodore

1979 GILTONIAN WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP FOR 18FT SKIFFS SYDNEY HARBOUR Just before Christmas I received an invitation from the New South Wales 18 footers Sailing Club in Sydney, to participate in the forthcoming Giltonian World 18 foot Skiff Championship, to be sailed in the Harbour. With snow lying thick on the ground I decided that, in spite of a very pregnant wife, and an imminent house move, this was an offer I couldn't refuse. Travelling expenses were to be met by British Airways, who had also chartered the Australian "Overseas Containers Limited" boat for the event — all I had to do was get in it and sail it. Unfortunately my crew once again were to be left behind. Sailing an Eighteen is very much coordinated teamwork by 3 specialists, all jobs are equi- important and a scratch Australian crew, however good, would not substitute for the 4 years that Bob Fawkes, David Elphinstone and myself have sailed together. After the snow and 24 hours sitting in a 747, stepping into the Sydney sunshine was like stepping into Paradise. All the British team had arrived at least one week previously and had quite established suntans, made me feel like a maggot by compar- ison’ After the initial Board of Control meeting - the Board governs the affairs of the "Titles" and is comprised of the member clubs throughout the World, I went to see "British Airways". The boat was beautifully turned out sporting the British Airways logo lettering up the side in red and blue, and 8ft diameter smiling cartoon Jumbo's, B A's latest advertising gimmick, on the mainsails. The boat was of very light wooden construction - about 160 lbs with rope and fittings, excellently built using Cedar and Gaboon ply. A glance around the dinghy park however, showed that in the past year tremendous advancements have been made, particularly with plastics and foam on paper honeycomb cores. At Plymouth, all the Australian contingent with the exception of "Color 7" were wooden, now all the top twelve boats are plastic reinforced with aluminium "space" frames to take the stress points. Mechanical rig tensioning gear, has in many cases been dropped, in favour of hydraulic mast jacks. "Color 7" still retains a mechanical system at 64:1 on each shroud, but has boxed the whole tension system in along the hog in case one of the muscle boxes ‘explodes’ damaging someone's foot. Masts are now moving aft, and so correspondingly are rudders, which are being slung from sponsors about 9" to 1' behind the transom, and of course, they're still getting lighter - or so any true Australian Eighteen sailor would have you believe. Ingenuity is the watchword. Simple ideas such as sprinkling sugar on to wet varnish or resin to create a nonslip finish, the sugar simply disolves away, leaving a rough finish, but no messy sand for fitting out next time round. "Clam Cleats" are extensively used (metal version), however the Australians streamline them by filing away unwanted metal and drilling lightening holes in them. Just a few grams saved, but the top racing is very, very close and no gear lightening is too much trouble. Incentives to win are high, an Australian 18ft Champion is ranked among the leading sportsmen, and will undoubtedly be featured sometime on Television and in the papers. He also has to consider the new boat for the coming season, which may cost over $35,000 (approx £18,700) for one year, poor results will mean the sponsor will either pull out, or look for more promising materials - only the winners get publicity.

5 Innovation in the Eighteens, for many years was slow in coming. Like so many classes the crews were not prepared to look around for inspiration from other dinghy sailors and failed to take stock of the changing techniques. Bruce Farr arrived on the scene in 1970 and developed a line of light weight, wooden, functional thoroughbreds for 3 handed sailing, 70 lbs lighter than anything designed before. Furthermore, the bouyancy incorporated into the hull shape of each design was geared to fit the crew weight expected to sail in the boat, along with the exact requirements and details for the sailplan and the rig change and wind speed. Farr's designs reigned supreme for 5 World Championships until 18 year old Iain Murray appeared with a radical, 10ft beamed boat, sponsored by Color 7 TV. The Murray/Color 7 combination have now won 3 World Titles in succession, and Murray has led the Eighteens from "night" into "day", by revolutionising construction methods and making the glass fibre/paper honeycomb core construction work. His designs are faster than Farr's and carry incredible amounts of sail - almost as much as the old 4 handers. He is a crack 12 footer sailor (much harder to sail than an 18 footer), and bared his ideas on the radical Twelves. He incorporated high freeboard, hitherto frowned on because of the extra weight of higher sides, wide aft chines and a very 'U' shaped forward entry for improving "nose-dive" characteristics. Perhaps this progress is the good side of sport sponsorship, development has now reached fever pitch and the money is there to see new ideas succeed or fail, anyway, new ideas have now come along to benefit all dinghy sailors - if they care to look that is, and progress makes development in the 470 and Flying Dutchman look Medizwval. I won't bore you with details of my efforts in Sydney, fact is we weren't so hot, but certainly one of the biggest problems for all competitors were the washes set up by the spectator craft. Hundreds of people turn out in craft of all shapes and sizes to watch the Eighteens. The water's natural wave pattern soon gets broken up into large confused sease On the fourth race British Airways was doing about 18 knots with the biggest Spinnaker set, and the crew all trapezeing ("three stringing under the biggy" - Australian slang), when we happened upon two large converging washes. I had no option but to steer for the centre of the subsequent eruption, only to find as we careered over the crest there was no water beyond, just a large trough. With nothing under the keel of course we just nosedived and that was that. The following race we found ourselves on the wind with "ITEL Computers" just above us. Gear failure aboard "ITEL" caused her to capsize slowly, but as she did so her mast head picked up my trapeze wire. The next second I was hoisted 15ft in the air as the wire was pulled by British Airways across ITEL's mast head. I must have hit a shroud on the way up, as my face felt as if it would fall in two. With no one at the helm, and my Aussie crew, Phil and Les looking extremely worried, British Airways never faltered, and sailed straight and true. The next second I was back in the drink and swinging back to my position on the side. Undamaged, I might add! However, while British Airways fuddled about, the real battle was between "Color 7", "Steelstocks" and "KB". The racing was filmed by the "Color 7" Helicopter and Launches, and we were able to view the smooth operations of the leaders on TV in the evening sport's bulletins. I'm afraid to say that we in British Airways did not do so well, finishing 3rd out of the 4 British Skippers and 29th out of 34 overall, a result which will take a lot of living down. Entries were received from America, Italy, France, New Zealand, Australia and of course Great Britain, and the Eighteen now appears international if only in small quantities. Bruce Long

SECURITY It is a sad thing, but we live in days of turmoil and unrest, what with vandalism and thieving, and one thing and another. I think probably that we are all conscious of the exposure of our club to these unfortunate facets of our society -— particularly during the week when often there is nobody at the site. We rely very much upon the integrity of our members to support and motivate the club, but there is no way we can have an on site Security Guard, let alone a Caretaker, and a Guard Dog would upset the Sheep! Anyway, in my capacity of Club Security Officer, I have approached various branches of H M Services like the Police, River Police, Coast Guard etcetera, to see whether they are able to help us with our Security during "Off-Peak" periods. They all seem particularly anxious to engender a spirit of trust and cooperation. Certainly it is pleasing to know that Customs Officers visit the Club at all hours of the day and night on a fairly random basis and report to the Police anything which is obviously wronge The Police will then get in touch with me and hopefully take some action. They will certainly do what they can, but it would be nice to reciprocate by helping them. I can help the Police by reporting in Navigans or placing on the notice board items or events which they are keen to get information on, and you can help by keeping your eyes open for those people or craft and reporting events which you think are suspiscious or definitely covert. It would be good to have the Police actively on our side, and I know they would be very grateful for our help. If you wish to discuss matters on Club Security please give me a ring and I will be delighted to talk to you. COMMODORE 'S NOTES The view was expressed to me quite recently that the discipline and involvement of Club Members is declining. My reaction to this was one of disbelief, fortunately, in view of the achievements of the past month. On reflection however, I feel certain that you must have some suggestions for improving the quality of our Club - if so, please tell me, or any committee member, of your views. One area where I believe that we can all help to make our surroundings more pleasant and hygenic is to take our personal litter and rubbish home with us. Also, as we are strictly a "Do it Yourself" organisation, if you see anything in need of cleaning or repair, please D I Y, help to get it done. As I mentioned we have several achievements to our credit since I last wrote in Navigans. All those members and friends who helped in anyway towards the running of the Regatta have my grateful thanks, and they can take pride in the fact that it was a great success, despite the rain, mud and wind. Anybody who read their local newspaper will realise that we had several anxious moments, but good sense, fortune and humour prevailed throughout. The Camping Week and Social Activities were well supported and the highlight of the final weekend was the visit by our President and his team from Rochester. We beat them again, of course, and it is rumoured that our President enjoyed himself so much that he decided to stay and guide our dinghy fleet through the fog at the Bench Head Buoy = or was he lost too? Sorry Jack, Louise and I might never have made it back without you. The road is being resurfaced as I write these notes, and I hope it will make driving to the Club more comfortable for several years to come. Don't forget to let me have your views, but above all ENJOY YOUR SAILING. Ron Greygoose Commodore rr REGATTA BAR I would like to express my sincere appreciation to all members who helped with the Bar. Pleased toreport record business, profits from which, as you know, go a long way to offset club running expenses. My thanks also to John Wilson and Mike Walton of the MASC for their help in organising the supplies, etc, and to Bernard Lingwood and Murray Bates for arranging transportation. David Harper Vice Commodore

REGATTA REPORT As usual the Regatta, held over the Spring Bank Holiday weekend had it's fair? share of Wind, Rain, Beer and Social Activities. The Club received more than 250 visitors over the weekend, and there were 224 dinghies entered in races. The Pennant race held on the Saturday, in aid of the R NL I, raised nearly £30.00, even though high winds — up to Force 6 = and choppy seas prevailed. Sunday began with light winds, Force 2, and the day passed with frequent rain, despite which sailing proceeded and 2 races were held. Monday proved a little different, however. The morning race, with winds up to Force 5, against a flood tide proved exhilarating, although a little wet for some. With an imminent Gale Foce 7 forecast, the afternoons racing was unfortunately cancelled. Classes racing, and the numbers in each class over the weekend were as follows: Class Total Entries Marconi Entries Enterprise 43 Fireball 27 0 420 15 11 GP 14 19 2 Handicap 21 0 Hornet 15 8 Int Moth 13 0 Kestrel 5 0 Laser 22 6) Mirror 28 8 Solo 17 7 Altogether over 20 clubs particpated in the racing, and as the results show, no one club had a monopoly on the prizes. Sadly only two of our members were in amongst the prize-winners, congratulations to them both. I have included two sets of "Regatta Results", one an overall summary of the ist, 2nd and 3rd positions, and the other a complete list of Marconi Club Members results. Well done everyone! John Weedon asked me to put ina "Thank You" to everyone who did something toward the Regatta weekend, so — Thank You to all concerned.

CRUISER RACING = 1979 In view of the renewed interest last year, we have decided to hold six races for the Barnacle Series this year (see Year Book), the four best out of six races to count. Those who raced last year will start with the handicaps derived by the end of the season, newcomers will be given a handicap according to class. Handicaps will be adjusted after each race, as the least unfair way of achieving some competition with such a range of performance. Three of the races are intended to be quite short, either to Maldon or Bradwell, on a Saturday. The other three are established club events in which placing will count towards the series. I hope that a number of you will participate - it's quite good fun and ‘'m sure improves one's overall sailing performance. See you on 16 June. Ron has asked me if I can persuade more Fleet Captains to contribute, don't you have anything to say to those other wet, tired people who are sailing alongside you? "Starboard" or "Water" is OK on the river, but I feel sure that there must be something else to say. The same goes for anyone else who has a few moments to spare, to jot down an article, sea-faring tale or anything which you feel "we" might like to read, and which would make Navigans more a magazine and less an "Official Notice Board". See you sailing. _Last date for August Navigans: Saturday 4 August. TO JOG YOUR MEMORY A reminder to all the recipients of Navigans who "pop the magazine into the briefcase", and leave it there. Please let your families see it promptly, and don't forget to read it too. The closing date for Mamgu entries is ist October. Entries may be sent to the Editor for typing, if required, or direct to the Commodore. (Entries for typing must be received in advance of the closing date). COMMODORE 'S NOTES This copy of Navigans should reach you just about on Barbecue weekend. As suggested by a number of members, we are trying a different layout this year in an attempt to reduce both the work involved and the disruption to club sailing activities. It is particularly relevant this year as the day following the Barbecue is the Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championships at Stone, and I hope that as many of you as possible will participate. The holiday season is on top of us and we are having the usual difficulties in providing cover for all the club duties. The Galley is the main problem and will not open on 12, 19 and 26 August, unless volunteers are forthcoming. We are making an effort to make Fun Day an enjoyable and "Relaxing" day out for all the family, so do come along and join in. Ron Greygoose Commodore sf. et *#®hUcaetmhUchhUCUc OhUcOrmhUlUcrhrChUcrLhUhOorUhUchrhUh# + FC HH FH FH FH # SOCIAL SCREED Fun Day this year is to bo on August 4. Club Policy for the Fisherman is that it is a back up rescue vessel, and as such must always be under the direction of the OOD. However, the safety of the Cruiser Fleet is important and if, for example conditions are too bad to row the family ashore in the dinghy, then ask the OOD if you can borrow the Fisherman. Be prepared for delays however, as crews of upturned dinghys are at more immediate risk than the cruisers on the moorings. Concerning safety, may I again remind members of the inadequacy of plastic row- locks. In my opinion they are unsafe for use at Stansgate. CADET NEWS I know the Regatta seems a long time ago, this is the first opportunity I have had to look back for Navigans. Whilst only two prizes were collected by M S C, one was a Cadet, congratulations to Mark Savill in the Solo Class, with Chris Weedon narrowly missing a prize for 5th overall in the large 420 fleet. Colin and I had 3 days with the Cadets after the Regatta and spent this time with 12 Cadets, some novices, some able to take on most senior club members - and winj and other friends of the families staying for the Camping Week. Once again my thanks to Colin for his help and patience. The next event for Cadets is the National Under 21 Hornet Championships being held at the Club. I know technically 21 is considered an elderley Cadet, those taking part are from the Marconi Cadet Fleet. Please come along on July 21 and 22 and cheer Colin, Chris, Mark, Stephen, Deborah and those others representing Marconi. Happy Holidays to you all. Rick Anstey Cadet Fleet Captain net tc ttmhUhrmhUc OhrmhUCUc OrmhUchOOOT HT THT ee +e Fe ee Fe CRUISER RACING Although we managed a trio of cruisers to run the ist Barnacle on 16 June, a postponement of only 15 minutes on the start, plus a wind change of 180 with the tide within a stones throw of Bench Head prevented everyone from making the mark, and so the race had to be abandoned. However, we had a jolly good sail, and this race will now take place at 1030 on Saturday 22 September. The 2nd Barnacle on 2 July was also eventful. One cruiser helm arrived for the race and the sight of his cruiser reminded him that his main sail was still at Taylors at Maldon. This led to a 30 minute postponement which made the course of Herring Point via the Stumbles quite tense, and the beat down to Colliers Reach against the tide fairly challenging. In spite of a variety of start times due to the failure to recognise the start flag, the sailing committee assure me the race is valid, although I am slightly embarrassed to claim a win. The moral so far is that we must try to start on time. Full results have not yet been received, but will be displayed in the Clubhouse as soon as received. On the Sunday the annual Rum Tub and Bung race from Stansgate was raced in misty conditions, Phil Kenworthy in his G P 14 being the overall winner. The remaining other finishers from the club were as follows: 6th Ron Greygoose 420 7th P Gray 420 8th Colin Leveridge 420 14th Mike Taylor 505 19th Murray Todd Hornet 20th Mike Williams Hornet 23rd P Schuster Hornet The remaining members could not find the Bench Head due to FOG! Whilst doing my housework the other Sunday morning, relatively simple - just a case of sloshing a couple of buckets of seawater round the sidedecks in the sunshine, I ruminated on the fact that the time of year had come around again, for the Cruiser Fleet to demonstrate their culinery skills to the rest of the Club Members; and prepare that gastronomic delight, the food at the Barbecue. Contemplation of this lead onto other thoughts about food and it's preparation, apropo, as Mr Harper would say, small cruising boats. Man has invented fewer more subtle forms of sadism than that of asking his mate to "knock something hot up" in the galley of a small cruiser, while he stands heroically at the tiller and beats up the Wallet to Walton; thereby ensuring that whatever she starts preparing, it will end up ina mesSe Imagine an area the size of your average sink unit, supported on a cake walk, containing a cooker, a sink (or bowl) and a minute work surface, with food and utensils stored in cupboards that require the dexterity of an ambidexterous gorilla to reach, and the rider that, at any given moment in time, when the cook is clutching a saucepan in each sweaty palm, and has both feet braced against the floor, and a fork between her teeth; she will hear her ever-loving coo through the hatch, "Darling, could you come and eee. untangle the jib sheets/drop the anchor/pick up the mooring/put out the fenders etc. etce, and you start to have some idea of what its all about. Well, its not really as bad as that most of the time, although I hasten to add that it can happen. The sailing man like all others marches, or rather beats, tacks, runs and reaches (what an unfortunate word), on his stomach. Food, hot or cold n,is an ~ im a ctor to the well being and safety of the ship, A hungry crew becomes irritable and tired, and fatigue is as great a hazard cruising, being without chart or compass. So passage making, the cook has an important job to do. However, most of us are just faced with the problem of feeding starving hordes each weekend, with very limited facilities. If you are going to cook, the most essential piece of equipment is a cooker. How's that for logical thinking. Cookers on boats are fueled either by Calor Gas or Methylated Spirit. People will argue the merits of both, Tijo has Meths, Jestabel - Calor Gase They both appeal equally to me, one blows the boat up, the other burns it down, but I use Calor Gas as I think that it is cleaner. My galley boasts better culinary equipment, (apart from electrical gadgets) and more cookbooks on the shelf than I have in the kitchen at home. Many make do with battered pans and utensils, that are long passed their best, in my humble opinion, a mistake, as I think you need all the help that you can get, and good equipment makes life that much easier. Basic stores are easier and often cheaper bought in bulk. Chat up your nice kind friend with a Cash and Carry Card, or ferret out the large economy sizes in Tesco's. As to food, well, everyone has their own ideas, and I have been rummaging through my brain trying to remember some of the recipes swopped and meals eaten on board other people's boats, over the years. Breakfast is important, and there is absolutely nothing like the smell of gently frying bacon wafting across quiet waters in the fresh sunlight of the early morning. If I can have a fried breakfast, I alsays do. A real marine treat is fresh caught mackeral gently grilled or fried in butter and served with crusty bread and lashings of horseradish sauce. John Todds swears by porridge, great for lining the stomach, (pessimist!) and is an ardent campaigner against that dreaded modern evil mono sodium glutomate’ Others prefer Swiss Cereal, ideal to serve and very good for you, while Vic like his Force Flakes, and the pictures of Sunny Jim. Kelloggs Variety Packs usually please every one, and are easy to stow. We also treat ourselves to an exotic marmalade on the boat, and have lime and lemon or ginger, as a treat at the weekend.

10 Pete Clayton on Peace cooks fantastic scrambled eggs, not all runny like mine, and his hairy bread is a good substitute if you are low on antibiotics in the medicine chest. Actually, bread will keep for a surprisingly long time on board, wrapped in polythene, and kept in the cool it can still be quite palatable at the end of 3 weeks. Sandwiches are a test of the good cook's ingenuity. The secret is that they should be moist but not soggy.e You can easily tell if they're successful; unsatisfactory efforts are soon used as fish bait or thrown to the gulls. One of the best I have ever tasted was the incredible combination of strong cheese and home-made blackcurrant jam on wholemeal bread, served by John Hopper on Davolos II, somewhere near the Bench Head a couple of years ago, deliciously washed down with a crisp little red wine, fantastic! (You can tell I enjoy my food). Everyone wants something to nibble most of the time, and this is where standbys like flapjacks come in handye My sister-in-law, Francis Tate on Teal at Mersea makes a lovely light shortbread and Anne Tate on Tarka in Weymouth knocks up a very tasty Tea Loaf. Items all very easily packed and stored. Sailing usually takes place in the summer and salad is often the answer to feeding the family. And it can easily be expanded with odd tins of potato salad etc from your store cupboard, when you have the odd half dozen guests come aboard. To ring the changes on ham or corn beef as the main ingredient, why not be lazy and buy up a batch of Cornish Pastys from Rook's; just as tasty with baked beans if the weather turns cooler. Wemdy Cherry on Alpha Centura makes a mouth watering egg and sausage pie, again, equally good hot or cold. The simple solution to the problem of the main meal of the day is to head ashore for the nearest fish and chip shop. However, this isn't always possible and once again, the poor old cook, (usually Mum), is left racking her brain as to how to satisfy her famished family. The cowards way out is to chuck several tins of this and that, or what ever the ambidexterous gorilla can find, into a saucepan and gently heat them upe This can be surprisingly successful and gives hot filling meals in almost seconds, which keeps the crew happy. Pasta meals areonhe of the answers, and certainly "Spagetti Bol" is the favourite dish on Jestabel. And very nice it was too, with a splendid little red wine, which went straight to my head, and I ended up stubbing my cigarette out in the peanuts!! (A very alchoholic evening, we even had Pete Foreman smoking a cigar). Jack and Jackie Manning on the other hand prefer a nice cup of tea, and we all know what that means, Wink! Wink! Nudge’ Nudge’ In fact, to keep Jack's strength up Jackie gives him steak for breakfast! As well as cups of tea, Jackie makes delicious Pizza, and is the only person I know brave enough to use a pressure cooker on board. She is also a dab hand with eggs (did you know fresh eggs will keep for about a month in the cool), and I remember her frying a giant omelette into which she shredded corn beef and then served cut into wedges with fresh crusty rolls. The most important factor about main meals on boats is to try and only use one pan and cook everything together, saving fuel and the washing up. Often the best dishes are those concocted in a flash of inspiration "impromptu"ly. Margaret Campbell's Mullet a la Stanley is one of these. First get a handsome, tanned youth to harpoon you a mullet, preferably from the other end of the marina to the loos. Poach it lightly until the flesh flakes off the bone and then blend with a beaten egg and fold into some made up instant potato mix. Pat into a large round and gently fry in butter with some onions and mushrooms. Serve with grilled tomato's. Even Stan would agree, that it was just as good as a pair of pints. Brenda Tate (Editors Note: Sorry the Recipes came first = bute..)

COMMODORE 'S NOTES We are now at the height of the holiday season and the number visiting Stansgate is at a peak. I want you all to share in the enjoyment of our wonderful facilities but for this to happen we must all be mindful of our responsibilities as members. Here are some important reminders:- 1 Please close the gate every time. Don't leave it to somebody else. 2 Please keep Dogs on a Lead. Several instances of nuisance have been reported to me recently. 3 Please do not leave money or valuables in the changing rooms. Money has been taken from the clothing of several members whilst they have been out sailing. 4 Please keep a look out for strangers in our premises and report anything suspicious. 5 Please help to keep the Club clean and tidy by clearing up after you and taking home as much domestic refuse as possible. Food residues attract vermin and are a health hazard. Finally Fun Day was blessed with good weather and provided a fun climax to the Camping Week. Our thanks should go to Margaret Lingwood and her helpers for making it such a happy occasion. HELMSMAN OF THE YEAR FINAL The Helmsman of the Year Final will be held on September 22 (Saturday) starting at 1100. The following have qualified: Graham Mead (Hornet), Christopher Weedon (420), Geof Josey (Solo), Caron Stuart (Mirror), Phil Kenworthy (Handicap) and Peter Moselley (Enterprise). The final will be run as a series of handicap races with each helm changing boats, (and crew, where applicable), after each race, until they have sailed in every classe. The winner being the helm with the best overall result. Why not come along and support your fleet's representative. John Weedon Rear Commodore S42 22.2.6 9 £8 F @£& 6 @ Ce. 6B 2 A Bo A ew VISITORS The Lockable Gate to the sailing site at Stansgate was provided in an attempt to prevent unwanted visitors from making use of our facilities, or entering for other nefarious reasons. However, as a public footpath runs through the middle of the site down the road and thence along the sea wall in either direction, anyone on foot has a legal right to enter the site. On a few occasions during the season there are sailing events open to members of other sailing clubs, and on these days it is necessary either for the gate to be left open, or to be opened each time a visitor arrives or leaves by road. On Sunday 2 September, when the Club was organising an open Cruiser race, as well as an open dinghy event, I was dismayed to learn that a Club Member had ‘refused’ entry to a car driven by the wife of a Maldon Sailing Club member competing in the Cruiser race. I am sure that any of our own Club Members would be made welcome at other sailing clubs whether arriving by road or water at all times. John Weedon Rear Commodore SS BBR Se Re SC OD CS wh Be ABS SB Ces COMMODORES NOTES Having just returned from holiday and getting ready to sail again, it always comes as a blow to me to realise that the season is drawing to a close. We have to turn our minds to such items as Laying Up Supper, Working Parties, A GM, next years Committee and Officers, Mamgu Trophy, Christmas Dance etc. While you are making the most of what remains of this year, please spare a thought for the items I have mentioned. All are vital to the spirit and efficient working of the Club. Ron Greygoose Commodore

a DINGHY CHALLENGE CUP This year's Dinghy Challenge Cup was held on Saturday2 September in ideal sailing conditions, ise. warm and sunny with a good westerley breeze blowing straight down the river. The start was a "long line" using the majority of the width of the river and with a long beat against the ebbing tide the fleet immediately split into two, the majority choosing the Osea shore. Those selecting the South shore, however, as soon as they were past the narrows and into the slack tide in the bay soon reached the windward mark. The first to round with a substantial lead was the 18ft Skiff sailed by Bruce Long and Co., followed by Graham Mead and Dunny Lumley in a Hornet, then came Mike Williams and Liz Stannard in another Hornet, followed by a bunch of boats including P Newman sailing a Laser, Phil Kenworthy and Jeoff West in a GP14 and several 420's led by John Chisnall and Murray Bates with Pat Black and Tony Cockrell close behind. The leading Solo at this point was sailed by Roy Battye, then came the first boat to approach the windward mark from the Osea shore, this was the Laser of Ray Apthorne followed by 4 420's with Chris Weedon and Deborah Harper just ahead of the other 3. There were few changes in position during the following broad reach back to the channel mark No 1, but the next leg which was a close haul up Goldhanger Creek saw the 18ft Skiff's hopes dashed when its mast collapsed. A fast square reach out of the creek to Breezy Point on the Southern side of the river brought the boats back to another windward leg with a beat against the tide to finish the first leg. Two further legs followed with boats which had good speed to windward gaining on the long beats, and the planing classes making gains on the reaches. The first boat to cross the finishing line, after nearly 2 hours sailing, was the Hornet sailed by Graham Mead and Danny Lumley. 8 minutes later the other Hornet with Mike Williams and Liz Stannard finished, closely followed by P Newman in a Laser, which was just sufficient to win on handicap. Several minutes elapsed before the first of a string of 420's completed the course, the first of these being sailed by John Chisnall and Murray Bates, then Pat Black and Tony Cockrell ensuring 3rd and 4th places respectively, on handicap. It was significant that the first Solo home, sailed by John Rutherford only finished 12th overall, although this class is normally very competitive, the conditions were obviously unfavourable. There were 22 boats given finishing places and another 7 who either did not complete the course correctly or retired early. =o 4 = HORNET SUMMER The calendar says the holiday season is over and certainly the Hornet Championships have been won or lost for another year. I was lucky enough to be involved with the 3 Championships this year and have written down some impressions about them. Marconi Club kindly held the Junior Championships in July, drawing 14 entries, and was well appreciated by everyone concerned. The wind could have been kinder to first time Hornet sailors, but provided exciting sailing for competitors and spectators. The winner was Jeremy Newman, who later won the World Championships (some consolation to those who were beaten). Best placed of the 5 Marconi boats was Robert Tate with 8th overall. Chris Weedon was 9th, Colin Harper 10th, Simon Perkins 12th and Paul Shuster 14th. Many thanks go to the Club Officials for their hard work in organising the event, and special thanks to Ann Bates and her helpers Angie and Vanda for their steadfast work in the galley after Rosemary was unable to attend. The World Championships were held at Enkhuizen on the Ijsselmeer in Holland = which is a very beautiful area and could be strongly recommended for holiday visits (cruisers?). The Dutch boats had to qualify to enter and only six British crews made the journey, plus one Australian pair, so there was a disappointing low number of 35 entries altogether. Their so¢ial programme was non existant unfortunately, partly due to financial difficulties, but the racing itself was organised well enough. The weather had to be seen to be believed, varying from force 7 winds which cancelled the practice race, to gusting force 6 for the first few races. This also meant sailing through an electric storm with fork lightning hitting the water all around us. At the other extreme, the last race was sailed in brilliant sunshine, but a dead calm. My new boat had its trials there and managed a best position of 10th although we were 20th overall. It's boat speed showed great potential however, when the two on board were a sensitive team, so we came home optimistic at least. The European Championships were held at sunny Brightlingsea (there are no National Champs when Worlds or Europeans are held in England), and were billed as the event of the decade. They attracted 74 entries and did indeed have excellent organisation, particularly their social activities. Their welcoming review was a "not to be missed", and its celebreties, Steve Heppel - ex Marconi for example. They also organised two fringe coach trips for camp followers to Colchester Zoo and Constable Countryside, which was much appreciated by those families whose role is usually just to hang around waiting for races to end. Racing was very close and the ist place was still undecided by the start of the last race, when either Malcolm Goodwin or Duncan Nicholson could have won overall. In the end Malcolms experience prevailed and he won the last race, and the series. The weather progressed from no wind to speak of in the practice race (when we managed to finish 13th, still full of optimism) to gusting force 8 and rainstorms on the last day. There were four Marconi boats, and you'll forgive me if I'm not more expansive about what happened to my earlier optimism, if I just say Graham Mead and Danny finished 20th, Graham Richardson and Ken early 30s, Murray Todd and Tony 41st, Mike Williams and 1 finished 40th. With September, Marconi Hornets still have 3 local open meetings: Stone Hornet, Hallam Trophy and final fling at Thope Bay, as well as our own points series and Hornet Buoy to enjoy so we will look forward to as many boats as possible out on the water enjoying this competitive fleet we are lucky to have at Marconi now. Mike Turner

nN ae MIRROR FLEET NEWS At the time of writing 12 of the summer points races have been sailed and from a total of 51 Mirrors in the club the average turnout is less than 4 per race$ Earlier in the season I considered holding a meeting to discuss apathy in our class, but it was not really worthwhile in view of the lack of interesti!i I have deserted the sinking ship and many of you already know that I have sold M59995 and I am not getting another. One major problem this year has been finding people from the Mirror Fleet prepared to do race-box duties etc (with some exceptions). The duty list was prepared and on the notice board in early April and if you are unable to manage the date given then some attempt should be made as early as possible to swap with someone else or arrange a substitute. I have become very familiar with the interior of the race box this year, frequently covering for people who have made no attempt to make alternative arrangements. Of the summer points races so far sailed Vic Braybrook has won 5, Mike Taylor 2 wins in 2 races sailed, Deb Harper 1 win and Chris Cooper 1 win. Graham Williamson has quite a collection of 2nd places. Caron Stuart has missed only 2 races and a result of persistence is that she represents the Mirror fleet in the Helmsman of the Year Final. Well done Caron. I have received from the Mirror Class Association a request for relevant details for next seasons year book, and the club fleet should now decide who is to take over as Fleet Captain. Any volunteers for the job please contact me. Finally I still have a slin gaff complete with stainless steel short-—neck gaff band, and a boom complete with tack downhaul and clew outhaul track and can be persuaded to part with them in exchange for £10.00. CRUISER FLEET NEWS Once again laying up time approaches and we should all look out our trolleys to check they are ready. And if any are still to be constructed or modified remember the key to success is strength, large wheels and positive location for the boat. Keel boats must be adequately supported by the trailer, NOT by chocks which can move either in towing or when the boat rocks in the wind. Our meeting at the Generals Arms resume in October, remember it is now the first Wednesday of each month. At our first meeting we hope to show all the holiday slides, so please bring some along together with the funny accompanying stories. See you there.
