= Os A “FLOTILLA" SAILING HOLIDAY IN GREECE I had been to Greece on holiday on five previous occassions but I had never been sailing there, although I cast envious eyes at the "lucky ones" many times, so this year I chanced my arm and enrolled on a "Pot Luck" boat with the Flotilla Sailing Club, sailing from Levkas in the Ionian Sea. Pot Luck meant that the four people on the boat met for the first time when they arrived, four strangers, sailing a Westerly Pembroke. Personality problems were evident from the start, but it soon got sorted out. Ome crew member John, said he had once sailed a 420, but I did€n't believe him, one young lady sailed a Laser and was very good, the second young lady was from Sweden and sailed a Folkboat and I was the only member of the crew who had ever had experience in anchoring and kedging, and I didn't intend to spend my entire holiday anchoring and kedging for them, so there was a short lecture on “how to do it". The journey outward started badly from Gatwick when Laker cancelled our flight at 7 am and we all found ourselves on separate flights to Corfu, where we had to wait until about 6 pm when the rest of the party arrived in dribs and drabs. I should perhaps explain that the island of Levkas is difficult to reach, and from Corfu we had to get the ferry boat across to the mainland at Igoumaniza and then take a coach down the coast to Prevessa and finally another ferry boat across to Levkas, where we finally arrived at about 1.30 am, crawled aboard our boats and slept till morning. The Westerly Pembroke had six berths, two in the forepeak, two on the dinette, and two quarter berths aft, and I was frankly disappointed at the layout. I do not consider myself to be a tall person, but I could not stretch full length in my quarter berth, neither could the girls in the forepeak. The girls chose the latter for reasons of privacy, although to be honest after about three or four days cooped up together, modesty got you nowhere! The other boats in the flotilla were Jaguar 27's and although the Westerlys outsailed them, there was vastly more space and comfort on the Jaguars. We all set off next day about lunch time and motored through the Levkas canal, into the open seas between the various islands of the group, and sailed down the coast of Levkas island until we reached the small port of Nidri where we anchored for the night, and after a swim we adjourned to the local taverna for drinks, eats and some dancing to BOuzouki music. The weather was in the 90° + bracket and stayed there the whole fortnight, and we had problems of salt loss due to perspiration. Anyone who goes to Greece expecting calm seas and steady breezes is in for a shock, the pattern of the weather was most consistant during our trip and most mornings it was dead calm, and we had to start the engine and motor along, but in the afternoons it regularly blew a yachtsmans gale with wave heights about four to five feet with crests breaking. There was also alother phenomena which has to be experienced to be believed, and that is known as "Down Draughts", where the heat from the land causes the air to funnel down between the hills, and results in gale conditions in an area of about half a square mile, or less, whilst elsewhere it is dead calm, We experienced these conditions ourselves on the second day of our cruise when entering Sivota bay to anchor for the night. The entrance to the bay is hard to find, and access is through a "dog leg" channel which then opens out into a snug anchorage about 800 yds by 1400 yqs. We all followed each other into the narrow "dogs leg" in comparitively calm conditions, but as we turned into the bay, a "down draught" hit us and we scattered like confetti. One chap ran aground, one tacked in front of us, we were knocked down and by the time we had recovered, John had accidently dropped our anchor overboard, and we swung round like an express train. The sails have never been lowered more quickly — before or since. We motored the rest of the way, no one spoke to each other for a few minutes. Once inside the bay all was calm again. THAT was a DOWN DRAUGHT.

- 10 = Next morning we left Sivota to sail to Atoko, an uninhabited island, where we anchored for lunch and a swim. Here again we had problems with down draughts, the only bay offering shelter was a small ex-volcanic crater, which meant about 17 fathoms in the middle and steep shelving beaches. Anchoring was such a problem that we rafted up alongside Harry whilst we sorted it all out. Unfortunately Harry didn't want us, so he cast us off without a word, and the next moment we were fending off everyone else with as much speed and courage as we could muster. That night we had a Barbecue on the beach organised by the Flotilla leader. For about £2.00 per head we had Steaks, Chops, Chicken Jacket Potatoes, Garlic Bread, Salad, Fruit and several buckets of local Plonk. This local fruit drink was highly intoxicant and we paid about £1.00 for five litres, some people were less interested in the food, expecially as the local cognac was also flowing freely. Next morning fat heads were prevalent. At the beginning of the first week everyone sailed in the Flotilla together in company, but as we became familiar with the boats we were allowed to go off "Free Sailing" with the understanding that we would all meet again at an agreed place in four days time. This arrangment worked well because it meant that we were not constantly crowded on to each other and there was more room to manoeuvere. We were sailing in the Ionian sea and the islands in the group consisted of Levkas, Cephalonia, Megannisi, Ithaca, Zante etc, and we decided to make for Ithaca to seek out a bit of culture, after all this was where Homer and Ullysses roamed. On the way we passed the island of Skorpio owned by the late Onassis, no one is allowed to land there without prior arrangement, and speed boats buzz around all day, and a helicopter service ferries the VIP guests to and from the mainland at frequent intervals. We arrived at the island of Ithacain the middle of a rather hard blow and had to take down our sailsin the entrance to the Harbour Port Vathi and motor in for fear of more misadventures with down draughtse We anchored in a shallow corner of the bay and went ashore for a Taverna supper. I came back on board early with a touch of the dreaded screamers, dosed myself up with medicine and turned in. I awoke about 2 am to discover we were dragging our anchor and although conditions were calm, we were nudging the chap next to us (a doctor) and the rest of the crew were still whooping it up ashore. I climbed into the dinghy and laid a kedge off our bow, got back on board and by pulling on one and paying out on the other I managed to separate us enough for comfort. After breakfast next morning, we all went ashore and hired Vespa@s and climbed the local mountain roads and took loads of photographs. The scooters were so cheap - they cost just under £2.00 per hour including the petrol - that we decided to stay an extra day and sample the local archeological delights. We visited Arethusas Spring, where Homer drank his fill and I bought a pair of leather sandals. We decided to sail in company with another boat to the small port of Kioni. It was undoubtedly the prettiest place we visited. It looked as though it had fallen eff a picture postcard. There was one Taverna on the quayside and we flopped down for drinks. I don't think I have ever drunk so much liquid in such a short space of time as I did on this holiday. It was a constant battle against de-hydration and although we nearly all imbibed the alchohol, we also sank gallons of Orange, Lemon and bottled water.

os {t~ When the owner of the Taverna saw us arrive he nipped smartly out the back and re-appeared with a large lamb which he cleaned, greased, salted and spiced, and proceeded to spit roast it for our supper. The moment of truth came when he announced he was ready to carve it. I expected us to hold our plates up for large slices, but to everyones amusement he took the lamb off the spit, placed it on a large wooden table and chopped it up with an axe! Anyway it tasted delicious. Off again next morning to a place called Fiskardo on the island of Cephalonia. This meant a steady beat to windward up the narrow Ithaca channel average width 2 miles in a strong N W breeze. Very good sailing and we made the most of it. I should explain that all the boats of the Flotilla are equipped with two-way radio and once you are off on your own, free sailing, you are required at regular intervals to report yourself to base. This arrangement worked well, and also enabled us to ask about weather conditions and anchoring problems. We learned in this instance that they were short of fresh water at Fiskardo so we put into Port Polis, a small pleasant bay and drewwater from a local well, filled the boats tanks and spare containers before arriving in Fiskardo for the night. We set off next day to sail across to the island of Megannisi and we reached Port Spiglia by late afternoon. It was the roughest conditions we had experienced since sailing in the Ionian Sea, and we had all the usual arguments about reducing sail, because you will appreciate that one of the problems on a "Pot Luck" boat is that we had four skippers. Anyway the Swedish girl at the helm suddenly gybed the boat "all standing" and the main sheet caught me across the face and I received a rope burn across the forehead and on the bridge of the nose. I was not pleased. We were obliged to "sail" the boat round instead of gybing as we had a large beam sea bearing down on use Several hours later we reached Port Spiglia and tied up for the night "bows on" to the jetty. It was so hot we all jumped overboard for a swim. Most of the females in these places swum topless and in one or two of the more remote places it was starkers! The French and Italians being Very keen on the latter. Port Spiglia has a vast cliff across and down one side of the harbour and it is necessary to climb about 800 feet up a goat track to reach the village at the top, but it is a very clean pretty place and I discovered it was famous for its olive oil. I found a shop that sold empty tins with a good screw top and I went along to the olive oil press and bought about a kilo and a half for 75p to take home. It was "green" olive oil, first quality. We also found a very good Taverna run by a chap called "Billy the Greek". He cooked chicken so delicious that he stopped cooking any other type of meat and became "Billy the Chicken". He certainly lived up to his reputation, we had supper with all the trimmings and I got up early next morning and climbed back up the goat track and asked Billy for breakfast. To my surprise he produced the most massive breakfast I had seen in Greece} It consisted of pure orange juice, yoghurt with honey, buttered toast, bacon and two eggs, marmalade and coffee. That cost me 55 drachma (about 75p). We all met together next day in the bay after our days of free sailing and arranged a race. It was to be a long haul around three islands, Tiglia, Moodra, Sparti and back to the finishing line. The rules of racing were to be observed in principle, but if rules got in the way they were to be discarded in favour of skulduggery, e g if a boat came too close, chuck plenty of buckets of water over him just to discourage him, and if he came too close over the start line, fend his bows off with your feet so that he had to go about. The race started and we chose the wrong end of the start line, lost our wind and were last across. Instead of heading straight towards Tiglia we headed out into the bay where we found wind and to everyones disgust we were soon in the middle of the field.

Se 126 Twelve boats started and by the time we were halfway round we were sixth. Harry should have been disqualified because he forgot to go round Tiglia and headed off full pelt for Moodra, but cheats never prosper and he lost his wind and finished tenth. The home leg was a full run in a light breeze and we rigged Main and Genoa in the conventional way, with the working jib poled out goosewinged, the sail from our dinghy (about 30 sq feet) rigged as a mizzen, and the awning wrapped around the pushpit just to show off. About one mile from home, the wind died completely and we were lying fifth. We immediately started to kedge with a bucket over the bows. John was absolutely built for this job - six foot two, 15 stone, and we estimated that he could chuck the bucket at least the length of the boat each throw, but we lived in fear that he would let go the rope altogether and we would have to stop and recover it. When it became obvious we were not going to improve our position by this means alone we "persuaded" the two girls to put on their flippers and laying with their heads to our sternthey flipped the boat along at a steady half knot. By this time boats 1, 2 and 3 had crossed the finishing ling and No 4 was lying motionless about 50 yds from the line. As the gap between us shortened we observed feverish activity on board, including desperate attempts to paddle and row, but when we were only 10 yds from them they started their engine, shot across the line and claimed 4th place as they had urgent need to charge their batteries, which the race officer accepted as a valid explanation. So we finished 5th, boarded them and threw their skipper overboard. I don't think he cared very much. We all finished in the water anyway. We spent our last day anchored in a sandy bay having a regatta, with dinghy races and lots of fun, before making our final sail up the bay of Levkas into the canal and back to where we started. The channel in the Levkas canal is well marked, but John nearly put us on the putty, and we touched once, got away with it and sent him below to make some teal The coach arrived next morning to take us back to Igoumaniza, but when we arrived at Corfu once again we were out of luck with Laker and we were told that the flight had a six hour delay. Instead of arriving home at 6 pm we arrived at half past midnight, and I had to go to work next day$ Looking back on the holiday I would gladly do it all again, but I would endeavour to get a crew of friends instead of a "Pot Luck" boat as I felt that there were moments of embarrasment due chiefly to peoples lack of experience and being unwilling to admit it. The first time John climbed into the dinghy he swung his legs over the pushpit and down the ladder “facing the dinghy with his back to the transom". The dinghy shot away from him with his feet planted firmly in it, but he still had his arms around the pushpit. We explained the need to descend backwards into the dinghy, and to give him full marks he learned very quickly. The Swedish girl was asked to tie a fender on to the end of a long line and trail it over the stern whilst people were swimming so that they had a safety line for emergencies. Unfortunately she couldn't tie a knot between two ropes of unequal thickness and the fender floated away and had to be recovered later. My own personal failure was the sudden realisation during an immense water fight that my wristwatch was NOT waterproof. Anyway I've been meaning to treat myself to a new one for some time now. Les Mendoza (See Map (or Chart) on back page! - (Editor).

on AS THE WANDERINGS OF KALINKA Our family's first summer cruise was in 1976, that glorious summer when the sun kept on shining andKalinka was new. Since then summer cruises have been successively more enjoyable due to our increased experience, even though the weather has never been so continuously hot. Plans are never too firmly fixed since so many variables can arise and we regard the cruise as a relaxing pleasure trip rather than a death defying venture. The talk one often hears of "We were out in this Force 8" etc doesn't impress us at all — but everyone to his own choice. This year after much cooking, preparation of clothes and general packing, we transferred the family of 5 plus 1 dog to Kalinka on the evening of Friday 27 July about 8 pm. Forecast indicated 30 C for Saturday with light breezes and high tide at Stansgate was about 0400. All went to bed in good time - the boys excited at the thought of all those different places to re-explore. Saturday 28 July Dropped mooring at 0400, tide just turning. Quiet, still morning, slightly misty and not quite light. Saw a little phosphorescence in the water, but very soon too much daylight for it to show. Stone looked like a small town, but this turned out to be the anchor lights of all the Gaffers, due to race later that day. Bradwell Power Station abeam 0445 indicated speed of 6 knots. Visibility still poor though sky brightening - steer E for 2 M (20 minutes) before changing course for Bench Head etc. Passed the Bas Buoy at 0545 - sun red, slight mist - cannot see land, steer E again to pass N Eagle. Plenty of water over the bar — quite calm — we keep the echo sounder running continuously, it is a useful guide to location. At 0605 we put up the sails on starboard tack but continued motoring a little longer. Visibility to shore now about 600 yds enabling a mental note of progress to be made. The written log has a gap here, but I remember having two breakfasts during the trip - eaten in the cockpit. All this time Tim and Ben age 9 and 6 are asleep in the forecabin. John 14 reading and dozing on the starboard bunk, June and I enjoying a quiet sail. Hugged the shore along the coast, with about 8ft of water throughout, passed just a few yards off Walton pier. The intention is to go into Walton Backwaters, visibility about 600 yds and as water is still very smooth we held our course moderately near the shoré, which would have been impossible with anything of a swell in the water. Approaching Pye Sands we saw a local fishing boat pass through a gap in the Pye Sand close to the first red can Buoy, and could see the channel from the surface appearance of the water, so greeting the crew of anglers as they passed we also "crossed the bar" and into the channel without ever seeing Pye End Buoy. All the remaining bouys into the Walton channel were picked up easily and followed faithfully. Arrived at Stone Point 1000. Distance covered 27m in 6 hours, half sailing, half motoring. The boys were pleased to play on the sand at Stone Point all day while June and I took it easy after the early starte After tea we motored around to our favourite anchorage just south of Shippers Island - where we just stay afloat and are sheltered from all directions. Sunday 29 July Cool windy day. June and I took the dog ashore for a few minutes while the boys played in the boat, drawing etc - they have an assortment of games, felt tips, books which stay on Kalinka permanently. After lunch we all walked to Kirby Staithe and back. A repeat of a shopping expedition made last year. The four

Pan oe miles or so doesn't seem so far this year. Monday Much better day - bright sunny intervals, wind SW 3-4. Motored round to Stone Point and all went ashore. At the turn of the tide put up sails and had a good sail into Harwich Harbour. Very quiet, wind blowing strongly down the Stour, so continued for a mile up the Orwell, then anchored for lunch under the lea of the west beach. Forecast strong S-SW winds, in fact various forecasts indicated anything up to force 8. Motored up the Stour to get shelter from Wrabness cliffs. Water choppy and spray flying but not unpleasant as quite warm. Kalinka does between 5 and 6 hours per gallon of fishing diesel so we don't mind using the motor. At Wrabness we enquired of a local yachtsman who recommended anchoring at a suitable spot almost on the beach. This proved excellent, merely requiring forethought with one or two buckets before the tide dropped too low. The boys were very pleased to find a friend who they had met last year, on holiday in one of the chalets. We found the people very friendly at Wrabness, and the beach is nice, with clear water, very good for swimming. Tuesday Shopping expedition to Wrabness village - swimming in afternoon. Windy but warm. Wednesday Took family to Dovercourt by train. Children enjoyed the train ride, but Dovercourt was a wash out in the rain — perhaps we were short of local information. Return to Kalinka for lunch. In the afternoon boys played games, watched telly, read etc = still windy and raining, but we were protected by cliffs. Thursday Rain stopped, wind about force 4 W. Sailed to Shotley, landed again in lower Orwell and had a circular walk going behind the Naval training establishment and back along the sea wall. A pity the Navy have left HMS Ganges — the little town seems dead without them. Lunch aboard, then motored up to Wolverstone marina. We generally prefer to swing to an anchor, but the hot showers and easy landing are sometimes welcome. Walked to Pin Mill along very pleasant footpath, then back for teae John was very disappointed that telly signal was extremely poor, due, no doubt to ail the surrounding rigging and masts. Friday Raining so slept late. No wind - rain cleared so left marina about 1030. Down the Orwell on dropping tide - put up sails but needed motor periodically. Through Harwich harbour - up the coast for the river Deben. Had lunch on the way — soup from mugs. Low tide at 1330 - fiddled around while listening to shipping forecast, then decided to attempt entrance at 1400. There was no swell and although low water it was neap tides. One of the leading marks was obscured by dinghies on the beach, but in such calm conditions we just steered for the obviously deeper channel near the beach and were in with no problem. Kalinka only draws 24 ft and sits level so we can afford to be a little venturesome. Sailed up to the Rocks —- breezes light, mainly westerly. Removed plough anchor and put on fisherman prior to anchoring, as the bottom is very firm here, conditions which I find don't suit the CQR.

=- 15 = Saturday Motored to Woodbridge and after exploring the available space and depths, dropped anchor near the ferry hard. Stayed afloat and good holding with the fisherman with trip line fitted, although not used. Shopping in the morning we encountered a few of the greenfly which had been on the news = our only encounter with them. In the afternoon we all walked to Sutton Hoo and then in the evening June and I had a quiet walk around Woodbridge. There is a lovely atmosphere here when you have time to enjoy it. Sunday Dropped down to the Rocks again, passing through Waldringfirld, where we sheltered from strong westerlies last year. While the boys played on the beach, June and I walked to Ramsholt, going by road and back along the sea wall. They say the Rocks is inaccesible by car, but Ramsholt itself must be pretty exclusive, only one road and that gated. Very pretty and we got back within a few minutes of our predicted time. Hungry boys are very critical of that sort of thing. In the afternoon it was very warm at the Rocks. The sun was hot and the cliffs are good shelter from the northerly force 3. The cliffs here are full of fossilised shells, some of which are left handed whelks showing their age. Other shells are similar to modern ones but all are very heavy. Mid afternoon we set off down river to return to Walton Backwaters. Passed over the Deben bar at dead low water in calm conditions — minimum recorded depth was 34 ft, at a time when the Stansgate maximum was 4.8m. The important point really though was again the lack of swell which enabled us to clear so easily. Outside Woodbridge Haven found northerly force 3, rising tide, so up sails, off motor and sailed to Stone Point in time for 6 oclock tea. Monday Had a shopping trip into Walton, using Even and outboard, while boys played at Stone Point. Tuesday Up Walton Channel and anchored off entrance to the Twizzle.e Went for a walk and picnic on the Naze. On returning found Kalinka had dragged her anchor (CQR) due to a combination of factors, of which I believe the most important was the fact that I had dropped the anchor in the spit which came out at the meeting of the two channels. This would presumably be soft silt and give poor holding. The wind and tide had together moved the anchor although it had been motored in initially. We were very lucky - the boat was not quite aground and the anchor was not fouled with anything worse than polythene and tin cans! Wednesday Left Backwaters in the afternoon in order to re visit Wrabnesse- Again the cliffs gave protection from southerly winds. Picked up mooring adjacent to other visitors who later, over a drink, told us they were on their honeymoon. Thursday Rain and strong southerly winds. June and I put on Oilies and went shopping. 1350 forecast indicated NW gales - not suitable for a Wrabness mooring so moved out quickly after telling honeymoon couple of our plans - don't think they were very interested however. Tide good to Shotley, wind already strongNW, then turned into the Orwell for Wolverstone. Although motoring this was a very slow passage,

= 46 = against a wind of about force 5 and a foul spring tide. Engine developed a ticking sound which I diagnosed as a disintegrating dynamo drive belt. We just hoped it would last to Wolverstone, but 5 minutes later we had dropped anchor just out of the channel and were untangling the shreds of rubber and string. However, we soon reached Wolverstone and were lucky enough to be able to get a berth inshore. We tried to get a new drive belt, but chandlery was shut. (In fact we finished our holiday without replacing it - with gas lights and a diesel engine, electricity is almost superfluous). Although Wolverstone is exposed to the north, my reasoning was that the floating pontoons and boats would absorb the energy of the waves. For us they did except just a little at high tide, but we had some friends at the exposed end of the pontoon and they had a very rough night. Friday After a very wild night the weather was now calm with a forecast of NW 4 becoming SW 4. Decided to leave for Pyefleet at once. Made Harwich harbour by 0815 as tide began to flood on springs. Had full sails up but found it desirable to motor also as far as Naze tower as tide was setting strongly towards the Backwaters, and the breeze was still very light. Motor off at Naze tower and a good sail to Clacton pier, breeze now SW 4 and crew asking for dinner, and cook refusing to cook while beating, so motored to E Mersea point = arrived 1330. Later anchored in Pyefleet. Saturday Our final morning, sadly back to Stansgate. Beautiful day. Being low springs checked position of Molliette target wreck. It is 100 yds North of the red can Buoy. The little Buoy labelled Molliette is of no location significance as far as I could tell - merely identification. Arrived at Stansgate 1320. Total holiday Miles 163 Engine hours 30 Fuel 5 gallons Cost 2 nights in marina = £4.76 + Food While this trip will seem tame to our blue water members I hope the account of it will encourage others to venture further afield, showing as it does how one can shelter comfortably from the weather when necessary, and make good passages when conditions permit. Russ Fuller

SBx COMMODORES NOTES PETTY THIEVING I regret to have to say it, but we still have a thief amongst us. There have been several more instances of money being taken from the Mens Changing Room. Please keep alert to the situation and make sure that you do not leave any money or valuables in the changing room. ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING Wednesday 29 November Elsewhere in this issue of Navigans you will find the Notice of Meeting calling for nominations for the Club Committee Posts. As is customary it indicates those members of the present committee who are prepared to offer themselves for election. Whilst the situation varies from hour to hour, at the time of writing we are lacking candidates for the important positions of Honorary and Social Secretary. So please search your hearts and consciences and come forward with nominations and suggestions, always remembering that the committee is a "Working Committee" and that everyone elected will be required to undertake some post or task in the club. You will be pleased to hear that the returning committee has decided that it will NOT be necessary to propose any increase in subscriptions for next year. M AS C ELECTIONS Elections take place during the week commencing 5 November for 6 positions on the MASC Main Committe. As specified in the Notice of Election displayed around the Company, nominations were required to be handed in by 0900 on 15 October. Unfortunately this information has become available just too late to enable us to mobilise an effective search for candidates from the Sailing Section. Nevertheless I ask you please to exercise your rights by voting when the time comes. LAYING UP SUPPER I hope to see all the old faces plus some new ones this year. What about it? Ron Greygoose Commodore ed FAIRIES AT STANSGATE About the middle of September I was working on the forestay of "La Mouette" at her mooring and I dropped my pliers overboard into 5 feet of water. The loss was reported to Claude Emerson and he searched at the next low water, without success. Ten days later on our second successive visit we found our pliers lying in the cockpit. Will the good fairy who found them please make him or herself known so that we can celebrate together at a mutually convenient time. J O Dugdale Bradley [redacted]

a S = BY 420 TO BRIGHTLINGSEA Saturday 29 September High Water: 1824 Wind: NE F4-5 Clear and sunny 1230 Marconi Sailing Club 20779 “Blue Max" (Alan Mack Crew Phil Gray) 18973 "Over'n'Out" (Pete Chrystie Crew Anna Keeling) 17711 “Red Alert" (Russell Jeffries Crew Steve Hopcroft) We left the familiar waters of Stansgate to beat downriver against both tide and a brisk north easterly. Our intention was to reach Brightlingsea - a distance of some 12 miles = hy high water that evening. Assuming we reached our destination as planned, we would camp at the municipal site close to Brightlingsea Sailing Club and return with the tide the following morning. We thought ourselves rather unlucky to have a north easterly to sail against considering how often the club races have started west this season; however, the weather conditions certainly made for exciting sailing with crews constantly out on the wire. Passing Stone, Red Alert's crew was having problems with a slipping jib cleat and the boat was not going at all well to windward. Meanwhile Blue Max was almost over when a sudden lull in the gusty wind caught the helm by surprise, the crew, who had been on the trapeze was dropped into the water and the boat heeled violently to windward, but after some frantic scrambling the dreaded wind- ward capsize was averted. Over'n'Out had none of these interesting problems and waited on a convenient sand- bank for the others to catch up. We stopped for lunch on same mud flats opposite Bradwell, not the most desirable spot for a picnic, and discussed our position. We had covered about a third of the distance to Brightlingsea and it was now 1430. The wind was still from the north east and the open water east of Bradwell was flecked with white horses. The decision was made to continue. The intrepid fleet tacked out to sea, where the waves became bigger and the wind stronger. The sea was moderate, as they say on the shipping forecast, but there was nothing moderate about the way the waves slammed into the hull showering crew and helm with spray. Sometimes the waves phased together to produce larger ones, and riding these was quite an exhilarating experience. The boat would fly out from the crests of these waves to drop with an almighty crash into the trough beneath. We kept as close together as we could in these conditions to encourage each other. We passed a number of cruisers on this stretch and we met with looks of disbelief as we over= hauled theme They must have thought we were mad or suicidal, or both. Gradually we tacked up past Mersea Island and around 1800 we reached the mouth of the Colne and the sheltered waters of Brightlingsea Reach. Over'n'Out reached Brightlingsea Sailing Club first and obtained permission to haul our boats up to the dinghy park. Sunday 30 September High Water: 1941 Wind: SE F4 Misty, some sun After breakfast we broke camp and packed the van for Beth to take back round to Stansgate. We manhandled the three boats down across the long 200 yard mud beach to the water. The tide was well out and we realised how lucky we are at Stansgate to have such a relatively short haul down to the water at any state of the tide. We set off at 1100, Red Alert leading the way, setting course close towards Mersea Island, too close as the helm realised soon enough. After a close encounter of the muddy kind, Red Alert set out to sea, chasing the other two boats who had been watching with interest, from a distance; Once we had cleared the acres of mud flats exposed at low water off Mersea Island we turned towards the west. As yet no land- marks were seen since there was a slight sea haze. The sea was less rough than before and we were now running with the elements. The waves, however, were still big enough to provide opportunities for surfing and when the boat was brought on to a reach exhilarating planes were achieved. Red Alert and Over'n'Out hoisted their spinnakers to make up on Blue Max, which had sped on ahead. We made good time and soon Bradwell Power Station loomed out of the mistse We stopped for lunch by the power station on a shingle beach. From then on it was plain sailing with full canvas and we arrived at Stansgate in time to catch the bar before it closed at 1430. We all voted the trip a great success and perhaps next year we may venture out of home waters to places even more exotic. a cass CRUISER RACING They say that no two races are alike and this was certainly true of this year's Marconi Cruiser Cup race, compared with last year, when we had a near gale, about a dozen entries and plenty of casualties on the way round. In contrast this year we had 37 entries from clubs all round the Blackwater, and near perfect sailing, good enough to enliven even the Bench Head, Innes Bench, Bench Head routine. The committee boat start was excellently managed by Mike Vaughan, well supported by Jack Walker on "Goelette", armed with a brace of cannon. I'm afraid we didn't get many Marconi entries, except the usual stalwart support of "Rasputin" and 'Deben Copernicus", well helmed by Robert. For two euphoric days I thought the combination of a rotten handicap and lucky sailing had put "Roanoke" first. However, unwisely, (or wisely) I'd asked George Foster, Chairman of BJRC Cruiser Group to check the results and he discovered a handicap correction for "Temptation" (DSC) which then beat me by 15 seconds - in 5+ hours! However, our cruiser people are "Cruisers", not dedicated racing enthusiasts and we have usually been hard pressed to muster enough boats to just make the minimum three boats for a race in the series. In the circumstances, unless there is pressure to do otherwise, next year I propose to arrange four races, the best of three to count, giving one discard. i SE | COMMODORE'S NOTES The Laying Up Supper went with a swing, our guests were most appreciative, and those of you who were unable to come missed a real treat. The next important item on the Club Calendar is the AGM. This is your chance to show your Officers and Committee how you value their efforts over the past year. Please come along in good numbers and make it more of a social occasion. Once the formalities are over you can have a drink, and talk of sailing past and future, among yourselves and with your new committee. Elsewhere in this issue of Navigans is an account of an address given by Tony Mayhew at a recent Section Chairmans Seminar. It provides a potted history of the development of the M OSC and will, I hope make us more understanding and appreciative of the work and aims of our parent Club. Ron Greygoose Commodore ert ft &¢ * © © &* & * * © & & 8 & + FF * SAFETY The last day of the Dinghy season provided those that sailed, some of the most exhilarating and perhaps most difficult sailing since the Regatta. It also provided me with yet another reminder of the vigilance necessary if we are to avoid serious accidents. In this case my son Mark was knocked out of his boat after being hit on the head by the boom. The strong wind against tide soon separated him from the boat, and the rescue launch, already engaged with another dinghy, was not directly to hand. He was recovered from the very choppy sea some 15 minutes later, approximately 300 300 yards from his dinghy. The safety problem was simply due to his wearing a dark blue overall. In the difficult sea it was almost impossible to keep sight of him, even with binoculars. Orange colouring, at least for arms and shoulders would have greatly improved the situation. Another lesson learned’ Frank Savill ft + © © © © © &¢ & + #& +e * 8 ee Fe ee * CRUISER FLEET NEWS Our next meeting at the Generals Arms will be on Wednesday December 5. OLD FITZ Edward Fitzgerald, or "Old Fitz", became famous for his particular translation of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayam. However, he was also a famous character in the 1860's living at 'Woodbridge, and sailing the East Coast rivers. His yacht called "Scandal" naturally had a tender, with the appropriate name of "Whisper", tender to Scandal", what else? About 40ft in length this schooner accommodated Old Fitz for many summers. "I have been fool enough to order a boat to be building which will cost me £350.00" She was sailing till 1930 on the Thames. Fitz collected nautical terms and put them together in a dictionary "Sea Words and Sea Phrases", with many fragments of colourful descriptions and conversation. His calendar may appeal to yachtsmen 100 years later. "January, just gone’ February, only 28 days: them March with light till six p m: then April with a blush of green on the whitethorn hedge: then May, Cuckoos, Nightingales etc: then June, ship launched and nothing but ship till November, which is only just gone”. A fascinating book for East Coast sailors, written by Frank Hussey entitled "Old Fitz" is in the Essex County Library. This is really an account of the Planning and Funding Sub-Committee and how it has worked over the last eighteen months. Why a Sub-Committee? This is necessary because of the lengthy studies involved, sometimes down to fine detail, and the fieldwork - sometimes literally that, sometimes wandering round a building - to try to resolve problems. So the Sub-Committee was set up to study suggestions and make recommendations to the General Committee, which then approves, amends or rejects them. Who are they? I'm their Chairman and the others were originally Gerry Gilbey and Marcus Wood. Since last November we've been augmented by Bernard Lingwood and Mick Downes, and of course we always welcome Robbie's assistance ex officio when he can manage it. During this time the Sub-Committee has met fourteen times and a working party to monitor and promote the lounge and games area project has met sixteen times. The Functions Planning: We interpret this as the consideration of change: any sort of change, such as a new activity, the change of use of a facility, altering a building or fixture, or the acquisition of a new building or fixture. Funding: means paying for the change. Note our three main ways of raising funds: (a) Direct raising, such as subscriptions and gambling. (b) Hiring to the Sections, to Members, to Outsiders. (c) Trading - this covers the bar, the kitchen, Christmas Hampers and Hairdressing. Last year these contributed respectively 52, 22 and 25% of our income approximately. Alternatively, of course, we may take funds from our reserves, or we may borrow. Whose Ideas? They come from everyone: the Sub-Committee, the other Committee Members, the Manager and his staff, individual club members, the Sections, our suppliers and our consultants. Policy (and Priorities) About each suggestion we ask ourselves a number of questions, such as: is there a need or demand for it (or could this be generated), is there room for it, does it conflict with anything we already do and, if so, can the conflict be resolved, is it good value for money,(Gerry's favourite) will it bring in extra income, also can we afford it, and not least, is is lawful? (This is not frivolous when one considers bye-laws, safety regulations and planning law). Cont* deescoecesees

ta Priorities, of course, vary from time to time, At the moment we have no major proposals from the Sections, so the following relates mainly to Club Headquarters here at Beehive Lane. Number one priority we see as the provision of extra car parking, number two the re-vitalisation of the lounges and games area and number three the others. You might think that was all, but we think of a number four as being the long term. In this category come the suggestions that have been made for a changing room block, expanding the capacity of the hall, expanding the foyer (to include, perhaps, a cloakroom and a club shop), extending the Clubhouse (for which Planning Approval was obtained in 1975). This would give us kitchen facilities which would enable us to cater for major functions like Dinner Dances and not make profits for contractors. Moreover, it would enable us to provide extra toilet facilities. This place is miserably under-equipped in this respect. Last in this category is the acquisition of a part, or even the whole, of the Hampton property. The Archive (from 1962). It is instructive to look at the history of the Club from 1962, which was a watershed for us. In that year we first played tennis and cricket on the "new site at Beehive Lane". 1963 saw Swiftplan buildings installed as temporary changing rooms and also the move of the Sailing Section to the Stansgate Site. July 1965 saw the great leap forward when the new Clubhouse opened. In 1967 came our first squash court and in 1969 numbers two and three. 1969 also saw the opening of the hall and lounge extensions. 1970 was the year of the Camera Hut. In 1975 came the new Clubhouse at Stansgate, in 1976 squash courts four and five, with number six the next year. 1977 also saw the extension of the Billiard Room, and 1978 saw the opening of the new Bowls Pavilion. It is interesting to note that of all this, only two items were for, or partly for, the ordinary social (non-Section) member = the building and extending of the Clubhouse. This Committee In March 1978, when we started, the Bowls Pavilion was under construction, The parking problem here was obvious to everyone, from the newest Club Member to the Chelmsford Borough Council Planning Committee: in fact the Planning Approval for the Clubhouse extension was conditional on our solving the parking problem. The lounges and games area were showing their ages and varied careers and were unattractive. The whole place was uncomfortable in hot weather. What progress has been made? Firstly, the Bowls Pavilion has been opened, to the credit of our predecessors, and has been an outstanding success. That Section is thriving as perhaps never before. A new room has been constructed at the Rifle Range and we have extended the hairdressing salon,

=a Ge We have acquired the lease on the Water Board land and we have fenced this and piped the ditch. We have coped with a burst pipe in the car park and leaking roofs. A significant measure of the year 1978/79 is that while increasing our fixed assets by no less than £59,000 (mainly the Bowls Pavilion) we yet managed to increase our liquid assets by £1,000 to £91,000. In the previous year fixed assets increased £42,000, liquidity diminished by £11,000. More recently, we have built new office accommodation so that our staff can have proper working conditions and we are now near the end of the major project to rejuvenate the lounges and games area. This involves alterations, decoration, carpets, furnishing and air-conditioning. There have been unfortunate delays due to problems with ceiling tiles and doubts about the roofs. The latter could be very serious but testing has been satisfactory and we hope soon to get back to normal, or rather better than normalsservice. The builders will then get to work on the new car parke The Future "What next?" depends on which way we want to go, or rather grow, because like most of our predecessors we think that if the Club were to stop growing it would start to wither. This is up to all of us: Committee, Manager, Staff, Members, Sections. For the Committee one can sum up as follows: "Our policy is to promote the comfort and convenience of our members in the many ways in which they spend their leisure time, and to provide the best possible facilities and service for them from the resources available." This is, indeed, the duty laid upon us by the rule book. Epilogue That potted history I gave earlier only listed the major items. Over the years there have been many minor improvements that have not made headlines, not least in the Sections' areas. It all goes to show that the Club is a living organic body. Helping it along is a demanding task, but it's very gratifying and rewarding when you see results from your work and find that the members approve it, as so far seems to be the case. AMafhon A. The A GM appointed a new Committee who have already met and agreed to the formation of a Moorings Sub-Committee to co-ordinate on behalf of the Cruiser Fleet the allocation of moorings, storage in the boat park, and the provision and maintenance of associated facilities. The Committee who will meet under the Chairmanship of Frank Savill, our Rear Commodore, comprises:- Vic Tate Moorings Secretary Murray Bates Boat Park Secretary Gordon Pewter Associate Representative Russell Fuller Cruiser Fleet Captain Peter Clayton Work Boat Bosun This is a continuation of our policy to spread the work load and responsibility for running the Club, as widely as possible amongst the membership. The Committee vacancies for Social Secretary and the one Ordinary member have been filled by Pat Harper and Tony Cockrell respectively. Tony has also accepted appointment as Cadet Skipper. This New Years Day we are entering a team in the Annual Rowing Race organised by the Maldon Little Ship Club in aid of the RNLUI. (Full details are contained elsewhere in this issue). Please give your support by entering, sponsoring and coming along on the day. See you all at the Working Party on Sunday 30 December, and on the Quayside at Maldon on Tuesday 1 January. ao \Shies COMMODORE 'S REPORT — 1979 Last year I began my report with a little homily about lack of support and the risk of declining standards. This year it would be inappropriate to do this as the involvement and level of support by members has been all that one could reasonably hope for. The activities of the Club are roughly divided between those concerned with sailing and those associated withCivil Engineering or Home Economics. Sailing is why we joined the Club, the other activities are the price we have to pay if we are to achieve our Sailing. Mike Vaughan our Sailing Secretary will be giving his report on our Sailing Programme, and I will try not to Pre-empt anything he is going to say. I must however thank all those who associated at our Annual Regatta. As you know it is the traditional duty of the Commodore to be OOD throughout the Regatta Weekend. This year there were several mishaps and many anxious moments. Despite these and the appalling conditions, the event was judged a success by those who took part. Each year the Committee critically review the organisation and management of the Regatta and the lessons learned are incorporated the following year. I must also mention the visit of our President and his colleagues from Marconi Avionics, Rochester. We had a particularly enjoyable weekend with them and they are already looking forward to coming next year. On the Civil Engineering front the major accomplishment was the repair and resurfacing of the road. A tremendous amount of hard physical work was put in by members to widen and prepare the road before resurfacing was carried out. I am pleased to be able to report that due to the alertness of one of our Associate Members we were able to engage a Local Contractor who undertook both the repair and the resurfacing of the entire length of the road for no more expense than some other Contractors were quoting for dealing with just the bad sections. This coupled with the assistance and prompt payment by the farmer for his share of the costs, made for a most satisfactory result. We must however continue to earmark some £500- £600 per year for future road maintenance and improvement. Our Caretaker Claude Emerson re-decorated the Clubhouse Changing=-rooms during the winter, and has once again maintained the Club and its surroundings in a clean and tidy condition. Although I must say he has not been helped in this by the tendency of some members to deposit rubbish on the floor of the dustbin area. This has also lead to complaints by the local refuse collector who is not obliged to remove anything not placed in the plastic bags provided. The Committee, however, have plans to resite the bins away from the Clubhouse and hopefully this will improve the environs of the club by removing an eyesore and a potential hazard. Our Clubhouse Secretary, Cyril Drakeford has accomplished many other jobs, the most notable of which was the roller blind for the galley. In case you may think there is nothing else to do, just you have a word with Cyril and he will offer you such jobs as building a stile, a new flag mast, not to mention the dustbin area and effluent pumping arrangements. We are again endebted to Dug Bradley for his seemingly inexhaustible supply of young trees, and to Russell and June Fuller for planting and nursing them so care- fully. Rabbits were the main threat to their survival, but now they have called in reinforcements in the form of half a dozen piglets from next door. Last year I reported that relations with our immediate neighbour were somewhat strained. I am pleased to be able to tell you that we now have a much better understanding of each others problems and that no instances of trespass have been recorded and no further complaints have been made against use The Club has continued to support B AC S P A and the B J RC. BACSPA have been keeping a watching brief on the plans by the Maldon District Council to issue a licence for the use of the hard, but no further developments have occurred. That is, until this morning, when a new Licence Document arrived in my post. Stan Allerton

— has been our representative on this Committee for the past year and has expressed the opinion that BACSPA is in danger of losing its impetus and direction. The opportunity to correct this will come in April, when the new Officers and Committee are formed at their AGM. Perhaps we could take the lead once again. Security has again been a problem. The Clubhouse doors and windows, and the main gate are frequently left open. The change in the security codes and the issue of new Card Keys must, I am sure, have improved our security, but all this is wasted if members leave it to someone else to lock up after them. The most distressing aspect of this year has been the thefts of money from members clothing and belongings left in the changing rooms whilst they were out sailing. Unfortunately this sort of thing crops up from time to time and I sincerely hope that we shall be rid of it next year. The Club this year has benefitted from two major gifts, both im memory of members who died suddenly during the year. The Rescue Boat was equipped with a brand new Radio Unit with the help of a very generous donation from Betty Beavins and her children, and the Challenger Dinghy "Idle Vice" was presented to the Club by Gwynneth Bridges and her son. I hope the Club will cherish them for years to come. The Barbecue this year was blessed with fine weather and the new layout worked well. We hope to develop this theme again next year. Early in the season Shirley-Ann Wood resigned as Editor of Navigans after 24 years of good work. We were very fortunate to obtain the services of "Halo Sailor" - Ann Allen, who is carrying on the tradition in fine style. The Galley Ladies have again done sterling work against increasing odds. Jill Savill was forced by ill health to give up the post of Galley Organiser, and Ann Bates and Margaret Lingwood took over, despite their other commitments. This is the area of organisation where we expect too much from too few, and I hope that next year more help will be forthcoming. The Bar has again sustained us both financially and socially, and towards the end of the season was re-equipped by Charringtons as we have purchased our beers from them for some time now. The Laying Up Supper was enjoyed by those who came along but the numbers were down on last year. As you will have seen from the Agenda published in last months Navigans a number of people have resigned from Office or Committee membership, and we are still short of a Social Secretary and one Ordinary Member. Those who are standing down or changing posts are, however, all willing to help their successors and the new committee in every way possible. This particularly applies in the case of my Vice Commodore, David Harper, who through pressure of work and family responsibilities is unable to continue as a Flag Officer for the time being. It is very difficult to thank all the deserving persons in this report - you know who they are, Margaret and the Social Committee; Mike, John and the Sailing Sub; David, Jack, Joyce and Murray of the Bar - as I say you know who they are. I must however mention our Cadet Skipper Rick Anstey, ably assisted by Colin Leveridge. Rick is giving up after many highly successful years. Our vigorous and expert Cadet Sailors owe much to them both and they showed their appreciation at the Laying Up Supper by presenting Rick with a Trophy. Finally I would like to offer my personal thanks to the retiring committee and to the many members who have supported and encouraged me throughout the year. Ron Greygoose Commodore

THIS IS MARCONI RESCUE — OVER! So at the end of my second year as your Coxswain we have again managed to provide a duty driver for every single event and my thanks go to Ken Hughes and Albert Fuller who have shared most of the work with me and to Dave Ormerod, David Urry, Robert Tate and John Weedon who completed the team when needed. The new radio (or rather the 2nd new radio) is superb and again thanks to John Weedon and Mike Vaughan for their help in installing it. Even on low power we have been in contact with the Club from West Mersea and over the season have talked to and fostered a useful working arrangement with Stone, MBYC and the Coastguard. I rather foolishly agreed to take the competency exam on behalf of the Club and am now swotting away! Keeping to our minimum number of drivers has nursed the engine through what can only be described as arduous conditions for the whole season and the only major problems were a starter motor drive packing up and a fracturedwater pipe, neither of which proved too disastrous. As a result of the debate after the Saturday of the Regatta - and lets get it in perspective because in spite of our well reported problems we rescued 57 crews = the main committee endorsed their support of the service and made certain recommendations, one of which I feel should be known to you all viz; "whilst other people are in the water no boats should be towed". The importance of this is that I am told that a lot of you still do not carry anchors. Lets look back at what happened on the last afternoon. Aforce 4-5 against an ebb tide produced 6ft waves at Stone and we were attending one of our 420's, which by the time we took it in tow, was well below Stone. We then got the radio call to pick up Mark Saville from the water, and by the time we got back to the 420, Stone were picking it up off Peewit Island. Also whilst the Mariner has a very high speed it is not so good at towing partially submerged boats in heavy weather, so the obvious solution is to ensure the safety of the crew and radio for the workboat. Fortunately conditions as bad as the Regatta and last day only happen infrequently; my fingernails have grown again and I've got my voice back and subject to the MASC accepting me as an associate member I shall be pleased to continue next year. During the last 5 years Colin Leveridge and I have been fortunate in having a team of Cadets full of natural ability, enthusiasm and determination to sail new classes not just at Stansgate, but at open meetings throughout the winter at other open series. During the last 3/4 years, the results speak for themselves, with 30% of this years awards going to Cadets and numerous class winners in previous years. Ladies have featured in the awards, both as class winners and supporting crews. My congratulations to all those on the leader board and the Garrett Memorial Trophy winners. My personal thanks go to Colin Leveridge for his help in guiding Cadets through the Elementary and Intermediate Day Boat certificates and for those Cadets whose age was a little early to pass the sailing tests but who no doubt will be there on the water looking for their first successess. The Trophy Colin Harper presented to me at the Laying Up Supper made me very proud and in return I thank the Parents of the Cadets for their help, the Cadets them- . selves, the facilities of the Club and Colin for 5 years work.
